# Protocol (frontend/backend contract)

Timeouts, retention periods and count limits below are protocol or configuration values. All JSON fields are snake_case. Times are RFC3339 (UTC). HTTP `listen` defaults to `:18660`; TLS is turned on explicitly with `public.tls_listen` and serves HTTPS / WSS. Over the public internet IPv6 is preferred for configuration and firewall rules.


### Client password login

An administrator sets a connection password and turns the feature on in the admin page. The connection password is separate from the administrator password and uses RFC 9807 OPAQUE. The password is used only in the browser that receives it; the registration and login routes reject a `password` field. The server stores the OPAQUE registration record and server key material, never the password or a fixed password hash that could log in directly. The settings page checks password length; the server cannot check strength from a blinded message.

The server and the browser WebAssembly share one fixed `github.com/bytemare/opaque` configuration: suite `opaque-ristretto255-sha512-argon2id-v1`, context `persona/client-password-login/v1`, client identity `persona-client`, server identity `persona-hub:<hub_id>`. The browser computes in a one-shot Worker and destroys it afterwards; the password never enters a URL, storage or a network request. After a successful web login the browser keeps using its device token. The feature exists only on the central hub; a member hub returns `409 member_hub`, so connect to the central hub's HTTPS address.

The public routes sit under `/api/v1/auth/password`. They require TLS (loopback is allowed for local development or a local TLS-terminating proxy) and do not trust a caller-supplied `X-Forwarded-*`. Writes accept only same-origin JSON, and responses are not cacheable. Login starts are rate limited per source and globally, so a wrong password detected only on the client cannot bypass the limit.

| Route | Request and response |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /state` | `{enabled,suite,hub_id,hub_name}` |
| `POST /start` | `{message,name,kind}`, `message` is a base64 KE1, `kind` is `web`; returns `{session,message,identity,suite}` where the message is KE2 |
| `POST /finish` | `{session,message}`, the message is a base64 KE3; success returns `{token,id,hub_id,name}` |

Verification sessions are kept in memory for 5 minutes and are lost on restart; each is consumed once, whether verification succeeds or fails. At most 128 states are held. Changing the password or turning login on or off changes the settings revision, so earlier verification flows can no longer issue device credentials. Turning login off keeps existing devices; the administrator can revoke all devices at the same time, and after the transaction commits the auth cache is cleared and existing connections are closed. Issuing a device credential and changing settings coordinate through a database row lock, so an old password cannot issue a new credential concurrently with a revocation.

The admin routes use the administrator session and CSRF checks, under `/api/v1/admin/password-login`:

| Route | Request and response |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/v1/admin/password-login` | `{enabled,configured,revision}`; never returns the registration record or keys |
| `POST /register/start` | `{message,revision}`, the blinded registration request; returns `{session,message,identity,suite}` |
| `POST /register/finish` | `{session,message,revoke_devices}`; stores the registration record and turns login on; only the administrator session that started the registration can finish it |
| `PUT /api/v1/admin/password-login` | `{enabled,revision,revoke_devices}`; switches login, optionally revoking devices |

A settings revision mismatch returns `409 stale_settings`; a wrong password or an expired or repeated verification returns `401 bad_password`; login that is not turned on returns `403 password_login_disabled`.

## Authentication

- Prefer `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. The current implementation has not locked down URL tokens: when there is no Authorization value, every authenticated API (WebSocket included) still falls back to `?token=`, not only on loopback or for WS. Clients should use the header so credentials stay out of URLs.
- The `token` in hub.json is the master token. It is accepted only from trusted sources such as loopback / LAN; from the public internet it returns `403 master_token_local_only` even over TLS. Public clients should use a temporary pairing token or a device token. Plaintext API over the public internet is rejected by default with `403 tls_required`; the only exception is `GET /api/v1/health`.
- Per-device credentials: `POST /api/v1/auth/tokens {"name":"<device name>","kind":"web"}` → `{id,token,role,name}`. Device tokens start with `jd_`; the hub stores only a hash. The stored kind is `web`, `link` or `other`: `link` is a computer's Persona Link (below), and any other value is stored as `other`.
The web client may send `"replaces":"<this browser's previous device id>"`: once the new credential is created, the hub revokes that one (only if it is a `kind: web` credential not yet revoked; other kinds and unknown ids are left alone, and the new credential is issued either way), and the response gains `"replaced":"<id>"`, so logging in again from the same browser does not pile up devices. A `full` credential can create device tokens.
- `GET /api/v1/auth/tokens` returns `{tokens,current}`. `DELETE /api/v1/auth/tokens/{id}` revokes a credential, clears the cache (authentication results are cached for 30 seconds and cleared on revoke) and disconnects every long-lived connection opened with that credential: the main WebSocket, live screen, forwarded ports, dev server previews and extension relays. The node-side streams close too, ending screen input and releasing any keep-awake hold for those screen connections. Connections opened with other credentials stay connected. The web app manages these in **Settings › Devices**.
- Scoped device credentials: the hub’s master credential can send `POST /api/v1/auth/tokens` with
  `{"name":"Feishu Agent integration","kind":"other","scopes":["agents.read","agents.control"]}`.
  The response adds `role: scoped` and the granted `scopes`. Supply a nonempty array of distinct scope names.
  Verify both response fields before sharing the new credential: a hub without scoped credentials ignores the request's scopes
  and issues a full credential instead.
  These credentials work over TLS from external clients and are managed in **Settings › Devices**, which lists the
  grants and can revoke the token and close its socket. A denied request returns 403 `permission_denied`
  with `scope` when the route requires one.
  - `agents.read` opens Agent reads, plus the machine launcher and launcher model lists and `GET /api/v1/ws`. That socket accepts `subscribe`, `unsubscribe`
    and application `ping`, and carries filtered session lists and the subscribed Agent's chat events.
    The socket excludes conversations of tracks and does not replay the owner's event log.
  - `agents.control` opens the shared Agent control routes for starting, messaging and interrupting Agents and
    other chat actions. Only visible pending Agent questions can be answered. Terminal control characters are rejected.
  - `agents.permission_mode` is a separate grant required to change a session's permission mode or specify one
    when starting a session. Resuming a session also requires this grant because resume can retain its permission mode.
    It opens only the permission mode field on the modes endpoint.
  - `agents.a2a` opens the per-session Agent Card and A2A JSON-RPC endpoint on enrolled machines.
  - Machine-specific restrictions are unsupported. A request with `machines` returns 400
    `unsupported_machine_restriction`. Files, device administration and other ungranted routes stay closed.
    A scoped credential stays with the hub that issued it. After a mesh center migration, issue a new one at the new center.
- Credentials for a computer's link: `POST /api/v1/auth/tokens {"kind":"link","machine":"<a machine in hub.json with kind link>"}` → `role: link`,
  which can only open `/api/v1/link` and `/api/v1/link/stream`; every other API is 403. The list includes `machine_id`. When redeeming a pairing code generated for that computer (`{"machine"}` below),
  kind and machine are set by the pairing code; naming a different machine in the request returns 403.
- Extension tokens (starting with `pext_`): the hub issues them for the scopes the extension was granted (`permissions.hub`). They open only the routes registered for those scopes; everything else is 403 `permission_denied` (with `scope` when a scope is missing),
  and only requests from the local machine are accepted, unless they carry their manager's proof that they came through it (`X-Persona-Manager-Proof`, a relayed manager's extensions).
- Linked hubs: another hub's credential has kind / role `peer` (`machine_id` is the other side's hub_id) and can only open `GET /api/v1/peer`;
  a link code `jx_…` can only `POST /api/v1/peer/pair`; every other API is 403. In a group only the **primary hub** accepts device credentials: a member forwards client requests unchanged (with `Authorization`)
  to the primary, and when it joins it hands the credentials it has issued (hashes) to the primary, so devices paired with the member keep working. When the primary is unreachable, the member returns
  `503 {"code":"center_unreachable","center":{"hub_id","name"}}`.
- Public authentication failures are counted per IPv4 address and per IPv6 /64, and the ban check runs before the database lookup; `429 rate_limited` carries `Retry-After` in seconds. LAN / VPN is not counted.
- Services (separate processes such as the assistant) connect to the hub's bus with a different token (`jb_…`), which can only open `GET /api/v1/bus`. See "Bus" below.
- Requests may send `Accept-Language: zh-Hans|en|ja` (the full list a browser sends is also accepted; the first entry is taken and falls back per [i18n.md](i18n.md)): human-readable text in that response (`error`, status descriptions) uses that language. `code` does not change; clients still branch on `code`. Without it, the user's language is used (see `client_hello.locale` in "Client capabilities and heartbeat").
- Every response carries `X-Request-Id`. A request may send `X-Client-Request-Id` (4–32 hex characters / `-`), and the hub then uses it ("Operations").

### Agent session sharing

Manager hello capability
`agent_sharing.v1` negotiates the sharing routes; node capabilities `share_projection.v1`
and `creation_receipt.v1` negotiate complete source projection and durable new-start
receipts. Unlike ordinary legacy API routes, sharing management never accepts URL
tokens or a default manager, and the public route never inherits login credentials.
An explicitly configured independent HTTP **or** HTTPS origin is supported; HTTP
requires the localized transport warning and explicit risk acknowledgement.

### Agent session archives

Hubs advertising `agent_session_archives` in hello / health relay recoverable archives for Agent sessions to their owning manager: every runtime the lists show (Claude Code, Codex, the Codex App, Orca, Paseo, DSH, opencode, pi…), since the record is the manager's own. Persona's own conversations use their existing assistant API. Archiving does not move or delete the source transcript.

| Request | Response | Permission |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /api/v1/sessions/archived?machine_id=` | `{ "sessions": [Session] }`, newest activity first within each manager; clients sort merged results; machine filter optional | full, answer; extensions with agents.read see only their manager's machines |
| `POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/archive` | `{ "ok": true, "native"?: NativeArchive }` ("Native archive", below) | full |
| `POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/archive?close=1` | `{ "ok": true, "archived": true, "close": { "closed": bool, "outcome": "closed" \| "not_running" \| "refused" \| "offline" \| "failed", "reason"?: string, "detail"?: string }, "native"?: NativeArchive }` ("Archive and close", below) | full |
| `POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/archive?force=1` | `{ "ok": true, "archived": true, "close": { "closed": true, "outcome": "closed" } }`: cancel a confirmation-blocked Agent, close it, then archive it | full |
| `POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/unarchive` | `{ "ok": true, "native"?: NativeArchive }` | full |

Archived rows carry `Session.archived=true` and are excluded from normal whole lists, WebSocket lists/deltas and paginated indexes. To a hub that takes them apart, the manager sends them in `fleet.archived` instead of in the machine's list ("Computer events"). Successful writes refresh normal lists; clients refresh the archive list separately and retain errors. Clients hide archive controls when the feature is absent. A manager announces `agent_session_archives` in its bus hello; the Hub advertises the fleet-wide feature only when every relevant owner is connected and supports it. Mixed manager versions conservatively hide controls. Direct requests to a manager without the feature return 501 `agent_archives_unsupported`; an offline owner returns 503 `assistant_offline`. The combined archive list fails explicitly when an owner is unavailable rather than pretending a partial list is complete. Unknown sessions return 404, assistant conversations return 400, and busy sessions cannot be archived (409 `agent_busy`): starting, working, waiting for an answer (a card), background work, running subagents or workflows. A finished turn awaiting the user's reply (`awaits_reply`) is idle and can be archived. Read-only credentials cannot mutate archives (403). Storage failures return 500 without reporting success. Repeating either operation preserves the requested visibility.

The owning manager persists records keyed by machine and session IDs without expiry. Clients must use the session's Hub, which routes mutations by machine ownership and merges manager archive lists. Mesh requests follow the existing center routing. The manager retains a minimal offline, read-only snapshot when a source inventory ages out, including after restoration and restart. Live inventory takes precedence. Reading still requires the original transcript to exist on a reachable computer; restoring does not recreate files. The manager reports `archive_changed_at` so the Hub can apply the same deletion projection to normal and archived lists. A later explicit archive/restore supersedes an earlier deletion. Hub deletion timestamps do not expire: this preserves deletion across manager restarts and long-lived fallback snapshots. This deliberately trades bounded tombstone storage for preventing old conversations from unexpectedly reappearing; no new Hub business store is introduced.

New source activity (an advancing update timestamp, running or waiting for input) permanently restores the session; becoming idle again does not re-hide it. A session archived with no update timestamp of its own (an Antigravity CLI pane's row has none) counts a timestamp after the archive's as new. Only a list read after the archive was written counts: one read before it (a list publish or another request that read the session while it still worked or waited for the user, then waited for the archive's lock) cannot restore it. Failed automatic restores are retried without committing the failed write in memory. Archive storage and lock waits have a three-second deadline, bounded further by the request context. Opening an unchanged archive list does not rebuild or broadcast normal inventories.

`archive_changed_at` is a strictly monotonic per-machine/session generation across explicit archives/restores, automatic restoration, force-close provisional records and rollback, including after a manager restart and when the wall clock repeats or moves backwards. A failed force close leaves a restored generation rather than deleting its marker. Rollback and close completion match the generation that started them; stale ones leave newer state untouched. Close completion retries native archiving only when its generation still matches, so it cannot overwrite a newer restore's native intent.

The manager also archives closed sessions by itself once they have been idle for `archive_closed_days` and no open to-do counts on them, through the same record (`server/internal/assistant/agent_archive_auto.go`). Such a session is restored like any other.

A record under an id a listed row's conversation went by (that row's `aliases`, set by the node: a Paseo Agent's transcript or an earlier fork of it; the terminal pane rows and the own id of an Antigravity CLI conversation; or a transcript a Claude desktop app session went on from) is neither an archived row nor a row of the inventory while that row names it: the row listed under its own id is the conversation. Whether that row is archived is the newest record among its own id and those ids: an archive made under one of them, such as one kept under an Antigravity CLI pane's id, holds for the row listed now. New activity in the row restores it under the row's archive key (below), newer than the record that archived it, which is kept as it was and listed again once no row names its id.

A row's archive is kept under its own id, its archive key, except an Antigravity CLI pane's row (`agy-<workspace>-<pane>`), whose key is its conversation's own id, `agy-<conversation id>`, the first of its `aliases`. An archive or a Close made on the pane's row then follows the conversation to whichever row lists it next: the companion's row once the pane is gone, or another pane's row. Its restore, the tool's archive (`native_archive`, which Antigravity answers `unsupported`) and a restore after new activity use that id too, and the Archived list shows it once. No record is kept under a pane's id, which the engine gives to another conversation later.

Archives made only in the tool (archiving in the Codex App) are not listed here; existing source-discovery rules still apply. Every runtime uses the same manager-owned archive semantics. In the manager, ordinary archive callers (these routes, "Archive and close", the assistant's tools) go through `setAgentArchive` (`server/internal/assistant/agent_archives.go`); the native archive below follows from the record it saves (`noteAgentArchive`).

**Cancel a stuck confirmation** (`?force=1`, main-chat `agent_archive` with `force: true`): only a currently blocked Agent without other active work is eligible. The manager and node recheck the state. The node closes its terminal with Ctrl-C and closes the pane, or asks its runtime to close; Paseo uses the same archive request as its CLI's `archive --force`, which closes the provider and rejects outstanding permissions. No permission or plan is approved. Permission/plan cards are rejected, screen cards cancelled, and the transcript is kept. Working, starting, background work, running children/workflows, loops, queued messages, and serving ports remain protected. Questions and forms are not confirmation overrides. Before closing, the manager persists the archive with a future close timestamp in one write, then replaces it with the actual close time on success. A failed close replaces that provisional archive with a restored generation and leaves the session and cards visible. The web screen card offers **Close Agent**, explains the cancellation, and asks for **Close and archive** or **Cancel**; the existing archive toast offers Undo. The cached blocked snapshot from before a successful close cannot restore the archive; new activity still can. Ordinary archive and archive-and-close keep their existing busy restrictions.

**Archive and close** (`?close=1`, hello / health feature `agent_session_archive_close`): archives the session, then closes its agent and its terminal on its computer, since the user asked for it (node `session.retire` with `close_terminal`): the tab and the agent process go, the transcript and how it was started stay; it is read-only from then on, and Resume on its terminal page brings it back (`claude --resume`, `codex resume`). A runtime's session that declares `capabilities.close` is closed through it (`session.close`) instead: the web offers that for an Antigravity CLI conversation's own row, the companion's, as it offers its pane's row, and a message continues the conversation in the companion after either. Restoring it reopens nothing. Implemented by `archiveAndCloseAgentSession` (`server/internal/assistant/agent_archive_close.go`).

- A busy agent is refused before anything changes (409 `agent_busy`): the archive's busy rules, plus a `/loop`, queued messages or a server it runs (`ports`), since closing would stop what the user may be using. Only when the plain archive guard permits it does the refusal suggest archiving without closing. A blocked dialog is not necessarily an approval request: inspect it on the computer, dismiss a read-only Settings/Status screen without approving anything, handle queued messages deliberately, then exit the agent safely and retry. A duplicate-delivery notice alone does not establish that a queued message was removed; archive never clears that queue or relaxes its guards.
- The archive comes first and is never undone by the close. When the close does not happen, the answer is still 200 with `closed: false`, the session stays archived and still open on its computer, and `reason` says why in the request's language (`detail`: the node's own words): `not_running` (it was not running: nothing to close, no reason), `refused` (the node will not close it: its engine or another tool keeps it, a runtime's or the Codex App's session, Codex started outside Persona so its launcher is unknown, the agent turned busy, a node without `session.retire`), `offline` (its computer is not connected), `failed` (the call failed). The user can close it from the computer or restore it.
- Only an agent of a terminal engine (herdr, Herdr App, Orca, Tern, Rex) that is still is closed: Claude Code, Codex or a compatible CLI, not another tool's session or one of an engine that runs Agents itself. Clients offer the action only for those; the node decides.
- Activity the agent writes while it is being closed does not restore the archive: the record keeps `closed_at`, and only activity after it counts.
- The hub forwards `?close=1` only to a manager that names `agent_session_archive_close` in its hello; a manager without it would archive and leave the agent open, so the hub answers 501 `agent_archive_close_unsupported` instead, and advertises the feature only when every owner has it.

**Native archive.** After Persona's own record is saved, the manager also asks the tool that owns the session to archive (or restore) it with the tool's own reversible archive, through the node's `session.archive` / `session.unarchive` ("hub ↔ node RPC"). Persona's archive is the source of truth: it succeeds whatever the tool answers, and nothing is ever deleted. `native` (`NativeArchive`: `{archived, state, error?}`) is what the tool has: `state` `done` (the tool has it the same way), `pending` (not yet: the machine offline, the Agent working, Codex still open in a terminal, the last error in `error`, diagnostic text that is not localized: clients word the state themselves; the manager tries again whenever that machine's session list arrives, backing off from 1 to 30 minutes), or `unsupported` (the tool has no archive Persona can drive, such as Claude Code, or the node cannot drive one: the archive is Persona's alone, and `error` may say why). The request waits a few seconds for the tool before answering `pending`. Archived rows from `GET /api/v1/sessions/archived` carry the same object as `native_archive`; it is absent when the tool was never asked. The manager keeps these records in the setting `sessions.archived.native`, beside `sessions.archived`.

What each tool does: Codex threads are archived with the app-server's `thread/archive` / `thread/unarchive` (the rollout moves to `<CODEX_HOME>/archived_sessions` and back, and the Codex App lists it as archived). A runtime does it only when it declares `caps.archive` (`docs/integrations/runtimes.md`); none does: Paseo's and DSH's bridges archive only as their `close` (Paseo's archive stops the agent and only a re-import brings it back; the DSH plugin has no unarchive), and Antigravity's "archive" is a list in its bridge, not Antigravity's own. Claude Code (no archive for local sessions; the Claude desktop app's archive is the app's private record), Orca, opencode (its archive column is only in its database, which Persona does not write) and pi have no archive Persona drives. A Codex thread archived in Codex leaves the node's list (the same rule as one archived in the Codex App); the manager's offline snapshot keeps showing it as archived and restorable. When new activity restores a session in Persona by itself, the manager asks the tool to restore it too (already restored answers done). After "Archive and close" has closed the agent, the tool is asked again at once: a Codex thread whose terminal was still open is archived in Codex once it has closed.

### Agent naming metadata

| Manager capability | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `agent_naming.v1` | Full-user ordinary Agent renames persist manual intent in the manager before node dispatch. A manager without it, or an offline one, keeps the native node path; ordinary extension calls retain the existing node authorization boundary. |

Session rows may carry `title_source` (`manual`, `auto`, `prompt` or `runtime`), `title_manual` and cumulative
`output_tokens`. These are additive node facts, not instructions to rename a session. Absent or unknown
provenance never proves that a title was not manually chosen. The manager uses them for guarded naming,
then publishes the resulting name in the existing `title` field; no client-side renaming algorithm is needed.

### Agent naming tools

The assistant-only `agent_autoname` MCP tool lets a Persona conversation name a coding Agent session at the user's explicit request. It takes exactly `{"machine":"<machine id or name>",
"session_id":"<full session id>"}` and rejects other fields, prefixes, ordinary coding-Agent callers and Persona's
own conversations. A permission card confirms the write on every invocation; declining or not answering makes
no model call and changes no title. The text result is a JSON object with `{"ok":true,"title":"<new title>","title_source":"auto","changed":true|false}`, or
`{"ok":false,"code":"<failure code>","retryable":true|false,"error":"<localized sentence>"}`. It has
no URL, header or token parameters and grants no standing permission.

`agent_autoname_receipt` is an assistant-only, read-only evidence lookup (`agent_naming_receipt.go`), not a new
client dependency or an execution receipt for a particular model call. Its input is only an exact machine and full
session id, plus an optional bounded `since`/`before` window `[since,before)` (both required together, at most 24 hours). It reads
only the real calling conversation's permission history through the owning manager, never another caller's cards
or arbitrary transcript text. `confirmation: found` requires one exact target match in the original two-field
`{"machine","session_id"}` card input, independent of JSON field order or layout, with complete bounded-page
coverage; the four-field evidence query is not matched against the card. The first history read and every later
page use the exclusive upper bound and the `(created_at,id)` cursor, so equal timestamps at `since` are not
mistaken for the window's end. It returns `{id,status,allow?,resolved_at?}` only; multiple matches are `ambiguous`, and no match, a
read error or partial coverage stays `unknown`. `naming` separately reports the exact target's current
`{status,requested,title?,named_at?,observed_at}` (`status` `current`, `not_found` or `unknown`). That snapshot is
not proof this request started or finished a model call and is not associated with its call id. `last_failure` is
not returned because it can belong to background naming. No `model_started`, execution-ended or `retryable` claim
is synthesized. The tool invokes no model, writes no settings, resolves no card, renames nothing and publishes no
session list. Ordinary coding Agents, extensions and work machines cannot call it.

### Health check and feature flags

`GET /api/v1/health` needs no authentication. Public sources get only:

```json
{"ok":true,"hub_id":"<hub UUID>","hub_name":"Home","tls_port":18662,"fp":"<SPKI SHA-256 base64url>"}
```

Trusted sources such as LAN / loopback also get `version` and `features`. The source is judged by the connection address, regardless of whether a token is sent; a public HTTPS health response is trimmed too. No source gets candidate addresses. When TLS is off, `tls_port` is `0` and `fp` is an empty string.

For trusted sources the health check also returns `channel` (`release` / `docker` / `dev`), `build` (UTC `YYYYMMDDHHMM`, 0 if absent), `protocol` (the client ↔ hub major version), `min_app_build` (the oldest client build it works with; 0 means no minimum), `commit` (the commit it was built from, `-dirty` after it with uncommitted changes, `""` when the build did not say; the assistant marks a task deployed only once this contains the task's merge commit), and `update.confirmed` (whether the process has finished confirming an update: true when there is no update to confirm; the watchdog waits on it). `channel` and `build` tell how this hub was built and whether it can update itself; WS `hello` carries the same fields. WS `hello` (after authentication) also carries `public_url` (hub.json's `public_url` with the trailing `/` removed; omitted if unset): hub links in assistant answers are built from it, and clients use it to recognize "links to this hub", even when they reach the hub through another address.

`hub_name` is this hub's human-readable name (hub.json's `name`, [config.md](../operations/config.md)). `hub_id` is a UUID persisted in the database's `settings`. Clients use it to tell hubs apart and to check they still reach the same instance after switching candidates. `fp` must come from a trusted QR scan or an authenticated trusted channel; never trust an arbitrary public health response to establish pinning.

The authenticated WS `hello.features` always lists server capabilities; trusted `/health` returns the same list. The hub builds it in `features()` (`server/internal/hub/extensions_link.go`): `proto.Features` (`server/internal/proto/proto.go`), then the flags the hub adds from its own state, then those the manager reports for the extensions. The full list:

- Message receipt transport (`proto.Features`): `message_send_state` (hub-received message feedback, "Message feedback") and `todo_send_state` (the same for a to-do's message or answer sent with an op id, its "To-do writes"). Their feature strings are informational; the dedicated current-socket hello versions establish receipt authority.
- Terminal Agent sends (`agent_terminal_send`) confirm the exact listed Agent before the terminal client uses the full-device message receipt route.
- In `proto.Features`, by area:
  - Connection and errors: `persona_contracts_v1` (the Persona naming contract: both sides read the old and the new names, and a client keeps sending the old ones to a hub without the flag), `tls` (the optional TLS listener and SPKI pin), `endpoints` (`GET /api/v1/endpoints`, see "Candidate addresses" below), `client_hello`, `heartbeat`, `app_ping` (see "Client capabilities and heartbeat"), `error_codes` (a stable `code` in error bodies, see "Error body"), `request_id` (`X-Request-Id`, see "Authentication" above), `client_ops` (see "Operation receipts"), `locale` (honors `Accept-Language`, `client_hello.locale` and the device's `locale`; human-readable text follows the language, [i18n.md](i18n.md)).
  - Devices: `ws_notify` (alerts over the WebSocket, see "Notifications over the persistent connection")

A feature flag means the implementation supports it; `tls` does not mean the listener is on, so also check `tls_port` / `fp`. A client talking to a hub without a flag falls back to the behavior without it. `node_version` / `node_mismatch` in the machine list flag whether the hub offers to redeploy the node: it runs another build than the one its platform gets (the hub's, or, with no build of the hub's version for that platform, the newest release its manager drives) (the personad on that computer was not deployed by this hub deployment, i.e. `deploy.sh` deployed only part of it, or it was installed on its own; the hub also logs a line when it connects), or its manager cannot drive it. Another build alone is an upgrade offer, not a fault: whether a node can be used is decided by the node handshake (`node_protocol`, `node_incompatible`; see "Node handshake"). New fields are optional, and clients check whether a field is present.

`ultracode` indicates support for Claude Code's independent session toggle (see "Claude Code ultracode" below). This is a hub capability: switching it on a computer with a node that lacks it can still return `409 node_outdated`.
`session_start_speed` (a per-node capability) indicates that node's `session.start` and `session.start.work` can carry `speed`: a new terminal Codex or Claude Code Agent's explicit start speed. Faster choices toward a node without it return `409 node_outdated`; omitted and `standard` keep the default behavior (see "Agent start speed").
`start_goal` (a per-node capability, not a hub feature) indicates that node's `session.start` can carry `goal`: a Claude Code (or, on newer nodes, Codex) `/goal` the node types and verifies after the first message is in the transcript (see "A goal set at the start" below). The hub answers a start carrying a non-empty `goal` toward a node without the capability with `409 start_goal_unsupported` before anything starts, so the caller can start again without it.

`launcher_switch` is a hub capability too: a computer whose node has not announced the `launcher_switch` capability (or that the manager has not reported yet) answers a `launcher` with `409 node_outdated`.

`engine_switch` is one as well: a launcher of the other engine to a computer whose node has not announced `engine_switch` is refused by that node (`switch_unsupported` or `switch_other_agent`), nothing changed.

`task_retry_launcher`: `POST /api/v1/todos/{id}/retry` takes `{"launcher","model"?}`, a failed start again on another launcher of the same computer, and a failed plan task carries `retry_with` (see the REST table and `TaskPlan` below). Clients offer "Use … instead" only when the hub lists it.

`todo_start_answer`: `POST /api/v1/todos/{id}/start/answer {"choice"}` answers the startup question a planned task's failed start stopped on (its plan task's `error_code: shell_waiting`, the question in `error_args`) and starts the task again in that tab (see the REST table and "Answering a start's question"). Clients show the question's card on a failed task only when the hub lists it; otherwise Retry.

`POST /api/v1/machines/{id}/deploy`: the hub installs the node build for that computer's platform and kind of program (its own, left by `deploy.sh` on the hub machine at `~/.persona/bin/nodes/personad-<os>-<arch>`, or the release's) on that computer over ssh (when it is going through tailcat, it is sent to the resident node through tailcat; the node replaces itself, exits and is restarted by launchd / systemd), kills the resident node (launchd restarts it with the new binary; `launchctl kickstart` over ssh does not always work) and reconnects. It looks the build up first (at most 20 s when that needs the release site), then runs in the background and returns `{ok}` (409 with a reason when it cannot start). Progress is in the machine list: `deploying` (in progress), `deploy_error` (why the last attempt failed); on success `node_mismatch` goes away. The web app shows a notice in **Settings › Machines** with a **Redeploy** button.

Persona Link's active `link` / passive `service` machines, and nodes forwarded through a member hub, are updated over the existing node RPC when they support the update protocol; no SSH is needed. `node.info`'s `node_update` / `node_update_reason` report the local update capability; the machine list's `can_deploy` / `deploy_reason` say whether that entry point can be used right now (also false when there is no node build for the machine's platform anywhere: no build of the hub's own, no release to fetch one from, or none whose node this manager drives; the reason says what to do, and `deploy_no_package` is true when the hub's side, no build it can send now (none, or a release site it cannot reach), is all that stops a node that could take an update, so a compatible node's card shows the reason instead of `error_code` `node_outdated`), and `deploy_phase` is `waiting_idle` / `transferring` / `restarting` / `confirming`. A node without the update protocol is first upgraded once locally. Deploy jobs are stored in Postgres and support waiting for idle, verifying the install, restarting the resident process, local rollback and confirming it is back online.

`POST /api/v1/machines/{mid}/link-switch`: a signed-in full device switches an ssh computer to Persona Link; the admin page's `POST /api/v1/admin/machines/{mid}/link-switch` does the same. Both answer 202 `{link_switch}` at once, 409 `{code}` when it cannot start (`in_progress`, or the reason below) and 403 for any other device, including one signed in with a pairing code it has not traded yet. Each machine in the list carries `link_switch` `{available, reason?, phase?, error?, rollback_unconfirmed?, at?}` for an ssh computer its manager connects itself, and for an hour after a switch ended: `phase` is `checking` / `installing` / `connecting` / `rolling_back` / `succeeded` / `failed`; `reason` (why not available) and `error` (why a switch failed) are codes the clients put in their own words (`offline`, `unsupported_os`, `link_unavailable`, `hub_old`, `pending`, `custom_node`, `busy`, `in_progress`, `no_systemd`, `linger_off`, `existing_link`, `no_node`, `unsafe_permissions`, `no_package`, `hub_unanswered`, `transfer_failed`, `install_failed`, `link_timeout`, `config_changed`, `interrupted`, `unknown`). A manager without it leaves the field out and clients offer nothing.

### Temporary pairing

`POST /api/v1/auth/pair-codes` accepts two kinds of callers: **loopback source + master token** (`personad hub pair`), or **a signed-in `full` device token** (any source: the web client's **Settings › Devices › Connect New Device**).
No request body is needed; when the body carries `machine` or `add`, it generates a pairing code for a computer's Persona Link (see "Computer pairing codes" below).
Link, peer and extension credentials, the temporary pairing token itself (one code cannot generate the next), and a master token from a non-loopback source all get 403.
A `full` device can already create long-lived credentials with `POST /api/v1/auth/tokens`; what this gives is a 10-minute, single-use code, so it does not widen permissions. The hub logs a line (device name and id) when a device requests one.
Codes without `machine` also return `qr: {size, rows}` (the QR code of the pairing link, one string of `0` / `1` per row, no quiet zone, same as `/admin`).
When the body also carries `"web": "<web URL>"` (an absolute http(s) URL with no `#` fragment and no user/password, otherwise 400), the response also includes `web_url` (`<web URL>#token=<temporary token>`: opening it signs in to the web client, and the part after `#` is not sent to the server) and its QR code `web_qr`. On success it returns HTTP 200 with:

```json
{
  "token":"<temporary token>",
  "expires_at":"<RFC3339 UTC>",
  "url":"http://hub.example.com:18660",
  "hub_id":"<hub UUID>",
  "fp":"<SPKI SHA-256 base64url>",
  "tls_port":18662,
  "alt":["https://hub.example.com:18662"],
  "pair_url":"persona://pair?..."
}
```

The response carries `Cache-Control: no-store`. The temporary token is `jp_` plus the hex encoding of 32 random bytes; the database stores only its hash. It is valid for 10 minutes and works as a `full` Bearer for the API / WS until it expires (see below).

It can **exchange for a device token only once** through `POST /api/v1/auth/tokens`; a second exchange returns `401 invalid_token`. After the exchange, other APIs keep working until `min(original expiry, exchange time + 2 minutes)`; then it expires, and WS connections already opened with the temporary token are canceled too. After a new device pairs successfully, the hub tries to send a pairing notification; if push is unavailable it logs instead.

`personad hub pair` calls the local API above and prints the temporary link and QR code; the running hub must be reachable over IPv4 loopback HTTP. `--legacy` prints the format with the master token offline.

The QR code keeps `url` / `token` and adds:

```text
persona://pair?url=<compatible URL>&token=<temporary token>&hub=<hub_id>&fp=<fingerprint>&tls=<TLS port>&alt=<HTTPS candidate>&alt=<HTTPS candidate>
```

This shows the structure; actual parameter values are each URL-encoded, and order does not matter.

| Parameter | Format |
| --- | --- |
| `url` | `public_url` or the local IPv6 address selected for a device QR (see below) |
| `token` | Temporary Bearer token; the master token with `--legacy` |
| `hub` | hub UUID |
| `fp` | SHA-256(SubjectPublicKeyInfo DER), base64url without padding, 43 characters; not a hash of the whole certificate |
| `tls` | TLS listen port, decimal |
| `alt` | Full HTTPS URL, repeatable; at most two, excluding `lan`. When both literal address families are available, the first IPv6 and first IPv4 candidates, IPv6 first; otherwise the first two eligible candidates in candidate order |

For a device pairing request made over loopback, a native HTTP-only Hub using its own bare hostname and listener port can use a
bracketed unique-local IPv6 address as the QR's primary URL. This applies when LAN discovery finds no private IPv4
address and all eligible IPv6 addresses share one /64. An explicit address or DNS domain in `public_url`, the
`PERSONA_PUBLIC_URL` override, or `public.advertise` takes precedence. The Hub does not write the selected URL
back to its configuration. Browser sign-in links, computer pairing, and requests relayed from a mesh member
keep their existing addresses.

Hostnames (`name` candidates) do not count as either address family because their DNS records may not support both. They remain eligible in the fallback order when one or both literal families are absent. Reserving an explicit IPv4 candidate alongside IPv6 lets IPv4-only clients attempt pairing even when earlier candidates are IPv6 addresses or an IPv6-only hostname. This selection applies to both device and computer pairing codes.

When TLS is off the QR code omits `fp` / `tls`; with no suitable candidate it omits `alt`. The API response still has the matching fields (empty string, 0 or empty array). Renewing a certificate with the same key does not change `fp`; changing the key requires restarting the hub and re-pairing devices through a trusted path.

#### Computer pairing codes (feature `machines_add`)

Request bodies:

```
{"add": {"name": "Lin's MacBook", "os": "mac", "icon": "laptop"}}   add a new "Computer connects" (kind link) computer and get its code
{"add": {"id": "macbook", "name": "…"}}                              same, with an explicit id (`personad hub pair --machine <id> --add`)
{"add": {"name": "…", "manager": "m-3fa21c"}}                        same, the computer belonging to that manager
{"machine": "macbook"}                                               another code for an existing link computer
```

- `add.name` may be Chinese (at most 40 characters). Without `add.id`, the id is derived from the name: the ASCII letters and digits in the name (lowercased, everything else becomes `-`); if there are none, `add.os` (`mac` / `linux` / `windows`); failing that, `computer`.
  On collision with an existing id, `-2`, `-3` are appended. `add.os` only decides which install instructions the client shows; the hub does not store it. `add.icon` is `laptop` (default) / `desktop` / `server`.
- The hub uses the same function as the admin page's **Add Computer › Computer connects** to write hub.json and hand it to the manager (effective while running, no restart).
  Computers added by a **device** are pending confirmation ("Computer trust" below); those added by **loopback + master token** are confirmed.
- When a device adds the same name again and that computer is still pending and has never connected, it is reused and a new code issued (`added: false`). A master token with `add.id` that hits an existing link computer also just reissues a code.
- `add.manager` (optional, a manager's id from `GET /api/v1/managers`): the manager the computer belongs to, normally the one the client is showing. The computer is that manager's from the start, never the carrier's first ("Moving a machine or a source"). The manager is checked before anything is written: a refused request adds nothing, leaves no pending computer and voids no code. `{"machine"}` takes no manager: the computer keeps its own.
  - Left out (or empty): the carrier's (`assistant`), and a reused computer (above) stays with whichever manager has it.
  - `"assistant"` is a valid value and not the same as leaving it out: a new computer is the carrier's, and a reused one that belongs to another manager is moved back to the carrier. Any other manager named: a reused computer that belongs to another manager is moved to it first.
  - An offline manager is accepted: the computer waits in hub.json and the manager takes it over when it connects. Until then it is not listed in `GET /api/v1/machines` (the hub lists what a manager reports; the reply's `manager` says where it went), its Persona Link gets `503 assistant_offline` and tries again, and it can be confirmed (`POST /api/v1/machines/{id}/confirm`) only once its Persona Link has traded the code. Not confirmed within 24 hours, it is removed as any pending computer is.
- A device can only issue codes for **pending** computers (`machine` or reuse); a confirmed one returns 409 `not_pending`. Every code a device issues goes through "pending → confirmed"; re-pairing a confirmed computer is done on the admin page or on the hub machine.
  This is not a security boundary (a full device can already sign credentials for any link computer with `kind: link` on `POST /api/v1/auth/tokens`).
- When a device reissues a code for a pending computer (`machine` or reuse), the computer's existing Persona Link credentials are revoked first: whichever computer redeemed the previous code, it cannot get confirmed along with the one holding the new code.
- Success is 200 with `Cache-Control: no-store`. Besides the fields above (`token`, `expires_at`, `url`, `hub_id`, `fp`, `tls_port`, `alt`, `machine`, `pair_url`; no `qr`), it adds:

```json
{"machine": "macbook", "name": "Lin's MacBook", "trust": "pending", "added": true, "manager": "m-3fa21c",
 "pair_url": "persona://link?url=…&token=…&machine=macbook&hub=…&fp=…&tls=…",
 "command": "persona-link pair '<pair_url>'",
 "install": {"linux": "curl -fsSL <site>/install.sh | sh -s -- --node --pair '<pair_url>'"}}
```

  `trust` is `pending` or `confirmed` (always present here). `added` says whether this call added it (omitted when not). `manager` is the manager the computer belongs to now (on every computer code, `{"machine"}` too):
  the client compares it with the `add.manager` it sent and, when they differ, says which manager the computer is under. A hub that does not know `add.manager` ignores the field and
  leaves `manager` out of the reply: a computer it added (`added: true`) is the carrier's, and one it reused stays where it was, which need not be the carrier. A client that sent a manager and gets
  no `manager` says so: a new computer is under the carrier; for a reused one it can look it up in `GET /api/v1/machines`. No `hello.features` flag: the reply tells. `install` is present only when the hub knows which site it was published from
  (the build-time `publish.site_url`, [config.md](../operations/config.md); local builds and Docker images don't have it), and currently only has `linux`.
- Errors (`error` is localized per `Accept-Language`):

| HTTP | code | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 403 | `forbidden` | Not a full device: a link, a temporary identity from a pairing code, an extension; a master token from non-loopback |
| 409 | `tls_required` | The hub has no TLS and is not behind an HTTPS reverse proxy, so Persona Link cannot connect; carries `"action": "enable_tls"` |
| 409 | `mesh_member` | The device is connected to a member hub of a linked-hub group: add it on the primary hub |
| 429 | `too_many_pending` | The device is adding a new computer while 3 are already pending (reuse and reissue don't count) |
| 409 | `exists` / `not_pending` | The given id already exists (and is not a reusable link computer) / a device issuing a code for a confirmed computer |
| 404 | `not_found` | The `machine` a device sent is not a link computer in hub.json |
| 404 | `no_manager` | `add.manager` is not in the roster (or was removed meanwhile) |
| 409 | `installing` | `add.manager` is still being installed (its install code not traded yet) |
| 503 | `assistant_offline` | The reused computer is in the own list of a manager that is offline, so it cannot move to `add.manager` now |
| 503 | `owners_unknown` | The hub could not read which manager carries which computer yet (as for a move); try again |
| 503 | (any other) | The hub could not read the roster to check `add.manager` (its database did not answer); try again |
| 400 | `unknown_machine` | The `machine` sent with a master token is not a link computer in hub.json (`hub pair --machine` then suggests adding `--add`) |
| 400 | `invalid_name` / `invalid_id` / `invalid_os` / `bad_request` | Missing or too-long name / id breaks the rules / unknown os / `machine` and `add` sent together, or `web` included |


### Candidate addresses

`GET /api/v1/endpoints` requires authentication and returns `{hub_id,tls_port,fp,endpoints}`. Each endpoint:

```json
{"url":"https://[2001:db8::1234]:18662","kind":"ipv6","port":18662,"scheme":"https","seen_at":"<RFC3339 UTC>"}
```

The address is a documentation example. `kind` is `ipv6` / `name` / `lan` / `ipv4`, sorted in that order; within a kind HTTPS comes first. `scheme` is `https` / `http`. `seen_at` is when it was collected, not proof of reachability. Candidates merge `public_url`, `public.advertise` and qualifying local addresses; public IPv4 is published only from explicit configuration. When TLS is off, automatic candidates use HTTP, and clients must not send tokens in plaintext over the public internet because of that.

WS `hello` carries the candidates too. When the address list changes, the hub sends `{"type":"endpoints","endpoints":[...]}`, only to clients that declared `endpoints` in `client_hello.features` on that connection; a change in `seen_at` alone does not trigger the event. The event is the complete candidate list and may be empty; clients should replace the old list.

### Error body

The main API's shared error handling keeps the `error` text and adds a stable `code`. `retryable` and `delivered` are **optional** and only given when they can be determined. 404 / 405 on the main router also return JSON. Separate sub-handlers such as mail, and streaming responses, follow their own protocols; don't assume they all carry the new fields.

```json
{"error":"invalid token","code":"invalid_token","retryable":false,"delivered":"none"}
```

`delivered` is `none` / `unknown` / `yes`; absent does not mean not executed. In particular, a plain timeout never gets a made-up `none`. Absent `retryable` does not mean automatic retry is OK either. Node 409 details stay flat (e.g. `draft`, `clearable`) and are not wrapped in a new `data`.

| code | Typical HTTP status | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tls_required` | 403 | Plaintext public API rejected; `delivered: none` |
| `master_token_local_only` | 403 | The master token can't be used over the public internet; `delivered: none` |
| `invalid_token` | 401 | Credential invalid, expired, revoked, or a temporary token exchanged twice; `retryable: false`, `delivered: none` |
| `forbidden` | 403 | Permission or pairing-code source requirements not met; `retryable: false`, `delivered: none` |
| `rate_limited` | 429 | The source is banned after authentication failures; wait per `Retry-After` |
| `token_store_unavailable` | 503 | The hub could not look the credential up (its database did not answer), so this says nothing about the credential: never treat it as revoked; retry per `Retry-After`. Not counted as an authentication failure |
| `bad_request` | 400 | Bad parameter / JSON; `retryable: false` |
| `not_found` / `method_not_allowed` | 404 / 405 | Resource doesn't exist / method not supported; `retryable: false`. A node's `not_found` is 404 too: a session its computer does not have or has no transcript for (`…/items`, `…/items/{iid}/full`, `…/items/{iid}/image`, `…/items/{iid}/visualization`), a file that is not there. Through a node call `error` is a plain summary in the request's language and `detail` the node's words. For a session's history it adds `reason`: `no_transcript` (the computer has a record of the session, but no transcript to read: its file is gone, or it never got a message) or `unknown_session` (the computer has no record of the id; records older than 60 days are not loaded, so this does not mean it never existed), and `error` is the sentence for that reason. A node gives `unknown_session` only once its records have come from the hub on its current connection: none while they load, nor while a load that failed is tried again. It gives no reason for a conversation an Agent runtime runs (its history is the runtime's, also while the runtime is not connected). A `not_found` without a known `reason` (a node that sends none, an Agent runtime's own answer, a missing file) keeps the plain summary. An older page (`before_seq`) of a session the computer knows but has no transcript for is not an error: an empty page with `has_more: false`, which ends paging |
| `gone` | 410 | The interaction is no longer pending, etc.; `retryable: false` |
| `conflict` | 409 | A conflict with no more specific code |
| `input_draft` / `dialog_open` / `prompt_changed` | 409 | The send or answer was explicitly refused; `retryable: false`, `delivered: none`, see below. `POST /api/v1/todos/{id}/accept` answers these 423 instead: clients read any 409 there as "already handled" |
| `op_id_reused` | 409 | The operation ID was already used for a different device, target or parameters; don't blindly retry with a new ID |
| `send_in_doubt` | 409 / 502 | A to-do's message or answer whose words may already be with its Agent (`delivered: unknown`: the answer to the send, or to the start of a new Agent that takes them, never came, or the node isn't sure it typed them) or are (`delivered: yes`: what followed failed, such as recording the decision they answer). `retryable: false`; `error` says to look at the to-do before sending again, `detail` is what failed. 409 on the conversation route, as its other refusals; 502 on the accept and asks routes (and the Lark card's button and an "OK" reply say the same), whose 409s clients read as already answered. A client shows `yes` as delivered with no run named; it never sends either again by itself. Cases in `spec/fixtures/todo-writes` |
| `agent_start_stalled` | 409 | The agent opened but its session was not identified before the start deadline (Codex), or Claude ran but never showed its input box (`data.screen` holds the tab's last lines, and `pane` / `kept_until` say where the tab is kept open, as for `shell_waiting`). Launcher health is unchanged; no automatic task retry or detour. Uses the existing RPC error `code` and message, also carried in `start_error_code` and task `error_code`. Uncoded errors from nodes keep the generic failure handling |
| `shell_waiting` | 409 | A start's new terminal tab stopped on a question from its shell's startup files (an update prompt, `[Y/n]`, "Press Enter", compinit's insecure directories, ssh's unknown host key, zsh-newuser-install, powerlevel10k's wizard, RVM's project trust, a password or passphrase) before the start command was typed. Nothing ran; `delivered: none`. `data`: `line` (the question), `screen` (the tab's last 12 lines), `pane` and `kept_until` (the tab stays open until then, then closes unless an agent came up in it), and the answers a full device may give it (`kind`, `choices`, `line_mode`, `secret`, `default`, see "Answering a start's question"; no `choices` from a start that took a hand-off's values). Launcher health is unchanged |
| `start_line_rejected` | 409 | A start's new terminal tab did not take the typed start line twice: something before the shell's line editor ate its first characters, and the shell answered for the rest (`permission denied` for the start file, `command not found` for a cut word, a parse error, an open quote). The node types the line once more before giving up. Nothing ran; `delivered: none`; the tab is closed. `data`: `line` (the shell's answer) and `screen`. Launcher health is unchanged |
| `terminal_not_ready` | 503 | A start's new terminal tab did not take the start command: herdr refused the typed line (`pane_send_failed`), or, in an Orca tab, the start line never showed there and its start file was never read by the end of the wait for the shell (Orca does not say whether a send arrived). Nothing ran; `retryable: true`, `delivered: none`; the tab is closed. A task start retries it once and does not count it against the launcher |
| `node_outdated` | 409 | The node doesn't support the requested feature, e.g. file upload |
| `too_large` | 413, or 409 mapped from node RPC | Request / file over the limit |
| `images_over_limit` | 413 | A message carries more pictures than a message holds; `limit` (hello's `image_limits` set the message was held to) and `got.images` give the numbers; `retryable: false`, `delivered: none`. See "Pictures in a message" |
| `timeout` | 408 / 504, often 502 for node calls | Timed out; the outcome can't be judged from this code alone |
| `node_unreachable` | 502 / 503 | The node is offline or the connection dropped; when clearly offline, `retryable: true`, `delivered: none`; not necessarily so for a dropped connection |
| `no_machine` / `machine_pending` / `claude_missing` / `launcher_missing` | 409 | The main chat (and other assistant chats) can't start: no computer / the computer isn't confirmed yet / Claude Code isn't installed on that computer / launcher not found. `error` is a plain-language sentence the hub writes in the request's language (naming the computer), `detail` is the raw text (the shell's error, shown only under "Details"), `action` is the suggested action (`add_computer` / `confirm_computer` / `install_claude` / `connect_model`), plus `machine_name`, `launcher` (sometimes) and `delivered: none`.  **A start in a new terminal tab** (`POST /api/v1/sessions`, `agent_start`, a task) whose tab's shell said it can't run the launcher (`launcher_missing`) or the claude it runs (`claude_missing`) fails within seconds with the same codes plus `where: "terminal"`, `missing` (the command or path the shell named), `kind` (`not_found` / `no_such_file` / `permission_denied`), `pane_shell` (the tab's shell; absent when the node cannot tell, and the sentence says "the default shell"), `launcher_shell` and `rc_file` (where the node lists launchers) and `line` (the shell's own line); the sentence then says the terminal's shell lacks it and where the list came from. A launcher the node does not list either is plain `launcher_missing` without `where` |
| `launcher_missing` with `where: "terminal"` | 409 | A launcher the new terminal tab's shell could not run is the terminal's problem, not a model to connect: its `action` is `switch_launcher` (start it on another launcher of the same computer: a failed task's `retry_with`, the launcher picker) instead of `connect_model`, and the body also carries `summary`, a short line in the request's language for a list row ("“work” can't start in the terminal on Example box"), while `error` keeps the whole sentence for the details. A client that does not know `switch_launcher` shows no button, as for any unknown action; `claude_missing` keeps `install_claude` |
| `center_unreachable` | 503 | Connected to a member hub of a linked-hub group, and the group's primary hub is unreachable right now (carries `center: {hub_id, name}`); the member does not take over on its own; switch to another or wait for the primary to return |
| `internal` | 5xx | Other internal errors |

The table lists the shared handler and the main business codes; other explicit node RPC error codes are passed through too, usually mapped to 409 (`not_found` to 404, `conversation_deleted` to 410). Clients should branch on `code`, show `error` for unknown codes, and still handle a response that carries only `error`.

APIs that take a JSON body all have a size limit, from 1 KiB to 32 MiB depending on the API (`decodeJSONBody` in the hub, and the managers' copies of it): the manager join (`POST /api/v1/bus/join`) 1 KiB; small settings, card choices (`…/choose`) and pair codes 4 KiB; device prefs, notify and `POST /api/v1/admin/peers` 16 KiB; hub-to-hub pairing (`POST /api/v1/peer/pair`) 64 KiB; pin / mute / launchers / card answers (`…/resolve`) / connector replies 1 MiB; session messages and the starts that carry a first message's pictures (`POST /api/v1/sessions`, `POST /api/v1/assistant/conversations`), interrupts, keys and the other bodies the hub hands to a node as they are (git commit / push / pr, agent settings) 32 MiB (`proto.MessageBodyLimit`), which is also the hub's cap on any request it forwards to a manager. Over the limit returns 413 `too_large`; the hub stops reading at the limit instead of reading it all. Malformed input is still 400. Some manager routes still read with a plain size cap and answer an oversized body with 400 instead, for example `POST /api/v1/task-plans/{id}/start` (1 MiB).

## Portable configuration forms

Modules can supply a versioned, localized configuration document instead of a
client-specific settings page. The shared configuration contract (`schema/configuration`)
defines typed text, toggle, single-selection, multiple-selection and number
fields; ordered titles/descriptions; effective/default values; partial updates,
explicit resets, field errors and revision conflicts. The Go package
`server/internal/configuration` validates the contract and adapts an injected
resource provider to GET/PATCH at a module-owned authenticated endpoint.
It registers no global route or storage. Settings › Labs consumes the
contract through a browser-local terminal adapter; server-backed modules supply
their own persistence and authority. The web app renders the controls in its
design system.

## Operation receipts (client_ops)

Once the server declares `client_ops`, clients may send `X-Persona-Op-Id: <UUID>` on the following write requests:

| Operation kind | Path |
| --- | --- |
| `message` | `POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/messages` or the full-device Agent-only `/agent-messages` route (`agent_terminal_send`) |
| `start` | `POST /api/v1/sessions` |
| `assistant_start` | `POST /api/v1/assistant/conversations` (hub feature `assistant_start_ops`) |
| `resolve` | `POST /api/v1/interactions/{id}/resolve` |
| `clarify` | `POST /api/v1/interactions/{id}/clarify` |
| `choose` | `POST /api/v1/interactions/{id}/choose` (also accepts a body `client_id`; see "Answering a question from its notification") |
| `interrupt` / `close` / `rename` / `modes` | `POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/interrupt`, `/close`, `/rename`, `/modes` |
| `rewind` / `restore_model` / `fork` | `POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/rewind`, `/restore-model`, `/fork` |
| `keys` / `send_now` | `POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/keys` (keys pressed in the Agent's terminal) and `/queue/send-now`: a repeat is answered from the receipt instead of pressing the keys or sending the queued message again |
| `worktree_create` | `POST /api/v1/machines/{mid}/worktree/create` |
| `todo_route` | `POST /api/v1/assistant/conversations/{id}/route` (a message to a to-do): kept and replayed as `todo_answer` is, a recorded `unknown` included; relayed as a send, so one cut off while the manager had it is 502 `assistant_in_doubt` with `delivered: "unknown"`; one that never reached a manager keeps no receipt. The hub sends `todo_send_state` while it runs ("Message feedback") |
| `todo_create` | `POST /api/v1/todos` **with at least one image**: the first response is replayed to the same op id instead of creating a second to-do. Relayed as a send, so a response cut off while the manager had the write is 502 `assistant_in_doubt` and is kept, not retried as a new create; `assistant_offline`, which shows no manager took it, keeps no receipt and may be retried. An image-less create (no `images` field, `images: []` or `images: null`) is not covered even when it carries `X-Persona-Op-Id`: no receipt is claimed and no pending/unknown response is synthesized |

Every session write either keeps a receipt or repeats harmlessly; `server/internal/hub/session_write_receipts_test.go` lists which and why, and a new session write route must be added to one of its lists.

The UUID is case-insensitive. The hub builds a digest from the operation kind, path, normalized query parameters and JSON parameters, then claims the ID atomically. A repeated request reuses the receipt only for the same device, target and parameters; a conflict returns `409 {"code":"op_id_reused"}`. Message requests set `client_msg_id` to the operation UUID, overriding any value of that name in the body. Without the header or a route-specific body receipt ID, no receipt is kept; the non-UUID `client_msg_id` and `sent_messages` dedup apply as usual.

`GET /api/v1/ops/{id}` returns the record `{id,device_id,kind,target,digest,state,result,created_at,updated_at}`. `target` contains `path` / `query`. Once recorded, `result` is `{status,body,content_type?}`, where `body` is the base64 of the original HTTP response bytes. It returns 404 when the record doesn't exist or doesn't belong to the current device credential. The master token has no device ID, so its queries are not filtered by device ownership.

| `state` | Meaning and retry behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `pending` | Claimed, execution not finished; a repeated write waits for the receipt and returns `202 {"state":"pending"}` when the configured wait runs out |
| `done` | Success receipt stored; a repeated write replays the original HTTP status and body without executing again |
| `failed` | Definitely failed, receipt stored; a repeated write still replays the original result |
| `unknown` | Outcome unknown; for ordinary operations a repeated request returns `202 {"state":"unknown"}`. Query or check by hand; never treat it as success or resend automatically |

For ordinary operations, HTTP 400 / 409 are usually recorded as `failed`; other errors are recorded as `unknown` unless it can be shown they didn't execute. A to-do's writes (`todo_answer`, `todo_route`) are recorded by the rule of their final `todo_send_state` ("Message feedback", its "To-do writes"): `failed` only when the answer shows nothing was taken, so a manager's 409 or 502 that says nothing of delivery is `unknown`. On startup the hub marks leftover `pending` as `unknown` and does not re-execute them. After completion it still tries to store the receipt even if the HTTP caller has disconnected; if storing fails it returns 503 with `state: unknown`. Receipts are kept for 30 days from creation. That is a retention policy; dedup beyond the window is not guaranteed.

Lark sends and Inbox replies also derive receipts from the body's `client_id`; see "Lark API" below. They reuse `client_ops` too, but an existing upstream error response is replayed as-is. Don't apply that response rule to all ordinary operations.

When a new session is started with an operation ID, the hub keeps finishing an accepted start after the caller disconnects and stores the receipt. Replaying the same ID won't start it again; an existing HTTP result is returned as-is even if marked `unknown`, and leftover operations with no result still return `202 {"state":"unknown"}`. A client persists the ID and parameters before sending, and queries the ID if the response is lost. Neither a 404 nor an unknown result proves it didn't start, so the client keeps the pending-confirmation record and doesn't POST again. Only a clearly failed receipt allows editing the form and starting a new operation.

A new assistant conversation (`assistant_start`) works the same way: an accepted start finishes after the caller disconnects, a repeat with the same ID gets the first answer (also when it was `502 assistant_in_doubt`, recorded as `unknown`), and nothing is started twice. `503 assistant_offline` keeps no receipt (nothing reached the assistant), so the same ID can try again once it is back. A client sends one ID per first message and, on a hub with `assistant_start_ops`, tries it again through a gap (no network, a timeout, the hub restarting, `202 pending`) for up to a minute; without the feature it sends no ID and doesn't retry gaps.

## Device connections

### Connection records

The hub keeps connection records for authenticated device WebSockets for 14 days. Master tokens and
temporary pairing tokens do not create records. Only an IPv4 /24 or IPv6 /64 prefix is stored. When the
hub fixes up an unfinished record after a shutdown or crash, it records `hub_stopped`.

## Codex sources and capabilities

External Codex sessions keep using `(machine_id, session_id)`. The fixed legacy home keeps its existing raw thread IDs; threads in other canonical homes use an opaque ID of `c0de-` plus a deterministic digest. Changes in PID, endpoint or connection generation don't change the session ID. `source_thread_id` is the original thread ID; never put the opaque ID into `claude --resume`.

New optional Session fields: `source_kind` (`codex_history` / `codex_app_server` / `identity_conflict`; Agent runtime sessions are `runtime`, see "Runtime ↔ node"; Claude Code sessions outside Persona's terminals are `claude_bg` (a background session), `claude_desktop` (Claude's desktop app) and `claude_cli` (a terminal Persona does not drive), sending through the owner's tmux pane for verified `owner_input`, otherwise through the session's peer inbox when the node can use it (a tmux row lists send and terminal even without an inbox)), `source_thread_id`, `source_instance_id`, `parent_thread_id`, `read_only_reason`, `attached`, `capabilities` (six booleans: read/send/interrupt/approve/terminal/attach, and the optional `modes`, `close`, `rename`, `model`, `rewind`, `rewind_code`, `plugin_input` and `supervision_policy`, and the list `permission_modes`). `plugin_input: true` (a `claude_desktop` / `claude_cli` / `claude_bg` row with no tmux pane whose Persona plugin polls the node) means the owner's own messages go in as their input while the session rests. `supervision_policy: true` (a non-sub-Agent runtime row whose runtime declared both `caps.assistant` and `caps.supervision_policy`) tells the hub that this runtime implements a dedicated out-of-band supervision policy channel; absent or false keeps the conservative non-capable runtime boundary. Old sources lacking these fields stay compatible; new sources lacking capabilities default to refusing writes. Without the terminal capability, terminal / keys / close pane are not shown.

`capabilities.takeover` is an optional object `{running, can_resume, reason?, released_desktop?}`; `reason` is `encrypted_context` or `unavailable`. The signed-in full-device manager route is not an assistant tool, and generic device-call APIs deny it. GET `/api/v1/machines/{mid}/codex/{sid}/takeover` returns `{token, cwd, transcript_path, continuation_prompt}` with a single-use token valid for two minutes. POST requires `confirm_stop: true` only while the original writer is running; when it has exited, `false` is accepted. Takeover resumes the same thread and session ID in a new terminal tab. A separate continue option alone starts an independent session with context and attached to-do preserved. The `encrypted_context` failure permits continuation only. A `released_desktop: true` plan instead resumes the original native Desktop thread through its same-home local app-server. It has no continuation prompt and cannot stop any process. Preparation, commit and subsequent sends check native ownership.

`capabilities.rewind` permits `session.rewind` to before a user message. `capabilities.rewind_code` additionally permits
`code_and_conversation`. Absent values keep the Claude terminal heuristic. Codex advertises conversation rewind for a
shared app-server with persistent paginated history and a node able to materialize that history. Runtime rows report
`caps.rewind`, excluding sub-Agents. A runtime row may carry `capabilities` of its own for this: `rewind: false` takes
the rewind away from that session, and `rewind_code: true` offers file restoration with it (Paseo: what each agent's
provider can do); without it file restoration stays off. The web message menu reads both fields.

`capabilities.model` permits model changes through `POST …/modes`. Runtime rows explicitly report whether the runtime
advertised `caps.model`, excluding sub-Agent rows. Absent values preserve older clients' model-switch heuristics.
A runtime row may narrow `modes` and `model` for its own session the same way it narrows `rewind`: `false` in
its own `capabilities` takes them away (Paseo: an agent it keeps archived, which it changes nothing of), and a row that
says nothing keeps what the runtime declared, as an older runtime's rows do.
A runtime that advertises `caps.models` also handles `launchers.models` for live native model discovery.

`capabilities.modes` says whether the composer's permission mode and effort chips can change the session through `POST …/modes`. A runtime row carries `true` when the runtime declared `caps.modes`, the row is not a sub-Agent's, and its `agent` is `claude` (Orca, Paseo's Claude providers) or the runtime's own (`agy`; not Paseo, whose bridge calls every agent other than Claude Code and Codex `paseo`, and takes for those and for Codex only their own approval and Allow all, `capabilities.permission_modes` below); otherwise `false`. `claude_bg` / `claude_desktop` / `claude_cli` rows always carry `false`: the peer inbox carries messages only, and a message never gives such a session a pane, so their mode and effort change on the computer. Other sources omit it for now. Clients show the chips from it when it is a boolean, whatever the agent; when it is absent (an older node, or a source that does not say) they decide from `agent` and `source_kind`. The hub forwards it as the node sent it (a pointer in `proto.SessionCapabilities`, so an older node's row stays without it). An older hub, whose `proto.SessionCapabilities` has no `modes`, drops it on the way; clients then fall back to the `agent` / `source_kind` rule as for an older node. A change that reaches the node anyway is refused with `409 modes_on_computer` for such a Claude, or `409 modes_not_running` when nothing runs the session (Resume on its terminal page brings it back); both words come from the hub in the request's language (`rpc-errors.modes_*`), and the same refusals apply to `model` and `ultracode` on that endpoint. An older node answers both with its own fixed text and no code.
`capabilities.permission_modes` lists the permission modes `POST …/modes` can set on a session whose agent is not Claude Code, Persona's ids in their order: `default`, the agent's own approval, and `bypassPermissions` where it has an Allow all. A runtime row says it in its own `capabilities`: Paseo lists `["default","bypassPermissions"]` for an agent whose approval is Paseo's Auto Accept (Grok and its other ACP providers, OpenCode) or Codex's full-access, `["default"]` for its other providers. The node keeps Persona's ids alone and drops the list where it refuses `session.modes` (the runtime declared no `caps.modes`), where the row narrowed `modes` to `false` (an archived agent), and where `capabilities.modes` is `true` (Claude Code's chips stand there); `capabilities.modes` itself stays `false` on such a row. With two or more modes the web app shows a two-state switch in the composer's picker: `permission_mode` `bypassPermissions` is Allow all, any other or none is the agent's own, named "Launcher default", not "Ask", since the agent's own settings may approve everything. Going into Allow all asks first; leaving it does not. A hub without the field drops it on the way, and the web app then shows no switch.
`capabilities.close` says whether the session can be closed independently of terminal access. Runtime rows report their declared `caps.close`. The web app uses this value for the close action and confirmation. When it is absent, closing is limited to terminal sessions (older nodes). An explicit false refuses closing even when terminal access is available.
`capabilities.rename` says whether the session's title can be changed (`POST …/rename` with `title`) independently of terminal access. Runtime rows report their declared `caps.rename`, excluding sub-Agent rows (`is_subagent`, or a `<session>@<id>` id); a pointer in `proto.SessionCapabilities` like `close`, so the hub forwards it as the node sent it and an older node's row stays without it. The web app shows Rename from it when it is a boolean, renaming the title alone (such a session has no tab); when it is absent it shows Rename on a row that can send and is the user's own Agent or a Persona conversation. An explicit false hides Rename even on a terminal session.

`capabilities.queue_edit` and `capabilities.queue_send_now` advertise queue controls on runtime sessions. Runtime subagents do not support them. If a field is absent, clients keep their previous queue-control rules. A Claude Code session outside Persona's terminals reports both, false unless it runs in a tmux pane: its queue is on its own screen.

`capabilities.stop_cause` is node-owned stopped-session recovery provenance: `user`, `idle`, `task_completed`, `restart`, `resume_failed`, `compact_failed`, `usage_limit`, `transient_error`, or `exit` (the Agent was told to quit, `/exit` or `/quit` sent through Persona; like `user` it never authorizes a supervisor's resume). `restart` is recorded for an Agent seen running (`ran_at`) within 10 minutes before the node started and cut off since; `resume_failed` for the assistant's resume refused with nothing run (`delivered: none`, no kept tab; any other failed start stays unknown); `compact_failed` for an Agent that quit while it was compacted before a message. `usage_limit` and `transient_error` are recorded for an exited terminal Agent whose latest turn has the recognized gateway quota-reset or temporary-capacity 429 error, only with a live observation after the error and the original Persona terminal still retained; unobserved history and a closed/replaced terminal do not authorize recovery. An explicit stop cause always wins, and an error older than a consumed start cannot grant recovery again. These causes, like `idle` and `task_completed`, permit the assistant's resume.
