  `plan_first` a boolean. Effort and ultracode reach Claude Code starts only; a goal reaches new Claude Code and Codex
  starts of tasks with `done_when`.
- A candidate's weight roll comes from the operating system's crypto-grade random source (`crypto/rand`), never a
  predictable generator; weights only ever share starts inside the winning priority group.
- With no fitting rule naming `goal` for a task (no policy, none that fits, or every fitting one silent on `goal`), a
  new Codex start of a task with `done_when` carries that goal by default; a Claude Code start carries none.
  `"goal":"off"` in a rule is how the owner turns the Codex default off; any other value is 400. The default is not
  sent to a start in an engine runtime or through an app launcher, and a node's refusal of it is not put in the task's
  `why`.
- Rules are tried in order and the first that fits wins, except for `goal`: the first fitting rule that names `goal`
  decides it, whichever rule supplies the rest. A caller's own effort, ultracode, tier, model or launcher is
  never replaced. A rule's values apply to one start try: the next try starts again from what the task named, and for
  whatever a rule filled in the task in `TaskPlan` keeps its own value, never the policy's (its `why` names a preset the
  policy picked).

### Dispatch policy

The assistant can run under an optional dispatch policy: an organization rule for which conversations may hand out
work, so a conversation that is meant to only read and report cannot open tasks or push work into the main or a
leader conversation. With no policy stored, or one past its expiry, every conversation behaves exactly as without
the feature.

A policy is one setting on the assistant (`dispatch_policy` in `GET`/`PUT /api/v1/assistant`, full credentials) and
also has its own route, `GET`/`PUT /api/v1/assistant/dispatch-policy`, open to full credentials and to an extension
token granted the `assistant.dispatch_policy` hub scope. Its shape:

```json
{
  "rules": [
    {
      "conversation_class": "scheduled",
      "deny": ["task_plan", "agent_start", "send_to_main"],
      "message": "where the model should leave findings instead"
    }
  ],
  "expires_at": "RFC 3339, optional"
}
```

- `conversation_class` is one of `main`, `leader`, `background_supervisor`, `scheduled` (a scheduled task's own
  conversation) or `other`. Classes are resolved most specific first, so a conversation a scheduled task runs in
  that is later made the main conversation keeps that higher class.
- `deny` names what the class may not do: hand out work (`task_plan`, `agent_start`), or relay work with
  `conversation_send` to the main conversation (`send_to_main`). A send to any other conversation is not limited.
  A limited conversation also cannot cancel or delete its own scheduled task (`cancel_followup`,
  `delete_routine`): removing the task would take away the conversation's own class mid-turn.
- `message` is an optional short note (at most 300 runes) appended to the localized refusal that starts with
  "The current organization policy requires…".
- `expires_at` is optional for a full-credential write, which may also set one further than an hour ahead. An
  extension write must set it to no more than one hour ahead; an expired policy is treated as absent, so a stopped or
  uninstalled extension leaves nothing in force. Empty `rules` clears the policy.
- The owner's own words are never blocked: when a limited conversation relays something to the **main**
  conversation, the send is allowed if the current turn started with the owner's own message (a user text item with
  a client message id and no source marking it as a scheduled run, a supervision message, a relay or a system
  notice), or if the sent text starts with one of the owner's messages verbatim. If the conversation's transcript
  cannot be read, the send stays refused.

The checks run on the model's tool-call entry only: the hub's own internal starts are not affected, and the main
conversation, leader conversations and the background supervisor keep working unless a rule explicitly names their
class.

### Explicit dispatch guard

The explicit guard is separate from the class-based dispatch policy. It is off by default and applies only to targets
named by `machine_id + session_id`:

```json
{
  "enabled": true,
  "expires_at": "RFC 3339, required for an extension-written enabled policy",
  "targets": [
    {"machine_id": "example-machine", "session_id": "example-session", "deny": ["task_plan", "agent_start"]}
  ]
}
```

`deny` may also name `conversation_send`. No policy, `enabled:false`, expiry or a target that
does not match leaves behavior unchanged. `GET` / `PUT /api/v1/assistant/dispatch-guard` accepts full credentials or
an extension granted `dispatch.guard`; the legacy every-scope grant does not include it. An extension-written enabled
policy must expire within one hour, and empty `targets` clears the policy even when the request leaves `enabled:true`.
Requests must name `dispatch_guard`. Duplicate or unknown outer, policy or target fields, missing/null policies,
`targets:null` and non-empty policies without an explicit `enabled` are 400 without a Store write or a tool-list
notification. Complete JSON is walked for duplicate keys before any `RawMessage` occurrence can be discarded. Field
names are case-sensitive at every level; a differently cased alias (`DISPATCH_GUARD`, `TARGETS`, `ENABLED`) is an
unknown field and gets the same 400. Only an
explicit `enabled:false` or `targets:[]` clears. Validation responses use localized typed errors in English,
Simplified Chinese and Japanese.

`guardRefusal` runs at the model tool-call entry before business arguments are parsed. `guardTools` applies the same
decision to the actual `sessionMCPTools` list, while `assistant.tools` accepts an optional `{machine_id, session_id}`
and uses `ToolsFor`. Untargeted lists and other conversations stay unchanged. A stale client or direct invocation
still meets the call guard. `--allowedTools` is not used as evidence of tool-list narrowing. The discovery cursor
includes the effective filter state and heartbeat re-evaluates it, so natural expiry and Setting read recovery cannot
leave an old narrowed list cached as `unchanged`. Each returned list and its revision come from the same captured
effective guard decision, including when an admission read and the list read see a transient failure. An unreadable or
invalid enabled policy fails closed for the four dispatch tools; unrelated tools remain available. The localized refusal
contains no storage error, target, tool name, arguments, policy or credential.

## WebSocket `/api/v1/ws`

Envelope `{"type":"…", ...}`.

Server → client:

| type | Fields |
| --- | --- |
| `hub_restarting` | `back_in_ms`: the hub is about to restart (deploy, `systemctl restart`, update), followed by 1001 "hub restarting". The client reconnects immediately and keeps the UI as is. No `event_seq`, not replayed |
| `hub_update` | `update` (same as `GET /api/v1/hub/update`): checking, downloading, waiting for idle, restarting, confirming, rolling back; pushed whenever the state changes; after `restarting` the connection drops for a while, which is expected |
| `hello` | `server_version`, `client_id`, `features`, `hub_id`, `hub_name`, `endpoints`, `tls_port`, `fp`, `mesh`, `channel`, `build`, `protocol`, `min_app_build` (the last four same as `/api/v1/health`), `event_stream`, `event_seq`, `resumed` (see "Event resume" below), `locale` (the user's language, feature `locale`), `push_grading` (boolean, current hub push grading switch), `image_limits` (the pictures a message may carry, see "Pictures in a message"), `message_send_state` and `todo_send_state` (each `1`: the receipt versions only the hub writes, the proof a client trusts those events by; see their rows); the first message on every WS, not yet including the negotiated heartbeat. `mesh`: `{"hubs":[{hub_id,name,online,self,center,endpoints,tls_port,fp}]}`, every hub in the linked-hub group (including itself, `self: true`; paired but currently unreachable ones `online: false`; `center: true` is the group's primary hub, which clients prefer among those in the same group); without linking, only itself. When connected to a member, hello comes from the primary (`hub_id` is the primary's) |
| `push_grading` | `enabled` (boolean): hub push-grading switch toggled; open web and desktop clients update notifications, sounds, and alert badges immediately |
| `endpoints` | `endpoints` (the full candidate list, only sent to connections that declared the capability of the same name) |
| `client_hello_ack` | `heartbeat: {interval, pong_timeout}` (the seconds actually used after this negotiation) |
| `resources` | `resources`: registered runner definitions, last mirror with `observed_at` / `attempted_at` / `unknown`, versioned queue tickets and durable CI leases; emitted after each mirror refresh. Read once with `GET /api/v1/resources`. |
| `machines` | `machines` (also after a rename: the whole list, with the new `name`) |
| `managers` | No payload: the manager roster changed (created, renamed, connected, disconnected, deleted, new reported bot identities); clients re-read `GET /api/v1/managers` ("Bus" below). Only sent to connections that asked for feature `managers` (`?features=` or `client_hello.features`), not in the event log |
| `saved_agent_searches` | `revision` (decimal string): the default manager committed a saved-query mutation; re-read the collection while its view is open, respecting the message's manager stamp. No query/name payload; see "Saved Agent searches" |
| `navigation` | `start`, `pages` and / or `overview`, whichever changed (`PUT /api/v1/navigation`, "Navigation"): clients keep the start page for their next opening and draw the sidebar's arrangement and Overview's cards and sections |
| `todos` | —: pushed whenever to-dos or links change; clients re-fetch `GET /api/v1/todos`. From a manager that names `todo_view` also when what a row's `view` files it under (its phase, section, reason, ask ids, the Inactive, Can wait and seen marks, its steps' count) changes with no write to the to-do: one of its runs changed (a card came, its turn ended or was seen) or time alone moved it (its `next_change_at` passed). Never for a working run's latest line, `since`, `next_change_at` or `rank` alone: those reach clients with the list's next read. The seen mark counts, so the first step after the owner looked at a working row pushes once. Settled with the writes' pushes; a run's change waits a second for the rest, and for time alone the manager looks at most once a minute. What the manager told the clients lives in its memory, so the first views it works out after it starts push once |
| `extension_auth` | `extension`, `auth` (`ExtensionAuth`): an extension's sign-in state changed (sign-in finished, signed out, expired, the extension sent `auth.changed`) |
| `subscription` | `id`, `connector`, `revision`, `state`, `removed`: a source subscription was saved, ran or was deleted; clients showing it re-read `GET /api/v1/subscriptions/{id}` or the list |
| `extension_ui` | `extension`, then either `id`, `badge` (a badge change, as `plugin_ui`, which is sent first with `plugin`) or `id?`, `invalidate: true` (the extension's `ui.invalidate`, gathered for one second; no `id` means all its UIs; only this name is sent): clients redraw the pages they show |
| `plugin_ui` | `plugin`, `id`, `badge` (`{text, tone}`, `null` clears it): a plugin changed the badge on its main navigation entry (`nav_page`) |
| `extension_ui_stream` | `kind` (`snapshot` / `delta` / `receipt` / `error` / `closed` / `suspended`), the payload under the name of its kind (`session` for `closed` / `suspended`), `request_id?`, `manager` (set by the hub: the manager that sent it): a frame of a native extension page stream, sent only to the one connection that opened it (feature `extension_ui_stream_v1` and `context.stream`); never broadcast, not in the event log. The hub itself only sends `kind: error` with `error.code` `manager_unavailable` when the manager does not answer the request; every other frame is the manager's ([schema/extension/README.md](../../schema/extension/README.md) "Canonical main-app WebSocket envelopes") |
| `assistant_feed` | `conversation`, `item` (`FeedItem`): a new entry in the chat feed; kind `view` is a live card's original position, and body.view is the AssistantView |
| `assistant_view` | `conversation`, `view` (the schema's AssistantView: id, conversation, version, view, created_at, updated_at): an update to a live card already stored in the database; at most once per second per card, old updates ignored by version; no separate notification |
| `assistant_view_block` | `conversation`, `key`: a body card has been validated from a trusted assistant text item and stored in the database, so its single reply can be enabled; replaying the same source doesn't broadcast again; goes into the existing event resume, and if missed is filled in by the feed.view_blocks snapshot |
| `assistant_view_action` | `conversation`, `action` (ViewAction: key, action, page?, values, client_msg_id, status, revision, error?, at, updated_at, kind?, version?, text?): card submission and send status; `kind` absent or `action` means a declarative action, `html` is an HTML bridge reply (`action` is the component key, `text` is the confirmed text); `version` is the card version the user saw when submitting (older records don't have it); old states ignored by revision; goes into the existing event resume |
| `task_plan` | `plan` (`TaskPlan`): a plan handed to the user, started, dismissed, or one of its tasks failed to start (`tasks[i].error`) |
| `assistant_schedule` | No payload: the assistant's scheduled tasks changed; clients re-read `GET /api/v1/assistant/tasks`. From another manager it carries `manager`, and only the shown manager's counts ("Messages to clients" below) |
| `assistant_saved_prompts` | No payload: the user's saved prompts changed; clients re-read `GET /api/v1/assistant/saved-prompts`. From another manager it carries `manager`, and only the shown manager's counts, as `assistant_schedule` |
| `launcher_health` | `record` (one record as `GET /api/v1/launchers/health` lists it: `machine`, `launcher`, `state`, `kind`, `error`, `checked_at`, `source`, `fails`, `repair?`, `blocked_reason?`, `resets_at?`, `limit_models?`, `limit_resets?`): a launcher's health state changed; only to connected clients, not a push |
| `sessions` | `machine_id`, `sessions` (the full set for that machine, pushed on change, not pushed if identical to the last one; each session carries `rev` = transcript byte count, and a change means new content; optional `suggestion`: a suggested owner reply. A finished Agent can offer one in its final work report. Otherwise Claude can supply its terminal hint or the manager can use the opt-in `suggest.next` model for an eligible open chat; optional `suggestion_risky`: the suggestion names a command, a path, a link, a secret-looking string or a risky action, so clients fill it in but offer no one-tap send; optional `attention_reason`: when the session is in "Needs you", the reason the host gave (botmux's attention reason); optional `external_url`: where to open it outside Persona (the Lark thread of a botmux session)) |
| `revs` | `machine_id`, `revs` (`{session_id: rev}`, changed ones only; sent when the fields visible in the list haven't changed but the transcript grew, pushed to all clients, and clients fetch the increment in the background; an open web chat takes it as its session's rev moving, "The page's own fallback") |
| `sessions_delta` | `machine_id`, `upsert` (`[Session…]`, new or changed sessions, whole objects), `remove` (`[session_id…]`): only to connections that asked for `sessions_delta`, after one full `sessions` snapshot per machine on connect; not in the event log; see "Session deltas" below |
| `sessions_list` | `revision` (an opaque checkpoint): only to connections that asked for `sessions_list`, which get no `sessions` or `sessions_delta`; sent once on connect and again when the indexed session list changes. A hint to read the HTTP `since` page from the saved checkpoint, not a baseline itself; not in the event log; see "Bounded Agents lists" ("Lightweight WebSocket negotiation") below |
| `lark` | `feed_ids` (chats with new Lark messages / changes); `settings_changed` (optional boolean, default false; this batch includes a change to message display settings, independent of the chat IDs; the client also re-reads settings); `account` (the Lark gateway account number these chats belong to); `ol_account` (only present when not the default account, equal to `account`: the parameter needed to read these chats). The hub follows the live events `/agent/v1/events` of every signed-in account on the Lark gateway, sends at most once every 400 ms per account, and pushes to all clients. |
| `agents` | `session_ids` (personal Agent session ids, `<source>:<sessionKey>`, whose content changed; `[]` means the list itself changed): an extension's source reported changes (`agentsrc.updated`), a send went out, a source was removed, or a conversation was removed from or restored to the list; clients re-fetch `GET /api/v1/agents/sessions` (a bounded reader from that collection's own `since` checkpoint) ("Removing a personal Agent from the list" below) |
| `agents.prefs` | No payload: the personal Agent list preferences changed (`PUT /api/v1/agents/prefs`, a conversation hidden or unhidden); clients re-read `GET /api/v1/agents/prefs` ("Personal Agent list preferences" below) |
| `conversation_deleted` | `machine_id`, `session_id`: a permanent manager tombstone. Drop cached transcript, feed, drafts and outgoing messages for this chat; show Conversation deleted for an open reference. The hub ends existing subscriptions and refuses replay; regular session lists omit the tombstone. Manager transport carries an identity-only `Session` with `deleted:true`, `assistant:true`, `status:offline`, a generic localized title and optional space. |
| `items` | `machine_id`, `session_id`, `items`, plus this batch's position in the transcript (see "Continuity of items" below): `history`, `to_seq`, `from_seq` (only on continuation batches). Only pushed to clients subscribed to that session; lines with no item (ai-title and the like) also get an empty `items`, so clients know those lines have been seen |
| `message_send_state` | `machine_id`, `session_id`, `client_msg_id`, `state` (`processing` / `delivered` / `failed` / `unknown` / `kept`: nothing went in and the assistant chat's manager keeps it to send by itself), `at` (UTC RFC3339Nano): a transport receipt for `/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/messages`, only to that session's subscribers. Processing precedes manager preparation and node delivery; it is not a durable queue or execution state. Final HTTP remains authoritative. Not in the event log; reconnect/retry the original operation ID to reconcile. Trust only when the current authenticated `hello` has top-level `message_send_state: 1`, fixed by the hub, not the extension-merged feature array. No client feature negotiation; older clients ignore the unknown type. See "Message feedback" below. |
| `todo_send_state` | `todo_id`, `client_op_id` (the request's `X-Persona-Op-Id`, lower case), `state` (`processing` / `delivered` / `failed` / `unknown`), `at` (UTC RFC3339Nano): a transport receipt for a to-do's message on `POST /api/v1/assistant/conversations/{id}/route` (`todo_id` the body's) or an answer on `POST /api/v1/todos/{id}/asks/{ask}/answer` (`todo_id` the path's), sent with `X-Persona-Op-Id`. Only to full devices that declared `todo_send_state` (`?features=` or `client_hello.features`); not in the event log. Processing goes out once the hub has claimed the op id, before the manager has the write (none when the body names no to-do); the final state once the relay answered and the receipt is stored, `failed` only when the answer shows nothing was taken. Final HTTP (or the op id's receipt) remains authoritative. Trust only when the current authenticated `hello` has top-level `todo_send_state: 1`. See "Message feedback" below, its "To-do writes". |
| `delta` | `machine_id`, `session_id`, `text` (the whole text the headless assistant is generating; an empty string means the turn is over. A Claude session Persona started sends it too: the message Claude is showing in its terminal, as far as the transcript does not have it yet, "" once it does; whole lines every 0.1–1 s. The live text is never the source: the transcript's items replace it). At most one every 80 ms, and what came after the last one goes out 80 ms after it, so the end of a burst of model output never waits for the next burst. The web staggers new words at the stream's pace (`web/src/ui/stream/wordFade.ts`) |
| `live` | `machine_id`, `session_id`, `live` (`SessionLive` or `null`): the status line of a working Claude, only sent to connections subscribed to that session that declared `session_live`; see "Live status" below |
| `screen` | `machine_id`, `session_id`, `text`, `status`, `ts` (the node does not sample the screen per subscription: the terminal page reads `/screen` itself on demand) |
| `fs_changed` | `machine_id`, `cwd`, `dirs` (folders in this page's `fs_watch` that changed), `git` (the Git status of `cwd` changed). Only sent to pages that did `fs_watch`; not in the event log and not replayed on reconnect (the page refreshes itself once after reconnecting) |
| `terminal_control` | `machine_id`, `session_id`, `state`: `active` (took control, with `cols`, `rows`), `busy` (another program on the computer holds it; ask the user whether to `takeover`; mirror in the meantime), `taken` (grabbed by another device or program), `lost` (the node let go itself), `unsupported` (old node / herdr, mirror only); `error` is a human-readable reason |
| `terminal` | `machine_id`, `session_id`, plus a frame `epoch`, `seq`, `full`, `cols`, `rows`, `data` (base64 VT bytes), or `error` (the stream stopped: computer offline, session not running…) + `unsupported` (old node / herdr can't stream; poll `/screen` instead). See "Terminal stream" below |
| `herdr_state` / `herdr_data` / `herdr_end` | `id` plus `state: "open"`, `cols`, `rows` / `data` (base64, ≤ 32 KB each) / `error?`, `code?` (`forbidden` `too_many` `bad_request` `offline`), `unsupported?`: a view of the full herdr interface (the response to `herdr_open`). The hub ends the view when un-acked bytes exceed 1 MiB |
| `herdr_focus` | `id` (the view), `machine_id`, `workspace_id`, `tab_id`, `pane_id`, `session_id?` (the Agent session in that pane), `source` (`client`: some full client on this computer was just typed into / `persona`: requested by a `herdr_focus` / `other`: anything else), `mine` (done by this view itself): herdr's focus changed, pushed to every view on this computer. The web only follows ones that are `mine` and `client`; `persona` + `mine` is an echo; the rest only show a hint. Feature `herdr_focus` |
| `interaction` | `interaction` (a new pending one, pushed to all clients; carries optional `push_level` `"P0"|"P1"|"P2"` for push grading, absent defaults to `"P0"`). When a question is first answered by the assistant on the user's behalf, the same card comes twice: first with `delegating: true` (the assistant is looking; not pushed yet), then again when the assistant hands it to the user, without `delegating` and possibly with `delegate` (`what` / `why_now` / `recommend` / `cost` / `reason` / `deadline`, the context the assistant filled in); a question a supervisor passed up may carry `suggestion` (`RuleSuggestion`, "Tasks and the chat feed"), and the card comes again without it once the suggestion was answered with Always or Not now; overwrite by `id` |
| `interaction_resolved` | `id`; when the assistant answered on the user's behalf, also `answered_by: "assistant"`, plus `reason` (why it answered that way) and `answers` (what it answered; re-answering starts from here) |
| `interaction_reanswered` | `id`, `resolution` (`{answers}`): the user changed the assistant's answer, and the new answer has been sent to that Agent |
| `hook_event` | The node hook event's original fields; the hub adds `machine_id` and sets `type: hook_event`; used to refresh session run state; `Stop` carries `stop_sig` (a reply signature the hub uses to dedupe "done" pushes, see `agent-states.md` ("Hook turn signals")); global report-only hooks carry `report_only: true`, so the hub doesn't take them to mean the session has Persona's hooks; `UserPromptSubmit` carries `prompt_source`, who the prompt is from (its message source's kind, such as `conversation` or `task`; `notification` for a background task's report; else `user`), never the prompt itself |
| `notify` | `kind: interaction / done / assistant / alert`, `machine_id`, `session_id`, `title`, `subtitle`, `body`; a decision's push (an `assistant` notify) also carries `todo: {id, asked_at, recommend, manager, ask?, lockscreen?, options?}` (`TodoDecidePush`; the last three from a manager that says how the push may answer it); interactions also carry `interaction_id`, alerts the caller's `id` when it gave one, an extension's as `ext:` and a hash (`POST /api/v1/notify`); a manager push may also carry `level` (`P0`/`P1`/`P2`) and `related_key` for the hub's push grading filter (held P1/P2/dedup alerts are withheld from `notify` and Web Push while lists and held-push briefings keep updating); `quiet: true` when the device is inside its quiet hours (post it without sound); only sent to connections that declared `ws_notify`; one selected while a device without push was offline comes after its next `client_hello`, see below |
| `inbox` | No payload; a list-change hint, the client re-fetches the Inbox |
| `look` | `{"id","effective"}`: the selected avatar changed (chosen on another device, or back to the default after an extension was uninstalled); every client switches to `effective` |
| `personas` | No payload; the avatar list changed (a tiered avatar changed tier, an extension with avatars was installed / uninstalled / disabled); clients re-fetch `GET /api/v1/personas` and switch once the new package has fully downloaded |
| `error` | `machine_id`, `session_id`, `error`; e.g. a subscription replay failed, and the client checks the session against it |
| `pong` | `id` (a string, echoing the client's application-level ping) |

Client → server:

| type | Fields |
| --- | --- |
| `subscribe` | `machine_id`, `session_id`, `since_seq` (optional; the web passes its local `covered`; if present, all items after it are replayed, one `items` per page (`backlog: true`), at most 8 pages / 4000 items, and beyond that the last one carries `more_after: true`; otherwise the last two turns are replayed), `lazy_images` (optional; when true, items received on this connection carry no image data), `fold_work` (optional; when true, the last two turns replayed from the end on this connection fold their work; `since_seq` replays are not folded) |
| `seen` | `machine_id`, `session_id`; same as HTTP `/seen` |
| `unsubscribe` | `machine_id`, `session_id` |
| `terminal_subscribe` | `machine_id`, `session_id`, `epoch` (optional), `after_seq` (optional): start receiving live frames of this session's terminal (only sent when the hub's `features` has `terminal_stream`); `control: {cols, rows}` (optional, `terminal_control`): the client takes control of the terminal at this size, and `takeover: true` grabs it even when another program holds it |
| `terminal_input` | `machine_id`, `session_id`, `text` (terminal bytes, written as is), `control: {cols, rows}` (optional, new size), `scroll` (optional, wheel lines, > 0 goes back, < 0 goes newer, feature `terminal_scroll`), `at` (optional, `[column, row]` from 0, which cell of the screen the wheel lands on: where the finger went down; without it the node uses the center of the screen), `click` (optional, `[column, row]` from 0, a left click on that cell, feature `terminal_click`), `mouse` (optional, `{action: down|up|drag|move, button: left|middle|right, at: [column, row], mods}`, `mods` bits: shift 1, ctrl 2, alt 4; one mouse event, feature `terminal_mouse`): only forwarded to the node when sent by the connection currently in control |
| `terminal_unsubscribe` | `machine_id`, `session_id` |
| `fs_watch` | `machine_id`, `cwd` (the session directory), `paths` (folders open on this page, absolute paths, at most 32), `git` (whether the Git status of `cwd` is shown). Replaces this page's whole set for this machine and this `cwd`; empty `paths` with `git` false releases it (so does disconnecting). Only full-access devices can send it |
| `herdr_open` | `id` (chosen by the browser, ≤ 64 characters), `machine_id`, `session_id` (optional, a session id or a `pane:` address, whose tab is focused first), `cols`, `rows`, `focus`: have the node run herdr's own client in a PTY and stream the bytes back (feature `herdr_client`, `full` devices only) |
| `herdr_input` / `herdr_resize` / `herdr_ack` / `herdr_close` | `id` plus `data` or `b64` (≤ 1 MiB) / `cols`, `rows` / `bytes` (cumulative bytes parsed) / —: only the connection that opened the view can use it |
| `herdr_focus` | `id` (the view's id), `session_id` (a session id or a `pane:` address, ≤ 256 characters): the page now shows this pane, so move herdr's focus there (feature `herdr_focus`, `full` devices only, only the connection that opened the view; it changes state on the computer, since focus is shared by the whole herdr session). No reply; if focus actually changes, it comes back as `herdr_focus` (`source: "persona"`). section 28 |
| `register_desktop` | `device_name`: a desktop client registers as a desktop client (`hub/desktops.go`); `device_id` (the device id used for push: while it's connected, the hub doesn't push "Needs You" or "Agent finished" to this desktop, and it posts local notifications itself). Signing it out means revoking its device credential (`DELETE /api/v1/auth/tokens/{id}`; the hub then drops its connection and deletes the push registration it made) |
| `unregister_desktop` | No fields: withdraw this connection's desktop registration while the client is locked, idle or unable to notify. The socket stays connected; an active desktop may register again on the next authenticated hello. A hub without the message ignores it, and closing the socket withdraws the registration |
| `client_hello` | `device_id`, `platform`, `version`, `build`, `os: {name, version, sdk}`, `features`, `heartbeat: {interval?, pong_timeout?}`, `locale` (`zh-Hans` / `en` / `ja`, the UI language), all optional, see below |
| `extension_ui_stream` | `manager?` (the manager to route it to; default the default manager), `request` (`UIStreamRequest`: `request` is `open` / `close` / `suspend` / `resume` / `event` / `snapshot`, with `request_id` and the fields that request needs): a native extension page stream request. The hub forwards it with this connection's authenticated identity to that manager, whose frames come back to this connection only (`extension_ui_stream` above). Only from full devices on a connection that declared `extension_ui_stream_v1`, at most 64 KiB and at most 16 managers per connection; anything else is dropped without a reply, and a ninth request while eight still wait for their manager closes the connection ([schema/extension/README.md](../../schema/extension/README.md) "Native UI stream protocol 1") |
| `ping` | Must carry a string `id`; an empty string is allowed; no reply if it's missing, null or not a string |

### Event resume (`event_seq`)

Broadcasts the hub sends to all clients (everything in this table except `hello`, connection snapshots, `sessions_delta`, `sessions_list`, `managers`, `extension_ui_stream`, `items`, `delta`, `terminal*`, `notify`, `pong`, `error`,
`client_hello_ack`, `hub_restarting`) carry `event_seq`: it increments by one per event within a stream (`hello.event_stream`), and numbering continues after a hub restart.

- The client remembers `event_stream` and the highest `event_seq` it received, and passes them when reconnecting: `/api/v1/ws?event_stream=<stream>&event_seq=<n>` (both are required).
- `hello.resumed: true`: right after hello, broadcasts with `event_seq > n` are replayed (in order, no duplicates), then live ones follow; the client doesn't need a full re-fetch. Connection snapshots are sent as usual (full state, applied silently).
- `resumed: false` (the stream changed: the hub crashed; what was missed is no longer in the last 2000 events / 15 minutes the hub keeps; more than 400 events) or a hub without these fields: do a full refresh.
  `hello.event_seq` is the last event at this moment; after the full refresh, keep counting from it.
- Permission cards that need filling in (elicitation `interaction`s) are not replayed; they come from the pending-interaction snapshot after connecting.
- After a subscription (`subscribe`) replay, a headless assistant session that is still generating is followed immediately by one current `delta`.

### Notifications over the persistent connection (ws_notify)

`notify` is the event name; `ws_notify` is the capability name both sides declare. The hub applies the push decisions for questions and completions, mute rules and device preferences, and sends it to a connection only when `c.has("ws_notify")`.

`interaction` means an interaction that needs handling, `done` means an Agent finished, `assistant` means the assistant finished, and `alert` is a reminder an extension sent via `POST /api/v1/notify` (or a script's `personad notify`) (clients ignore unknown kinds). Preferences are read from `/api/v1/devices/{id}/prefs` by the authenticated device ID: interactions follow `input`, completions follow the completion policy; quiet hours (`quiet`) drop completions and mark interactions and reply reminders `quiet: true`; machine and space mutes use the existing checks. Completion events are decided by the hub, and a client should not generate another one from session state changes. The web declares `ws_notify` only while its alert sound or system notifications are on (saying `client_hello` again when they change) and shows only what it does not work out from session states itself: the assistant's conversations' cards and reminders, `assistant` and `alert`. The raw `interaction` and `interaction_resolved` events are still sent, for request cards and withdrawing notifications; don't treat both as new reminders.

**Kept while offline**: a device (a browser) hears of a question or a finished turn only on this connection. So, for each device, the hub keeps the `notify` events it selected for that device while the device had no `ws_notify` connection or every eligible connection synchronously rejected the event because its outbound queue was full, and sends them right after the `client_hello` of its next connection that declares `ws_notify`, oldest first (not ordered against `client_hello_ack`):

- They are the same events a connected socket would have got, with no new fields. The device's settings (`input`, the completion policy, manager mutes, quiet hours) were applied when each event was selected and are not applied again, so one selected inside quiet hours still carries `quiet: true`. They are written in the language of the device's last `client_hello`.
- An `interaction` notify whose card was resolved in the meantime is skipped. Other kinds are sent as kept; clients collapse them with their usual notification tags (the interaction id, the session, an alert's `id`), so one already shown is replaced rather than repeated.
- Bounds: at most 50 events per device for at most 30 minutes (the oldest go first), for the 32 devices whose last `client_hello` declared `ws_notify` most recently. A `client_hello` without `ws_notify`, or revoking the device's credential, forgets the device and its events.
- Memory only: a hub restart loses them, and a device is known only after it has said `client_hello` with `ws_notify` to the running hub. An event sent to a socket that was already dead but not yet detected (before its heartbeat times out) is not kept. An offline device kept only for replay does not count as selected in `POST /api/v1/notify`'s answer. A connected recipient whose queue rejects the event still counts as selected and also contributes to `kept`; neither count proves delivery. When another socket for that device accepts the event, no replay copy is kept.

Events don't prove a notification was actually shown; after a disconnect the client must still fetch interactions and sessions to reconcile.

### Web Push (browsers)

A browser that turned on **Settings › Notifications › When Persona is closed** gets, while no page of it is connected, the `notify` events a socket would get, as a Web Push (RFC 8030) encrypted to it (RFC 8291 `aes128gcm`) and signed with the hub's VAPID key (RFC 8292). `server/internal/webpush` encrypts and signs with the standard library only; `server/internal/hub/webpush.go` decides and delivers. Push delivery is the hub's own: full devices only (an extension's token, an answer-only device and Persona Link are refused).

`/api/v1/push/grading` is the neutral alias of `/api/v1/push/ln-mode`: both paths use the same handler, request / response shape and authorization. The older route and the `ln_*` reason values below are legacy wire identifiers retained for compatibility; the feature is named push grading.

| Method | Path | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GET | `/api/v1/push/ln-mode` | Push grading switch state: `{"enabled": bool}` (default false). Full credentials and an extension token with the `notify` scope may read it |
| PUT | `/api/v1/push/ln-mode` | `{"enabled": bool}` → the same shape; full credentials only (extension tokens get 403, even with `notify`); stored in `hub_settings` |
| GET | `/api/v1/push/intercepts` | `{"intercepts": [{"at","level","reason","title"?,"body"?,"related_key"?,"todo_id"?,"machine_id"?,"session_id"?,"manager"?,"also"?}]}` newest first, at most 200, the pushes the grading filter held back (`reason`: `ln_p1_held` / `ln_p2_silent` / `ln_dedup_12h`; `also`: titles merged into one same-minute P1 entry). `todo_id` and a complete `machine_id` + `session_id` pair are optional sources the clients follow. Full credentials read every manager's. An extension token needs the `notify` scope **and** its extension ID in `hub.json` `intercept_readers`; any other extension token gets 403, and a listed extension still reads its own manager's only (the manager filter runs **before** the 200 limit, so other managers' bursts cannot push its entries out). `body` is a stored summary, not the full text: title plus at most 140 runes with an ellipsis when cut, because bodies can contain the owner's decision questions, agent replies or notify_user text |
| GET | `/api/v1/push/stats/daily[?days=N\|&since=RFC3339]` | `{"since": RFC3339, "days": [{"date","manager","sent","intercepted","by_reason"?}]}` per UTC calendar day and manager: `sent` counts logical alert pushes allowed through to delivery (one entry however many devices were targeted, regardless of per-device mute/quiet filtering or push-service acceptance; counted with the switch off as well as on, including the hub's own pairing / joining receipts with `manager` empty; silent background pushes are not counted), `intercepted` with `by_reason` counts held pushes. Counts read the hub's full in-memory records (up to 500 held / 2000 delivered, 14 days), so they stay exact past the intercepts' 200-entry limit. `days` is 1 (today) to 14; `since` takes an RFC3339 timestamp and wins over `days`; windows older than 14 days are clamped; bad params get 400. Full credentials read every manager's; an extension token with the `notify` scope reads its own manager's only. There is no "opened / handled" count: card-resolution events are not stored per push |
| GET | `/api/v1/push/web` | `{key}`: the VAPID public key (uncompressed P-256, base64url), the browser's `applicationServerKey`. Made the first time it is asked for and kept in the hub's settings (`hub.web_push.vapid`); 503 when it can't be read or stored |
| GET | `/api/v1/push/web/{device}` | `{subscribed, service?, host?, browser?, current?, endpoint?, created_at?, updated_at?, last_ok_at?, failed_at?, status?, error?}`. `{device}` is the browser's notification device id (`web-<uuid>`, the id its prefs go by). `service` is `FCM` / `Mozilla` / `Apple` / `Windows`; `current` false: made with a key the hub no longer has (the page subscribes again); the last delivery (`last_ok_at`, or `failed_at` with the push service's `status` and `error`) is kept in memory |
| PUT | `/api/v1/push/web/{device}` | `{endpoint, keys:{p256dh, auth}, key, locale?, features?, browser?}` (`PushSubscription.toJSON()`, the key it subscribed with, the page's language, its `client_hello` features, "Chrome · macOS") → the status above. 400 `bad_device`; 400 `unknown_push_service`: the endpoint must be https on 443, without credentials, at FCM (`fcm.googleapis.com`), Mozilla (`*.push.services.mozilla.com`), Apple (`*.push.apple.com`) or Windows (`*.notify.windows.com`), so a device can't make the hub post to an address of its choosing; 400 `bad_endpoint`, `bad_keys`; 409 `key_changed` with `key` (subscribe again with it); 403 `owned`: another device credential made it, and the request doesn't present its endpoint (the same browser signed in again does); 503 when it can't be stored. `features` keeps only `elicitation`. At most 32 browsers, kept whole in `hub.web_push.subscriptions`: one more drops the one renewed longest ago; the same endpoint under another device id replaces that row |
| DELETE | `/api/v1/push/web/{device}[?endpoint=]` | `{ok, removed}`; 403 `owned` as for PUT |

**What is pushed, and when.** `notifyWSFrom`, after the sockets and the notify ring, picks each subscribed browser that has no connection whose `client_hello` named its device id (or, for a page whose `client_hello` named none, no connection with the credential that subscribed), that has the capability the event requires, and whose prefs take the event: the decision a socket gets (`input`, the completion policy, manager mutes, quiet hours). So cards, finished turns, reply reminders, decisions and `POST /api/v1/notify` alerts; not an extension's own `hub.push_localized`, pairing receipts, hub updates or withdrawals (the page takes back what is over when it opens). The browser's service worker gets:

```json
{"v":1,"kind":"interaction","title":"Needs your permission","subtitle":"Fix the login · Laptop","body":"Bash: npm test","machine_id":"laptop","session_id":"<id>","interaction_id":"<id>","quiet":true}
```

with `id` (an alert's), `todo_id` (a decision's) and `recording_id` when the event has them, written in the language it subscribed in, the texts shortened until it fits 3,993 bytes (one 4,096-byte record). `TTL: 1800` (what the notify ring keeps); `Urgency: high` for `interaction`, `reply` and `assistant`, else `normal`; `Topic` a hash of the notification's tag (`<machine>/<session>#needs` or `#finished`, `card:<id>#needs`, `todo:<id>`, `alert:<id>`), so pushes waiting at the push service replace each other as the notifications do; a notification with no tag (`notify_user`, a to-do reminder) has no `Topic`, so none replaces another. The VAPID `sub` claim names the project, never the user. A 429, 5xx or network error is tried again after 1 s and 4 s; 404 or 410 drops the subscription, and so does revoking the credential that made it. The push service sees ciphertext, its size and timing only.

### Client capabilities and heartbeat

Once the client sees that the server supports `client_hello`, it may send:

```json
{"type":"client_hello","device_id":"<device id>","platform":"web","version":"<version>","features":["endpoints"],"locale":"en","heartbeat":{"interval":240,"pong_timeout":15}}
```

`locale` is the resolved UI language (`zh-Hans` / `en` / `ja`, [i18n.md](i18n.md)), not "Match System". The hub uses it for the text of `notify`, `error` and the like on this connection. A `full`-role connection's value also decides the **user language** (Postgres `settings.user_locale`), used for assistant answers, injected messages, task notifications, bot replies, and pushes to devices without their own `locale`: the first device to report one sets it, and after that only a device reporting a different language than it did before changes it; another device connecting in its own language does not ([i18n.md](i18n.md), "Protocol: telling hub the language"). If no client has ever reported one, it's `zh-Hans`. Omitting `locale` changes neither. When the user changes the language (or the system language changes under Match System), send `client_hello` again right away (with the other fields as before; omitting `features` clears the capability set).

The web client's `device_id` is its notification device id (`web-<uuid>`): while a connection that named it is open, the hub pushes nothing to that browser's Web Push subscription ("Web Push (browsers)" above). This metadata is only recorded on the current connection and doesn't change the authenticated device identity or permissions. `build` currently accepts any JSON.

Each `client_hello` replaces the client's capability set, and omitting `features` clears it; don't substitute the server's capability list for the capabilities the client itself supports.

The seconds below are the negotiation bounds and timer settings in the code.

- Without negotiation, the hub sends WebSocket protocol pings every 20 seconds and waits 15 seconds for the protocol pong.
- `heartbeat.interval` is in whole seconds, first clamped to 10–900, then jittered downward only: a random integer in `0..min(interval-10, floor(interval/10))` is subtracted. It's drawn once per negotiation, and `client_hello_ack` returns the value actually used.
- `heartbeat.pong_timeout` is in whole seconds, clamped to 5–60; an omitted item keeps the previous or default value. An empty `heartbeat` object also marks it as negotiated; omitting the whole field keeps the previous negotiation state.
- The web client sends `heartbeat: {"pong_timeout": 45}` (no `interval`): the 15 s default is too tight for high-latency public links whose outbound path changes, and 45 s still sits under the page's own 70 s quiet limit.
- After the writer goroutine applies the new settings, it returns `{"type":"client_hello_ack","heartbeat":{"interval":<actual>,"pong_timeout":<actual>}}`. The client can send it again to renegotiate; even sending only metadata without heartbeat gets an ack with the current values.
- After negotiation it also tries to adjust TCP keepalive: Idle uses interval, Interval uses pong_timeout, Count is 3; this depends on whether the underlying connection supports it. A protocol pong timeout closes the connection. Only one protocol ping is outstanding at a time, and it doesn't block application-level replies.

Application-level probes use separate client-initiated JSON messages:

```json
{"type":"ping","id":"probe-1"}
{"type":"pong","id":"probe-1"}
```

The first is sent by the client, the second is the hub's reply, with `id` echoed as is. Check the server's `app_ping` capability first; it's independent of WebSocket protocol control-frame ping / pong, and neither replaces the other. The hub never sends JSON `ping` on its own and doesn't handle client JSON `pong`. A client that doesn't send `client_hello` doesn't receive the `endpoints` event or the negotiation ack.

New fields must be optional, and an existing key keeps its type; for example, `id` stays a string.

### Codex questions and approvals

Codex / compatible forks have no hooks in the terminal, so the node reads questions from the rollout itself (`request_user_input_async` / `request_user_input`) and approvals from the screen, turning them into ordinary
`question` / `permission` interactions with `agent: "codex" | "traex"`; permission cards also carry `reason` (the reason Codex gave) and `always_label` (what **Always Approve** would allow;
without this field there's no **Always Approve**). The answer format is the same as Claude's: `{"answers":…}`, `{"allow":true,"always":…}`, `{"allow":false,"message":"…"}`
(with `message`, the turn stops and the message is sent in as the next message). Answers are synchronous: the hub hands it to the node (`codex.answer`), and the node checks that the computer still shows this question / this approval
and that the TUI is back in a state where it can be answered, types the input, then confirms Codex accepted it before returning success; otherwise it returns 409 `input_draft` / `dialog_open` / `prompt_changed` (nothing typed),
and the card stays (except for `prompt_changed`).

### Permission cards that need filling in

A `permission` interaction can carry `fields: [{key,label,placeholder?,secret?,optional?}]`; the web fills in passwords with a secure input field and on approval sends
`{"allow":true,"values":{"password":"…"}}`. If a required field is missing, the hub rejects this approval and keeps the card; secret fields in the interaction history are recorded only as `<redacted>`,
and the raw values only go to the waiting tool. The list doesn't approve them directly.
Values for keys the card does not declare are dropped when it is answered. Everyone else told of the answer gets the redacted copy: the `interaction.resolved` / `interaction.ended`
events (the channels, the task feeds), and a second answer's `{"already":true,"resolution":…}`. Such an answer is never held for redelivery, and the hub's operation receipt for `resolve`
(`client_ops.digest`) covers the answer as the hub reads it (`proto.Resolution`, field names in any case) with each value replaced by its key, and one fixed body for a body that
is not an answer. Lark and plugin channels can only decline such a card. The assistant's `secret_run` card (`tool_name: "secret_run"`, one secret `password` field) is one of these: the web fills it in on the card itself. Only the assistant's tool
makes it: a card with `tool_name: "secret_run"` from a node (`interaction.create`, a Codex list) or from `fleet.ask` is refused.

### Commands waiting for input (`command_input`)

A command an Agent runs that stopped at a prompt (an Antigravity background task asking for a password, a token or a sign-in code) is a `permission` card that needs filling in, so the rules above apply: its
one field is secret and required, its value is recorded only as `<redacted>`, and no quick path answers it.

```json
{"id": "ci_…", "kind": "permission", "tool_name": "command_input", "tool_title": "Command input", "agent": "agy",
 "agent_label": "Antigravity", "summary": "A command is waiting for your input: Enter the authorization code:",
 "tool_input": {"command": "example-cli login", "task": "task-7", "prompt": "Enter the authorization code:",
                "output": "<up to 20 lines before the prompt>", "masked": true},
 "fields": [{"key": "input", "label": "Enter the authorization code:", "placeholder": "…", "secret": true}]}
```

- `tool_input`: `command` is what runs in the Agent's words (absent when unknown), `task` the engine's name for it, `prompt` the line it waits
  on and `output` the lines before it (escapes and blank lines removed, at most 2 KiB); `masked` says the prompt reads as secret, so the web hides the line
  while it is typed and offers Show. `summary` and the field's label and placeholder are in the owner's language (the manager rewrites them).
- Answers: `{"allow": true, "values": {"input": "<line>"}}` types the line and Enter into the command; `{"allow": false}` (Not now) and
  `{"dismiss": true}` type nothing, and the same prompt is not asked again. A line is one line of text: no line break or other control
  character, at most 4096 bytes. The answer is synchronous, as a Codex card's: the manager hands it to the node (`codex.answer`), and the hub
  answers the client only once the node typed it or refused. Refusals keep the card and come in the owner's language: `prompt_changed` (the
  command no longer waits on that prompt: the card ends), `command_input_line`, `command_input_unreachable` and `command_input_refused`
  (nothing typed), `command_input_unconfirmed` (the line went out and the computer did not confirm it: look before sending it again).
- Only a node's card list (`codex.interactions`) makes one, in this shape (`proto.IsCommandInputCard`): a card with `tool_name: "command_input"`
  from `interaction.create` (a hook, a runtime, a daemon) or from `fleet.ask` is refused, as the password card's is, and so is a listed card
  in another shape. A command-input card is not the Agent's own screen: a screen card of the same session stays beside it.
- The web draws any permission card with fields as a form (summary, the field, Deny / Fill In & Allow), so it answers it as it is.

### Secret hand-off cards (`secret_handoff`)

A `permission` interaction with `tool_name: "secret_handoff"` asks to hand secret values to one Agent run as environment variables
. Its `tool_input` is `{"variables":[{"name","provider","provider_name"?,"title"?}],"agent"?,"machine_name"?,"cwd"?,"prompt"?}`
(the item as its provider describes it, its detail on one line of at most 40 characters; never a reference or a value). Its `summary` (also the push's text and the "Needs you" row's title) leads with the Agent and how many secrets it asks for, and says "an Agent" when the Agent has no name yet; the items are on the card only. Only the manager's Agent start makes it: a card with that tool
name from a node or from `fleet.ask` is refused. Only a `full` device approves it, by a `resolve` request that itself carries
`X-Persona-Features: secret_handoff`; a client sends that header on the card's own approve request only (not from a notification), and the feature in `client_hello` does not count. Any other approval of such a card
(an extension's token, the hub's own token, a request without the feature) gets 403
`{"code":"secret_handoff_elsewhere"}` with a localized message saying where to approve, the card stays pending, and the refusal is recorded in each
provider's audit log. A plain no (`{"allow":false}`, with or without `message`; `{"dismiss":true}`; `{"cancel":true}`; nothing else set)
goes through from any client. `…/choose` answers 400 `not_choosable`.

### Terminal dialogs (screen interactions)

When an Agent is blocked without a hook interaction, the hub reads the screen once (`session.screen`, 40 lines) and builds a `screen` card:

- The node reads those 40 plain rows the same way for the card and for its answer (`node/hosts.go` `dialogScreen`). When herdr can't send them whole (a wide pane full of CJK text is past 8 KB in 30 plain rows),
  both take the most bottom rows that fit (30, 24, 16, 12), and a dialog is read from them only when they show it whole, from the rule that opens it (`screen.DialogWhole`).
  Then it is the dialog a whole screen shows, with the same `rev` whatever rows fit at the card and at the answer. A dialog taller than those rows stays unreadable as before:
  no card, and an answer presses nothing, since part of it (a permission's command) would be neither shown nor in `rev`.

- When it's built: for Claude Code without Persona hooks (started from the user's own profile), it reads the screen and builds the card as soon as it's blocked; for sessions with hooks (that sent a hook event since this hub started,
  or that Persona started), it first waits 1.5 s so the hook's own card arrives first (3 s for Codex / compatible forks). If the hook's card arrives late, it still replaces the screen card.
  A hook card answered with an allow that Claude doesn't take (its own safety checks) leaves the dialog on screen: node then lists the
  session as blocked by it (`docs/protocol/agent-states.md`, "An allow Claude did not take"), and the screen card follows the same way.
- After a screen card is answered, the hub looks at the screen again every 250 ms for up to 2 s: when the Agent asks again right away (the next AskUserQuestion question, the next permission), herdr may stay blocked
  with no state change, and this check is what builds a card for the new dialog; if it still sees the one just answered (the keys haven't landed yet) or no dialog, it keeps looking, and stops once the Agent is no longer blocked or another card exists.
- The hub parses the dialog with `server/internal/screen` and puts it into `interaction.dialog`: `header`, `question`, `detail`,
  `options[{key,label,detail,kind,keys}]` (`kind`: `type_something` / `chat` / empty), `rev` (a hash of the question and options, excluding the cursor and spinner).
  Numbered options are chosen by number; unnumbered lists like Claude 2.1.312's trust-folder prompt are computed as `up/down` + `enter` from the cursor. The card id includes `rev`: a changed dialog is a new card,
  and what was selected on the previous card doesn't carry over.
- A client's answer carries `option` (plus `text` for `type_something`) instead of guessing keys itself; the hub passes `rev` and `option` to the node's `session.keys`,
  and the node **re-reads the screen, re-parses and compares `rev` before pressing any key**; if they differ it presses nothing and returns 409 `{"code":"prompt_changed"}`, and the hub then builds a new card from the current screen.
  The keys are also computed on the node from the screen at that moment (so it won't pick the wrong thing if the cursor was moved on the computer).
- Compatibility: a client that doesn't know `dialog` parses `screen` and sends `keys` itself; the hub adds `rev` to those too and checks it the same way; a node that doesn't know `rev` / `option`
  gets the computed `keys` from the hub. Cards where no dialog was parsed (only the terminal and the key bar) aren't checked.
- Screen card answers are synchronous: the hub waits until the node has pressed the keys before replying to the client.
- `rev` hashes the header, what is asked and each option's label and detail with all white space and ANSI escapes left out, so the same dialog redrawn at another pane width (the web viewing the pane resizes it) keeps its `rev`.
  The card takes the `rev` the node will check: `session.screen` with `lines` 40 (plain, visible) also returns `dialog_rev`, the node's own parse of that screen, so a hub and a node of different builds still agree.
  A node that returns no `dialog_rev` gets the legacy formula (`LegacyRev`, which keeps the wrapped rows), and a node also accepts that one.
  A `prompt_changed` refusal's data carries `rev` (the card's) and, when a dialog is on screen, `seen_rev`, `seen_question` and `seen_options`. The node logs the same with the pane the answer read and the agent's pane (the one `session.screen` reads for the card), and the hub logs the refusal's data.
  The card the hub makes after a `prompt_changed` is named by the node's `dialog_rev` too, so a dialog the node reads differently gets a new card rather than the old id again.
- **A permission prompt for a shell command** (Claude Code's "Bash command", its description, the command between dashed rules `╌╌╌`, a boxed warning, a countdown): `dialog` also carries
  `command` (the command, its wrapped rows joined back where the screen shows they were wrapped), `description` (the agent's words for it), `warning` (the boxed note as Claude Code words it),
  `risk` (what the warning is about, for clients to say in plain words: `delete` for "Dangerous rm operation …"; empty for any other warning, shown as it is),
  `deadline` (the countdown sentence as on screen), `deadline_action` (`deny` when it blocks the request, `allow` when it lets it through) and `deadline_at` (RFC 3339, when it runs out by the hub's clock at the read).
  `detail` still holds "Bash command", the description and the command, for clients that don't read `command`. The command is in `rev`; the warning and the countdown are not, so the card stays answerable while the clock runs.
  The countdown is read as one sentence across the two or three rows a narrow pane wraps it onto, so its seconds never change `rev`.
  Claude Code 2.1.322 draws a `│` before each row of the command, as before the warning; the rows between the dashed rules are the command whatever they start with.
- **Multi-select** (AskUserQuestion `multiSelect` in Claude Code 2.1.316): `dialog` also carries
  `multi: true`, `submit` (`Submit`, or `Next` when more questions follow), and options also carry `checked` (already checked on the computer) and `text` (what's already typed in the free-answer box);
  with several questions, `steps[{label,done}]` is the tab bar at the top; the confirmation page before submitting is `review: true` (`incomplete: true`: some questions unanswered), with options "Submit answers / Cancel".
  `checked`, the cursor, typed text and tab checkmarks don't go into `rev`.
  A client's answer carries `options` (the keys of options to check; unlisted ones get unchecked) and `text` (the free answer; empty means don't check it). The hub passes it to the node's `session.keys`
  (`multi: true`, `options`, `free_text`), and the node presses one key at a time, re-reading the screen after each, and finally presses Submit / Next; on the confirmation page, if all questions are answered it presses "Submit answers" too.
  A single `option` sent for a multi-select card is treated as checking just that one.
- Passwords: when the last line on the screen is a password prompt (`[sudo] password for …:`, `Password:`, an ssh passphrase, the passwd, mysql/psql, ssh-keygen, ansible-vault and openssl/keytool prompts…; the rules are deliberately narrow, and the word password in body text doesn't count), the card carries
  `secret: true` and the client uses a password field (not saved to drafts). Password or not, `text` in terminal card answers is always stored as `<redacted>` in the database;
  the terminal panel's key endpoint (`/keys`) isn't stored at all, and the hub's request log only records the path and status code.

### Session deltas (`sessions_delta`)

- When connecting the WebSocket, a client adds `?features=sessions_delta` to the URL. If the hub has the capability (`sessions_delta` in `hello.features`), it:
  1. On connect, sends one full `sessions` list per machine as a snapshot, **without Codex history sessions** (`source_kind: codex_history`; clients get them from `GET /api/v1/sessions`);
  2. After that only sends `{"type":"sessions_delta","machine_id","upsert":[Session…],"remove":[session_id…]}`: new or changed sessions (the whole object, not half of it) and the ids that are gone;
     nothing is sent if nothing changed. Codex history sessions only appear in deltas if the client already has them (a live Codex session ends and the same id becomes history).
- The hub tracks, per connection, every session of every machine each client holds (`client.have`); snapshots and deltas are computed and queued under the same lock, so a delta is always computed against what the client really has.
- Reconnecting after a disconnect means a new snapshot, which fills in any missed changes.
- Compatibility: a client that doesn't send `features` gets full lists (identical ones not sent); a hub without `sessions_delta` in `hello.features` sends full lists, and the client handles them as full lists.
- The web (`web/src/lib/sessions-delta.ts`): a snapshot replaces this machine's list but keeps the existing Codex history; `wsQuery` adds `features=sessions_delta` on every connection, `store.ts` merges by `upsert` / `remove`, and `refresh()`, while connected to a delta-capable hub, only takes Codex history from `GET /api/v1/sessions`, replacing existing history with the copies in the response (pushes don't carry history, so seen / went offline can only be updated from here).

### Bounded Agents lists (`sessions_list`)

**Choose the right collection.** Claude Code, Codex (including history), terminal-host and contributed-runtime sessions use **`GET /api/v1/sessions`** and snake_case `Session` rows, identified by `(machine_id, session_id)`. **`GET /api/v1/agents` is source/setup status**, not those sessions. Extension personal-agent conversations use **`GET /api/v1/agents/sessions`**, camelCase rows and the opaque `id` (`<source>:<sessionKey>`). The two collections are not combined or renamed.

#### Opt-in parameters (both session collections)

Any of `limit`, `cursor`, `since`, `summary`, `state`, `project`, `group`, or `counts` opts into the bounded API. `pane_source`, `roots`, `parent_session_id`, `place`, `space`, `catalog`, `todo`, `waiting`, `exclude_pane_source` and `include_hidden` also opt in, but are supported only by the runtime collection (see below). Without them the legacy request shape remains unchanged: runtime `machine_id` filtering still returns the complete list; personal-agent `source`/`provider` filtering still returns the complete list; personal-agent `q` alone still searches messages and returns `items`. The runtime collection's legacy answer carries the same bounded rows a `summary` page does (cut text, task arrays only as counts); a row's whole chat detail is in `GET /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/info`.

| Parameter | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `limit` | Integer 1–200, default **50**. Full and delta pages both use it. A delta removal consumes one slot, just like an upsert. |
| `cursor` | Opaque `next_cursor` from a preceding page. URL-encode it and repeat all original filters, `summary` and `since`; `limit` may change. Empty/invalid cursor is rejected, not treated as a first page. |
| `include_hidden` | `1`/`true` includes directory-hidden runtime rows for temporary user inspection; default false. Applies before rows, totals, counts, catalog and search, binds cursors and deltas, and never changes saved rules or Assistant observations. |
| `summary` | `1`/`true` for list-row summaries, `0`/`false` for complete rows; default false. Does not change row identity or filter membership. |
| `state` | Exact unified state: `needs_you`, `working`, `unread`, `idle`, `offline`, or `unknown`. Omit for all states. No user-specific mute/pin ordering is implied. |
| `machine_id` | Exact runtime machine id. Personal-agent sources do not expose a machine, so this filter matches no personal-agent rows. |
| `project` | Exact runtime `repo_root`, falling back to `workspace_cwd`, then `cwd`. This is the node's supplied path, **not** a guessed repository. Personal-agent rows have no project. |
| `group` | Runtime `space_id`, falling back to `workspace_id`; personal-agent `accountId`. Machine-local space ids can overlap: use `machine_id` with `group` when expanding a particular computer's group. This does not represent personal-agent custom preference sections or to-do group ids. |
| `source` | Runtime `source_kind` or personal-agent contribution id; unchanged transport/source semantics, never a pane origin. |
| `pane_source` | Runtime only: exactly `terminal`, `feishu`, `desktop`, or `unknown`. Requires the independently advertised `sessions_pane_source` capability. See pane/host origins below. |
| `roots` | Runtime only: `1`/`true` leaves the child sessions folded under a listed parent out of the rows, `total` and every count, and filters and counts the others by their folded state; `0`/`false` is the same as no key. Requires the independently advertised `sessions_hierarchy` capability. See "Session hierarchy" below. |
| `parent_session_id` | Runtime only: a session id, with `machine_id` (400 `invalid_query` without it, when empty, or with `roots=1`): only the sessions folded under that session, all depths. Requires `sessions_hierarchy`. See "Session hierarchy" below. |
| `place` | Runtime only, repeatable (1 to 64 values): each value is a JSON array `["<machine_id>","<project>"]`, and the sessions at any of those directories are selected: one project's checkouts across computers; an empty project selects that computer's sessions in no directory. Requires the independently advertised `sessions_catalog` capability. See "Projects and spaces" below. |
| `space` | Runtime only, repeatable (1 to 64 values): each value is a JSON array `["<machine_id>","<group>"]`, and the sessions in any of those computers' spaces are selected; an empty group selects that computer's sessions in no space. Requires `sessions_catalog`. See "Projects and spaces" below. |
| `agents_only` | Runtime only: `1`/`true` excludes assistant and track conversations from the list, totals, counts and catalog. Requires `sessions_agents_only`. See "Agents-only sessions" below. |
| `catalog` | Runtime only: `1`/`true` returns the filtered list's projects and spaces instead of rows; `0`/`false` selects a normal page. Requires `sessions_catalog`. See "Projects and spaces" below. |
| `todo` | Runtime only: a to-do id selects the sessions on that open to-do (`Session.todo.id`); `none` selects the sessions on no open to-do (a done to-do's included). Empty or repeated: 400 `invalid_query`. Requires the independently advertised `sessions_todo` capability. See "Sessions by to-do" below. |
| `waiting` | `1`/`true`: only the sessions that only wait in the background (`Session.background_waiting`, by the folded state with `roots=1`); `0`/`false`: the others. With `state=working`, the two halves of the working sessions. Requires `sessions_quick_filters`. See "Quick filters" below. |
| `just_finished` | `1`/`true`: only the Just finished sessions (`work.just_finished`, by the folded state with `roots=1`: a parent showing its children's work is not one); `0`/`false`: the others. With `state=idle`, the web's Just finished and Seen sections. Requires `sessions_just_finished`. See "Just finished rows" below. |
| `exclude_pane_source` | Runtime only: one of the `pane_source` origins; the sessions of that origin are left out of the rows, `total` and every count. Empty, repeated or unknown: 400 `invalid_query`. Requires `sessions_quick_filters`. See "Quick filters" below. |
| `manager` | Runtime only: a manager's id; only the sessions on its computers. Requires the independently advertised `sessions_manager` capability, and does not opt into the bounded API by itself. See "One manager's sessions" below. |
| `provider` | Runtime `agent` or personal-agent `provider`, exact and case-sensitive. Runtime accepts one value. A paged personal-agent request may repeat it for OR-set matching only with `agents_provider_or`; see "Personal-agent provider OR sets". Empty values on older runtime nodes stay empty; no agent name is guessed. |
| `q` | Case-insensitive substring, at most 256 Unicode characters. Runtime title, cwd, repository, branch, space/slot/agent names and last preview; personal-agent title/provider/account id. With an opt-in parameter this is **row search**, never remote transcript/message search. |
| `search` | Runtime only, opt-in ranked search, 1–1,024 UTF-8 bytes. Requires `sessions_search`; separate from legacy `q`. See "Ranked runtime search" below. |
| `counts` | `1`/`true` returns aggregates instead of rows. `0`/`false` selects a normal page. The same filters apply. With `roots=1`, current hubs include `active_agents_by_machine` in standalone and inline counts. It counts roots whose folded state is not offline and excludes Assistant conversations. An absent machine in the map has zero matching Agents. An absent map means the count is unavailable. |
| `since` | Opaque `revision` from the completed baseline/previous delta. Returns only changed rows and removals, including state/title-only changes when `updated_at` did not advance. Keep the same filters; changing a filter requires a new first-page baseline. |

Repeated recognized parameters that are not explicitly documented as repeatable, malformed booleans/page sizes/states and malformed tokens return HTTP **400** with `code: "invalid_query"`. Unknown parameters are ignored for compatibility. Responses retain the usual localized `error` field.

#### Page and ordering

```http
GET /api/v1/sessions?summary=1&limit=50
GET /api/v1/agents/sessions?summary=1&limit=50&source=demo
```

```json
{
  "sessions": [],
  "remove": [],
  "has_more": true,
  "next_cursor": "<opaque cursor>",
  "revision": "<opaque checkpoint>",
  "total": 8000
}
```

`total` is the number of matching sessions in the **whole collection**, not the page length or number of changes. Empty arrays are `[]`, not null. `next_cursor` is absent on the final page.

- Order: newest `updated_at` first for runtime rows, newest `rankTimeMs` first for personal-agent rows, then composite identity ascending for ties. This is a latest-update timeline, not the clients' state-rank/pin sort.
- A cursor traverses a **frozen filtered snapshot**: updates, deletions and inserts while scrolling cannot duplicate, omit or reorder rows in that snapshot. Every page returns its snapshot's same `revision` and `total`.
- Snapshot retention is five minutes, with at most 32 active views per collection. A restart, expiry or eviction returns HTTP **409**, `code: "cursor_expired"`; restart at page one. Cursors bind filters and summary mode; a mismatched/tampered cursor returns 400.
- The runtime collection includes Codex history. It uses the manager's already-decorated state, ownership, hidden/deleted-session rules and task metadata; it does not recompute business state in the hub.

#### Personal-agent provider OR sets (`agents_provider_or`)

When `hello.features` advertises **`agents_provider_or`**, a client may repeat the existing `provider` key on an already paged personal-agent request:

```http
GET /api/v1/agents/sessions?summary=1&limit=50&provider=provider-a&provider=provider-b
GET /api/v1/agents/sessions?counts=1&provider=provider-a&provider=provider-b
```

One to 64 supplied values form an **OR** set: a row matches when its `provider` exactly equals any member, case-sensitive, and that set combines by **AND** with every other filter. Set order and duplicate values have no semantic effect. The limit applies before duplicate canonicalization, so 64 copies are valid but 65 are not. A single nonempty value keeps the existing exact-match behavior. The legacy single-empty `provider=` remains unfiltered; an empty member of a multi-value set, a zero-length value list or more than 64 supplied values returns **400 `invalid_query`**. No value is trimmed, case-folded, comma-split or silently discarded.

Pages, full-set `total` and counts, and `since` deltas all use that same membership. The canonical set binds the frozen cursor: reordered or duplicated spellings of the same set may continue it, while adding, removing, replacing or omitting the set returns 400. A provider edit upserts a row that enters the set and removes one that leaves it; counts describe the complete matching set at the same revision, never only the loaded page.

`provider` alone does **not** opt into paging. Without another paged parameter, the personal-agent endpoint keeps its legacy complete-list envelope and first-value behavior, including an unpaged repeated key. The runtime collection keeps its singleton behavior and rejects repeated `provider` on a paged request. Old hubs can reject a paged repeated key or use only its first value on the legacy route, so clients must gate this contract on `agents_provider_or` and retain the legacy full-list fallback, applying their own complete-set OR filtering there.

#### Ranked runtime search (`sessions_search`)

The runtime collection advertises `sessions_search` independently. It searches the hub's already-indexed Agent
metadata and latest available text, including unloaded historical sessions. It does not fetch transcripts, call models,
search every past message, or search the separate personal-agent collection. Assistant conversations are excluded:
the existing `assistant_search` contract owns them. Older hubs can ignore unknown parameters, so clients must gate
on the capability and require `search_hits` in a successful response before calling the result complete.

```http
GET /api/v1/sessions?search=machine%3Astudio%20parser&summary=1&roots=1&limit=40
```

`search` accepts one nonempty, valid UTF-8 query of at most 1,024 bytes. The page size defaults to 40, with a maximum
of 100; `q`, `since`, `counts`, `with_counts`, `catalog` and exact `session_id` lookup cannot be combined with it,
even when those parameters are empty or false. Existing filtering and permission constraints still apply. Legacy
`q` remains a contiguous substring and existing list/delta ordering is unchanged.

The normal page fields are retained, with `search_hits` always present (an empty object for no matches). Its keys
are the same JSON-encoded `[machine_id, session_id]` tuples used by runtime removals. Each value is
`{score, evidence?: {role, before, match, after}}`; `role` is `user`, `agent`, `error` or `title`. Evidence contains a
bounded fragment of actual indexed text, not model-generated explanation. Its match may fall after the summary's
truncated title or preview, so a client must not discard the row by matching the compact summary again. The map
contains only identities in the returned page, not other matches or inaccessible sessions.

All whitespace-separated terms must match the same session, though different terms may match different fields.
Explicit operators use case-insensitive substring values except exact states; values within a dimension are OR,
dimensions and remaining words are AND. Unknown operators/values remain literal terms. Plain words never silently
become filters. Supported spellings follow the existing web matcher:

| Dimension | Operators |
| --- | --- |
| Computer ID/display name | `machine:`, `host:` |
| Project name/folder | `project:`, `repo:`, `cwd:`, `path:` |
| Agent runtime ID/name | `harness:`, `agent:`, `launcher:` |
| Model | `model:` |
| Unified state | `state:`, `status:`, `is:<state>`; `is:unknown` remains literal |
| Pinned session | `is:pinned`, `is:pin`; workspace pins do not imply session pins |
| Error or attention | `is:error`, `is:errors`, `is:failed`, `is:blocked` |
| Recent update | `since:`, `after:`, `updated:` with `24h`, `7d`, `30d` and existing aliases |

Time aliases retain current client behavior: `1d`, `2d`, `48h` select the 24-hour bucket; `1w` selects seven days and
`1m` thirty days. The last recognized time operator wins. This search's time window is unrelated to the legacy
`since` delta checkpoint. The shared corpus under `spec/fixtures/session-search/` checks client/server behavior.

Global ranking is title prefix 100, title substring 80, all terms in title/project/computer/space/tab/folder 60,
other indexed metadata/latest text 40, and operators-only 30. Add 5 unless the displayed state is offline. Sort by
score descending, then update time descending and composite identity ascending. This happens before paging, not
by sorting each newest-first page in the browser. `roots=1` preserves existing child-folding and folded-state rules.
With `roots=1` a hit in a side session folded under a listed row (`folded_as: "side"`) comes back as that row,
filtered and ranked by its folded state, with **`hit_session_id`** in its `search_hits` value naming the side and the
evidence the side's own text: a client opens the row's chat with that side shown at the hit. The row is listed once:
by its best hit, its own on a tie, else the side whose id comes first. Other rows folded under it (children, workers,
a side's own children) are not searched as it; without `roots=1` every row answers for itself and carries no
`hit_session_id`.

The first page freezes its ranking, evidence, membership, machine-name/pin/attention context and time cutoff.
Continuations repeat the same query and filters but use that frozen result. Normal five-minute/32-view cursor limits
