The machine list says why in `node_incompatible`: `node_protocol_old` (update the node) or `node_protocol_new` (the node needs a newer manager).
- Optional features check capabilities, not builds: a nonempty `service_tier` on a new conversation's `assistant.send` needs `assistant_service_tier` (the manager answers `node_outdated` before any thread or turn starts; an omitted tier keeps the old behavior); `fast` or `ultrafast` `speed` on `session.start` / `session.start.work` needs `session_start_speed` (the same `node_outdated`; omitted and `standard` keep the old behavior); a model on `assistant.send` / `assistant.warm` / `session.start` / `session.send` needs `model_configuration`; `"ultracode":true` on `session.start` needs `ultracode` (a node from before the handshake has none; `false` asks for nothing and is never refused); a non-empty `goal` on `session.start` needs `start_goal` (the hub answers `409 start_goal_unsupported` before anything starts, and the start goes on without the goal); `resume_outside_health` on `session.start` needs `resume_outside_health` (the hub sends it only to a node it saw announce it, and the manager answers `node_outdated` if the node it reaches does not, a node from before the handshake or a test's included: an older node would resume unchecked); `deny_dirs` on `assistant.prepare` (`[{dir, track}]`: the track directories, relative to the home as `dir`, that the assistant's other conversations' Read and Edit are denied, in addition to every manager's track the node finds itself; the node also tells a conversation in one of them as that track's, `Session.Space`, since a track's directory is data and never told from its path; a later list for the same prepared directory replaces the earlier one, and a conversation in a listed track is never denied its own) is read only by a node with `deny_dirs_v1`, and an older node ignores it (it knows a track only, so no conversation of another track is started on it); `space` on `assistant.prepare` (`{slug, initial_space_md}`: the directory is that track's own, `tracks/<slug>`; the node makes `inbox/`, `recordings/` and `.space/history/` there, all 0700, writes `SPACE.md` from `initial_space_md` only when there is none, and writes `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` as `claude_md` followed by the `SPACE.md` it reads, only when they change; it answers `space_md_digest`) needs `track_spaces_v1` (the manager answers that the node needs an update before anything is written, and the hub refuses it with `node_outdated` for a node that does not announce it); `track_kind` on `assistant.prepare` (the kind of the directory's track: `orchestration` for the assistant's own, which the node gives the directory's processes as `PERSONA_TRACK_KIND`; a value that is not a kind's slug is dropped) needs no capability: an older node ignores it and its processes get none; `assistant.space_recording` (`{dir, slug, name, content?, remove?}`: a recording's transcript written into, or removed from, the `recordings/` of the track directory `dir`, which must be `slug`'s; `name` is `<YYYY-MM-DD>-<uuid>.md` only; written atomically, 0600, never through a link) needs `track_recordings_v1` (the manager saves no recording into a track before it, answering `409 node_outdated`); `assistant.track_inbox_write` (`{dir, slug, name, content}` → `{path}`: one quick capture written as `inbox/<name>` in that track's own directory, a real folder, the name a plain `.md` file name, the file written new and renamed into place, never through a link; the same bytes again succeed, other bytes under the same name are refused) is asked only of a node that announces `track_inbox_v1` (without it the capture waits in the list); `assistant.space_md` (`{op, dir, slug, state?}` → `{content, digest, state, refused?}`: `op` is `put_state` (only the text between the state markers, at most 2048 bytes and no marker; every other byte stays); `dir` must be track `slug`'s own directory; SPACE.md is read without following a link, at most 64 KB, written atomically after the file it replaces is kept in `.space/history/SPACE-<UTC time>.md`, the latest 20 kept; a write is refused with `refused` `managed`, `too_large`, `no_state_block` or `missing`, and nothing written) needs `track_space_md_v1` (the manager asks only a node that announces it, and the hub refuses it with `node_outdated` for one that does not); `clipboard.get` / `clipboard.set` need `clipboard` (`node.info`'s `clipboard: {supported, reason?}` says whether a clipboard is reachable there); an update over the node RPC needs `node_update` (and `node_update` in `node.info` saying it can run now), and with `node_update_idle` the manager waits until `sessions.list` answers `update_busy: false`, for every Agent to be idle without it or when the field is missing; `secret.run` needs `secret_run` (without it the manager answers `node_outdated` before the card is shown); `secret.stage` and a `session.start` with `secret_ticket` need `secret_env` (the same `node_outdated`: an older node would start the Agent without the values); `launcher` on `session.modes` needs `launcher_switch` (the hub answers `node_outdated`: an older node would drop it and switch only the model); `switch_now` on `session.send` needs `launcher_switch_now` (the same `node_outdated`: an older node would type the message on the old launcher and leave the switch waiting); `session.switch` needs `launcher_switch_idle` (the same `node_outdated`); a launcher of the other engine there is taken as a switch to that engine by a node with `engine_switch` only (one without refuses it with a `switch_*` code); `model.http` needs `model_http` and `model.run` needs `model_run` (the same `node_outdated`); `machine.diagnose` and `machine.cleanup` need `machine_diagnose` (the manager answers `node_outdated` before asking); `start.continue` needs `start_continue` (the same); `start.answer` needs `start_answer` (the same); `assistant_turn` on `launchers.check` goes to every node, which honors `model` either way, but only a node with `launcher_check_assistant_turn` runs the check as the turn and says so in its answer (`assistant_turn: true`), and on a Claude Code launcher the node runs itself only such a pass clears the main chat's own failed turn (a launcher of another agent, or a runtime's, gets the plain check, whose pass counts); the readiness step for a `tool_search_unsupported` turn says Persona sends every tool to that gateway only for a node with `assistant_tool_search_fallback` (it resends such a turn once with every tool loaded and starts that launcher and model so from then on), plain retry words for any other.
- **Ordinary Agent skills.** `session_skills_v1` adds `session.skills` and validated explicit skill selections to ordinary `session.send`. Managers refuse selections with `skill_unavailable` and `delivered:none` on older nodes, while ordinary text keeps working. Catalogs are partial when local adapters cannot enumerate every source.
- **Assistant profiles.** `assistant_config_dir` adds explicit `config_dir` to `assistant.send`, `assistant.warm` and headless `session.send`. The manager refuses a nonempty selection with `node_outdated` on a node without it, including pre-handshake nodes, before any process starts. Omission keeps an old node's behavior; there is no protocol-version bump. A new node preserves old conversation profiles by saved metadata or actual transcript discovery.
- **Scheduled prompt references.** The hub advertises `task_input` for the Web prompt editor. A leading file context carries `path`, `machine`, `cwd`, `launcher` and `runtime`. Skills retain their opaque `ref`. Nodes advertise `task_input` for content validation and file-reference delivery. The task picker requests `task_input=1` on the existing file-list endpoint so the node confines listings to the selected physical working directory.
- **Scheduled execution.** Node capability `task_execution` adds `assistant.directory` and strict `task_execution:true` on `assistant.send`. The manager refuses either on an older node before dispatch (`node_outdated`). During a scheduled run, that definite pre-delivery refusal waits up to `assistant.task_execution_wait_seconds` (default 600) for the capability, then records `task_execution_wait_timeout` wrapping definite non-delivery. Only attested inherited ordinary tasks may omit the capability earlier; actual omission is recorded as `compatibility_fallback: "legacy_task_execution"`. The node validates `cwd`, prevents resuming another directory/launcher, and permits same-model transient recovery only.
- **Assistant supervision instructions.** `assistant_supervision_instructions` adds manager-owned `supervision_instructions` to `assistant.send`, `assistant.warm` and headless `session.send`, and to `assistant.model` / send-parameter resolution. A nonempty policy is refused with `node_outdated` before dispatch to an older or pre-handshake node; ordinary messages with an empty policy remain compatible. New nodes apply the exact policy as Claude system instructions or Codex developer instructions, include it in the execution fingerprint and honor explicit empty metadata as role removal. The shared directory is never rewritten per role. The protocol version is unchanged.
- **Agent start speed.** `session_start_speed` adds `speed` to `session.start` and `session.start.work` for a new terminal Codex or Claude Code Agent. Codex validates the selected model's advertised tier; Claude Code writes one merged per-start settings file. Faster speed on any resume, another launcher or a runtime is refused. A manager returns `node_outdated` for `fast` or `ultrafast` on a node without the capability, including pre-handshake nodes; omitted and `standard` keep the old behavior. See "Agent start speed".
- **Assistant start speed.** `assistant_service_tier` adds `service_tier` to a new conversation's `assistant.send`. The node consumes it only for a new Codex conversation, waits for `thread/settings/update` to acknowledge the advertised native tier before the first `turn/start`, and leaves effort independent. It rejects the field on an existing session or a non-Codex runtime. The one-shot request is not retained in process state, execution fingerprints, warm starts or recovery; later speed changes still use `session.speed`. A manager refuses a nonempty value with `node_outdated` on a node without the capability, including pre-handshake nodes. Omission and the protocol version are unchanged.
- **MCP nested wait correlation.** `mcp_wait_v1` in `node.info.capabilities` means the target node preserves a valid `call_id` from `computer.call` into a nested `computer.elicit`. The manager sends that id only to a target advertising the capability with a nonzero protocol version. While an older target owns the RPC, the manager publishes `unknown`, then restores the previous live state; it never mistakes that target's silent elicitation path for `computer`.
- **External model inventory.** `external_launcher_inventory_v1` is announced only while the node has an enabled, trusted local adapter registration; it is not a required or permanently announced capability. The internal `devices.list` entry exposes `external_inventory:true` only for a protocol-aware node advertising it. Managers use `launchers.list {source:"external",refresh:true}` for this source without starting shell discovery, do not probe unconfigured/older nodes, and merge only that source's entries into the retained per-machine catalog. The flag permits discovery, not arbitrary commands or conversation execution; explicit main-chat scope and local registry checks remain required.
- **Lanes.** `node_lanes_v1` says the node frames its connection when the manager asks (`rpc.lanes`, "Lanes" under "hub ↔ node RPC"). The manager asks right after `node.info`, and only a node that announced it; a node from before the handshake never has it. Without it, or on a refusal, the connection stays JSON lines; the protocol floor is unchanged.
- **Backward compatibility.** A node from before the handshake leaves the three fields out (protocol 0): the manager drives it as before and reads the old `node.info` flags (`model_configuration`, `node_update`) for what it can do. A manager from before the handshake ignores the fields, and new nodes keep sending the old flags for it.
- **Resident reload handover.** `node.restarting` is an optional node-to-manager announcement. The resident drains admitted RPC replies and idle
  assistant processes before closing the current connection, and hands its attach listener/run lock through exec. The manager suspends new outbound calls and
  uses the following `state.load {restart_barrier:true}` request as a fence: `{restart_ready:true}` means every earlier registered call's reply arrived.
  `state.load {restart_barrier:false}` cancels that preparation and resumes calls. A manager from before the flag treats either as an ordinary read, so the
  protocol floor is unchanged. `node_restarting` means the operation was refused before execution and may retry; an unsent suspended call may retry too,
  but `rpc.ErrDropped` remains an ambiguous result and is never automatically replayed. Initial engine/node.info handshakes interrupted by exec retry within
  their existing bounded budget. A failed control exchange closes its physical peer, so a late announcement cannot leave a live manager suspended; an already
  published reply wins over a later connection closure. `node-update-check` adds optional `resident_handover: true`; resident uploads and ordinary reloads
  require it before installing or draining a replacement. Startup rollback to a legacy image releases, rather than inherits, the listener/run lock.
  This resident reload path retains the existing five-second reconnect grace; it is separate from slot blue-green promotion.
- **Node update preflight failures.** The optional node-to-manager `node.update.preflight_failed` event
  carries `{id, error}` after a committed upload fails the installed executable's resident reload check. The manager
  fails the deploy waiting on that transaction ID with the supplied error. Older managers ignore the event, while
  older nodes omit it and keep the existing confirmation flow. Local rollback and the protocol floor are unchanged.
- **Builds.** The build string (`version`, `node_version` in the machine list) does not decide compatibility. It is the upgrade policy: another build sets `node_mismatch` (the **Redeploy** offer), the hub's automatic redeploy after it updates itself (`devices.update_nodes`) and a deploy's wait for the node to come back on the hub's build. `node_protocol` in the machine list is the protocol the node announced (absent: from before the handshake).

## Engines

Each machine's node drives one "engine", that is, a set of terminal hosts: `herdr` (the classic herdr command line; the default, so existing machines are unaffected),
`herdr-core` (the runtime behind the Herdr desktop app, display name "Herdr App"), `orca` (the runtime of the Orca desktop app, display name "Orca"),
and `herdr-both` (display name "herdr + Herdr App"): the node **registers both herdr and herdr-core as hosts at the same time**, and sessions from both are shown merged.
This is for the case "use herdr locally, and have Herdr App connect remotely to the same machine". With a single choice the hosts are not used together: running them at once slows each other's refresh;
side by side, refreshes run in parallel and events are isolated per host, so they don't slow each other down (implementation in `node/engine.go`, `refreshHosts` in `node/placement.go`, `node/herdrevents.go`).

- The user picks per machine in the web app (at pairing, or Settings › Machines): `PUT /api/v1/machines/{mid}/engine`. The hub stores it in the Postgres settings, not in hub.json.
- **Host sets**: a computer can enable several hosts side by side, any subset of `herdr`, `herdr-core`, `orca`, `tern`, `rex`, `paseo`, `cindy` and `t3code` (or none at all),
  plus a **default host**: where sessions started or resumed from a client go (the empty set has no default). Each single engine above is a set:
  `herdr-both` is `{herdr, herdr-core}` with herdr the default.
  - `PUT` body: `{"hosts": ["herdr", "orca"], "default": "herdr"}`. Without `default`, the first host in the order herdr, herdr-core, orca, tern, rex, paseo, cindy, t3code;
    `"hosts": []` is the empty set. Older clients still send `{"engine": "herdr-core"}`, which stands for its set; a body with `hosts` is always a set.
    An unknown host, `herdr-both` as a member, or a default that is not enabled is a 400, and nothing is written.
  - **Storage**: the key `machine_engine_hosts` (machine id → `{hosts, default}`) is the choice. `machine_engines` (machine id → single engine) is written beside it
    with the single engine closest to the set (the host itself when there is one, `herdr-both` for herdr + herdr-core, else the default host, herdr for the empty set),
    so a rollback still finds the engine. A machine with only `machine_engines` reads as the set its engine stands for and is not
    rewritten; a machine in neither is `{herdr}`.
  - **Machine fields**: `engine` stays that single engine (older clients read it). `engine_hosts` and `engine_default` are the set and the default host (never null;
    `["herdr"]` when never chosen). `engine_suggested` (while online) is the set to preselect at pairing: the hosts the node reports available, herdr when none;
    a machine that already chose is never changed by it. `engine_sets_unsupported`: the node is online but too old for sets, and the chosen set is not one it can run
    as a single engine (herdr + Orca, say). It then runs `engine` alone, and clients say so until the node is updated.
  - **Choosing the host for a new session**: `POST /api/v1/sessions` (`session.start`) may carry `host`, one of the enabled hosts; without it, the default host.
    A host that is not enabled, or one that cannot start sessions, is refused with `engine_missing` and nothing starts. When the node is
    too old (its `node.info` has no `engine_hosts`) the hub answers `node_outdated` and does not send it: an older node would ignore `host` and start in its engine.
    Session rows carry `host` (the host they live in: the pane's kind, `paseo` for Paseo's) and `also_open_in` (the other hosts the same session is live in).
  - **`engine.use`** carries `{engine, hosts, default}`. Older nodes read only `engine`; newer ones report `engine_hosts` (the set they run) in `node.info`,
    which is how the hub knows they take sets. The empty set is sent as `"hosts": []`, never null.
- Every time the hub connects to a node, **the first call** is `engine.use` (before `node.info`), but only for machines with a stored choice. Machines never configured get nothing,
  so the node keeps using herdr and old nodes never receive a method they don't know. When the user changes it and the machine is online, it is sent right away; `engine.use` calls for the same machine are queued, and each sends the value stored at send time.
- After connecting, the node doesn't poll or subscribe to any engine's events until the engine is settled: it receives `engine.use`, or the hub skips it and calls `sessions.list` directly (never configured / old hub).
  It waits at most 3 seconds, then starts with herdr. So a machine set to herdr-core never flashes herdr sessions on connect, and never queries herdr.
- `engine` is the stored choice. If the node rejects `engine.use` (too old), the hub logs a line, the PUT still returns 200 and the choice stays stored; it takes effect once the node is updated.
- `engines` comes from `node.info`; each entry is `{id, name, available, version?, note?}`. herdr is available = it answers, or its socket file exists, or `herdr` is on PATH. herdr-core is available = its socket answers `hello`
  (a node using herdr asks herdr-core this only once, during `node.info`, and leaves it alone otherwise). `herdr-both` is available = both of the above are available (no version).
  Orca is available = `orca-runtime.json` exists, its socket answers `status.get`,
  and the protocol version is compatible (if incompatible, `available` is false, `note` is a one-sentence reason in Chinese for the user, and `version` is still included; also asked only once during `node.info`).
  Tern is available = `tern` is found and its session daemon answers `tern inspect`; its `version` is the binary's (`tern --version`), also while
  Tern is not running. Rex is available = `rex` is found and its server answers `rex --autostart=false api call server.status` (never starting one);
  its `version` is the binary's (`rex version`), also while Rex is not running.
  `version` is the version each reports; omitted if there is none. Old nodes only report the first two.
- **Named herdr sessions**: a node on the default herdr server also drives every running named herdr session (`herdr --session <name>`) as part of
  the `herdr` host. Their pane, tab and workspace ids (`pane_id`, `tab_id`, `workspace_id`, `space_id`, `slot_id`, panes and `pane:` addresses) are
  `@<session>:<id>`, the default server's stay bare; `host` and `space_kind` stay `herdr`, and the spaces are named `<session> · <label>`. Clients treat
  the ids as opaque.
- `home_real` in `node.info`: `home` with its links followed, sent only when that is another path (a home reached through a
  symlink). The hub hands it to the assistant with the machine (`devices.list`'s `home_real`), which compares a remembered kind's directory
  with a task's in either spelling. Old nodes, and homes that are no link, leave it out.
- `claude_plugin` in `node.info`: the Persona plugin for Claude Code on that computer as its resident node last checked it (`proto.ClaudePlugin`:
  `state`, `auto`, `version`, `bundled`, `claude_version`, `config_dirs`, `changed`, `error`, `checked_at`, `next_check`); the node also sends it as a
  `claude.plugin` notification whenever it changes, and the manager puts it on the machine as `claude_plugin`. Old nodes, and nodes that have not
  checked, send neither.
- `herdr_running` / `herdr_running_known` in `node.info`: whether the classic herdr server answers right now, and whether the node can tell (a machine using herdr-core
  has no such socket and sends neither). Old nodes send neither; the hub uses this to tell "not running" from "unknown".
- `builtin_programs` in `node.info`: the extension programs built into personad (`["cua", "ego", "imessage"]`; iMessage uses `connector.*` method names). For nodes that report it, the hub calls them via `plugin.node.call {id, method, params}`;
  old nodes don't send it, and the hub keeps using `computer.*`, `browser.*` (new nodes still answer those).
- `herdr.server.start` (hub → node, no params, returns `{running}`): the user tapped "Start" in the Agents list. Not bound by `herdr_autostart`;
  if it can't start, the reason is returned the same way as `engine_missing`. Old nodes don't have this method, and the hub returns 502 rather than claiming herdr can't start.
  If herdr isn't installed, a pinned version is installed first (waits up to 15 seconds; if not done, returns an "Installing herdr …" error, finishes installing in the background and then starts itself).
- `herdr.server.status` (hub → node, no params, returns `{running, known, installing, install_error}`): `installing` means the node is installing herdr,
  `install_error` is why the last install failed (empty string if it never failed); `GET /api/v1/machines/{mid}/herdr` passes them through as is (omitted when absent).
- `usage.windows` (manager → node, no params, returns `{enabled, collected_at, accounts: [UsageNodeAccount]}`): subscription quota windows from Codex app-server, Codex rollouts, Claude status line files, and local runtimes such as Antigravity. Each item has the established usage account fields and optional Codex `account_key` and `source_key` digests. These keys are for the manager's grouping and are absent from the client API.
  It only reads local files and never touches credentials. When `usage_windows` in `node.configure` (hub.json `machines[].usage_windows`) is false it returns `{enabled: false, accounts: []}`. Old nodes don't have this method; the hub treats them as having no data.
- Operations without a pane (new, resume session, rename) go to the set's default host (the node's `defaultHost` / `defaultKind`; classic herdr for
  herdr + Herdr App); per-pane operations (read screen, send, keys, close) are routed by the host kind of the pane id, and each host's panes are limited
  only by that host's capabilities. A session live in two hosts is listed once, in the host that owns it, and every per-pane operation goes there.
- **`paseo` (display name "Paseo") is not a terminal host**: the node registers no host and runs the Paseo bridge itself (`node/paseobridge.go`).
  The bridge is a runtime with runtime id `paseo` ("Runtime ↔ node" below), and its sessions are this machine's sessions.
  - **New session**: all handed to it. A launcher Paseo does not have (the login shell's, one kept in Persona, plain
    `claude`) goes with the kind of agent it starts (`agent_type`): Paseo runs one of its providers of that kind and says
    so (`instead`), or refuses (`launcher_kind_missing`), never another kind and never its default. Its providers are then all that `launchers.list`
    offers for that host.
  - **Resuming a Claude session that isn't running**: handed over with `session.start {resume}`; the session id stays the same. After the takeover, messages go over with `session.send` as usual.
  - **When the bridge isn't connected**, both new and resume return the error `engine_missing` and nothing is sent.
  - **Detection**: Paseo in `engines` counts as available in two cases. One: the bridge is connected; then `version` is Paseo's version, and below the oldest Paseo Persona is tested with (0.15.0)
    `note` asks to update it. Two: the address written in `paseo.pid` in the Paseo home responds; in that case `note` says why the bridge is not connected: why it could not start, the error it printed
    when it exited, or, once it has run for 30 seconds without connecting, the last line it printed.
    The node writes these notes in Chinese, from the hub's `node-engine` catalog; the hub words them in each reader's language in the machine list, `machines` events and the answer to
    `PUT /api/v1/machines/{mid}/engine` (`i18n.EngineText`). Other notes (Orca's) reach clients as the node wrote them.

## hub ↔ node RPC

> What connects to nodes is the manager (the assistant's process): "hub" below is the manager in production; hub calls and node events are relayed over the bus ("Computers (devices.*)" under "Bus"),
> and the protocol the node sees is the same, word for word.

`ssh <host> ~/.persona/bin/personad node --stdio` (on the hub machine itself a child process is started directly; it is a child of the manager). One JSON per line on stdin/stdout.
Both sides can send requests: `{"id":"h12","method":"…","params":{}}` → `{"id":"h12","result":{}}` / `{"id":"h12","error":{"message":"…"}}`;
one-way events: `{"event":"…","params":{}}`. Ids sent by the hub start with `h`, ids sent by the node start with `n`. stderr is the node log.

Cancellation: when the caller no longer waits for a request, it sends `{"event":"rpc.cancel","params":{"id":"n12"}}` and the other side cancels handling that request. The node sends it for `mcp.call`, and the manager for `model.http` and `model.run`. For `mcp.call`: when the MCP process or hook disconnects (the assistant's turn was stopped), the hub's `approve` ends with it, the card is recorded as cancelled and withdrawn, and answering it afterward returns 410, so a write nobody is waiting for is never executed (such as sending an outdated message). Old versions that don't know this event ignore it, and handling runs to completion as usual. Extension and connector connections don't send this event.

The ctx a handler receives **ends once the reply is sent** (same as being cancelled): work that continues after replying (`session.watch`'s transcript pushes, anything streaming) must not hang off it; use `rpc.ConnContext(ctx)` (the connection's ctx, which ends only when the connection drops).

### Lanes

One connection carries everything between a manager and a node. With JSON lines one writer at a time writes it: a pong, an answer to a user action, terminal frames and a 1 MiB `file.chunk` all wait behind the line ahead of them, and on a slow link the heartbeat can close a working connection behind a file transfer. Both ends can switch the connection from JSON lines to **frames** on four lanes (`server/internal/rpc/lanes.go`). The byte pipes in between (ssh, `node --stdio`'s relay, tailcat, Persona Link and its hub relay, a member hub) carry the bytes as they are and need no change.

**Switching.** A node that announces `node_lanes_v1` answers `rpc.lanes` itself (the rpc layer, before any handler); the manager asks right after `node.info`, before anything large goes out:

```
→ {"id":"h3","method":"rpc.lanes","params":{"versions":[1]}}     a line
← {"id":"h3","result":{"version":1}}                              the node's last line: frames follow
→ {"event":"rpc.lanes","params":{"version":1}}                    the manager's last line: frames follow
```

Each side switches its output under its writer's lock right after the line that announces it, and its input in its read loop right after the other side's announcing line, so a line in flight on either side is read the way it was written. A peer that does not know the method answers an error (`unknown method rpc.lanes`, or `lanes_refused` from one that will not switch now), and both sides keep lines. The answer switches the manager whether or not its call still waits for it; a manager that gave up waiting (10 s) still frames its own output, and logs that lanes are on after all. A machine whose connections broke on frames three times in ten minutes (`rpc.ErrFrame`: something in between that does not carry the bytes as they are) is not asked for an hour, which the manager logs. Extensions, connectors, runtimes and every other user of `rpc` never enable lanes, so `rpc.lanes` is an ordinary (unknown) request there.

**Frames.** A 16-byte header, then up to 32 KiB − 16 bytes of one line (its newline left out); a frame with its header is at most 32 KiB:

| bytes | data frame `D` | acknowledgement `A` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | `D` (0x44) | `A` (0x41) |
| 1 | lane: 0 control, 1 interactive, 2 events, 3 bulk | 0 |
| 2 | flags: 1 = the line's last piece; other bits 0 | 0 |
| 3 | 0 | 0 |
| 4–5 | slot (big endian): which of the lane's lines in progress this piece belongs to | 0 |
| 6–7 | payload length (big endian) | 4 |
| 8–15 | this frame's sequence number in this direction, 1 for the first (big endian) | the last sequence number read; every frame before it was read too |

An acknowledgement's 4-byte payload is when its sender read the last frame it acknowledges, in milliseconds of its own clock (big endian, wrapping; only differences between two of them mean anything).

A reader rejects anything version 1 does not write (an unknown kind or lane, a flag or reserved byte set, a length over the limit or an acknowledgement's not 4, a sequence number that is not the next) and closes the connection: two ends that disagree about where the frames are fail at once rather than read garbage. A line longer than a frame goes in several, each lane keeping at most 16 lines in progress (slots 0–15); a reader takes at most 64 at once. An empty payload with the last-piece flag is an empty line.

**Lanes.** Control always gets the next choice of frame. When bulk is queued, it gets a turn after eight interactive or event frames; it still needs credit. If it has none, eligible interactive answers and events continue immediately. This bounds scheduler starvation without holding a read-loop response behind credit. Within a lane, lines that fit in one frame take turns with the lane's oldest long line, and the other long lines wait until it is through, as on the one writer: a short answer is not held behind a long one, and long ones finish one after the other (taking turns, concurrent file chunks would each end only at the end, every one later than its caller waits):

| lane | what goes on it (`server/internal/nodeproto` `ControlLane`, `BulkLane`) |
| --- | --- |
| control | `ping` and its answer, `stream.ack`, `rpc.cancel`, acknowledgements |
| interactive | every other request, and its answer |
| events | every other event |
| bulk | `file.chunk`, `file.read`, `file.upload.chunk`, `node.update.chunk` (each request and its answer) and `stream.data` |

A method names a request and its answer; the answering side picks the lane by the method it answers. Lanes only order what one side writes: the reader puts lines together whatever lane they came on, and dispatches each when its last piece arrives, so a call whose write returned is read before anything written after it. Each side uses its own build's table; a name the other side files elsewhere only changes that side's order.

**The window.** What the transports buffer (ssh's channel window, TCP, a relay) lies ahead of every frame written after it, so interactive requests and bulk lines also wait for credit: only so many of their bytes may be sent and not yet acknowledged, and those never fill the buffer ahead of a ping (a large `model.http` body or file write on a slow link otherwise would). Large answers and events still go to the transport at once, as on the one writer, and a ping written after them waits behind them there; the middle of such a line still arriving excuses a late pong. A reader asks for an acknowledgement of the interactive and bulk frames it read each time it is about to wait for more input; a reader held up by its own side (a handler that does not return) stops acknowledging, and the other side's requests and bulk lines stop once its window is full, instead of filling memory. The window adapts by delay one way: an acknowledgement says when the other side read the newest frame with credit it covers, by its clock, which with the time that frame was written, by this side's, is the frame's delay one way plus the difference between the two clocks. The smallest such delay of the last five minutes, among frames of its kind, full or shorter (a shorter frame takes less time on the wire, which next to its own would make a full frame's look like queueing), is the link's own, and what a frame takes beyond it is time it spent queued on its way. How long the acknowledgement then waits on the way back, behind what the other side sends, does not count: a busy other direction does not close this one's window. Below 100 ms of queueing the window grows (about doubling a round trip while the queue stays under 50 ms), above it shrinks by a quarter (a half past 400 ms) at most once a round trip. It never falls below what the other side reads, at the rate it reads (from the spacing of its read times, the most of the last 10 s), in the time its bytes wait to be acknowledged, that queueing left out, plus 100 ms; the longest such wait of the last 10 s counts. An acknowledgement waits behind what the other side sends and covers everything read since the last one, so the first byte it covers waited longer than the frame it names, and the wait changes from one to the next: a window sized by the frame named alone runs out while acknowledgements are late, and the link idles. It grows no further than what the other side reads in 100 ms past that, since on a long round trip a queue shows only a round trip later. When the other side's queue drains, the acknowledgements it held come quicker than the frames were read, and a window still sized for the old wait would fill the queue on the way, ahead of pings, until that wait aged out: once frames queue past 100 ms, the window is held to what the other side reads in the latest wait plus 200 ms. Frames are not paced, so what one bunch of acknowledgements frees still goes at once. It starts at 32 KiB and stays between 8 KiB and 4 MiB. Frames with credit are cut to a quarter of the window and, once the rate is known, to what the link carries in 100 ms (at least 4 KiB), so on a slow link a pong behind one waits for a few KiB, not 32. Events of the events lane, interactive answers and control never wait for credit: a synchronous event handler can send an event from the read loop, or wait there for one of its side's answers to be written (`AfterReply`), and waiting for credit would wait for an acknowledgement only that same loop reads; on the one writer a pong waited behind a whole answer anyway. Bulk events (`stream.data`) do wait for credit: the port streams send them from their pumps, never from a read loop. A read loop must not wait for its side's requests or bulk lines to be written: a request from it would wait for an answer only it reads, and a bulk line for credit. The manager queues the hub's port streams for a node apart from its other events (`devices/notes.go`), so terminal input never waits behind port bytes waiting for credit; a stream's bytes and its close (every `stream.*` event but `stream.ack`) share that queue, so a close never overtakes the last bytes. The two queues hold at most 32 MiB together, and a note that has waited 30 s while nothing at all went out on the connection (`Peer.LastWrite`; a write waiting for credit while other frames go out is not stuck) gets the node connected again. The port streams keep their own window (`stream.ack`) inside it. A reader holds at most twice the line limit in lines still arriving on one connection. The manager and resident node accept RPC messages up to 128 MiB over established connections, including plain JSON lines. Other RPC peers default to 64 MiB unless configured with a different limit.

**Resuming.** A resident node that announces `node_resume_v1` keeps a framed connection when the transport under it ends (`server/internal/rpc/resume.go`, `server/internal/node/attach_resume.go`, `server/internal/devices/resume.go`). The manager asks for it with lanes, `{"versions":[1],"resume":1}`, and a node that grants it answers `{"version":1,"resume":{"token":"<random>"}}`; a side that does not know the field ignores it, and nothing below happens. From then on each side acknowledges every frame it reads, as its read loop takes it (an acknowledgement through the last frame read, beside the one through the last frame with credit that the window samples: version 1's frames, sent more often) and keeps each data frame it writes until the other side acknowledges it: at most 16 MiB, none unacknowledged for more than a minute. Past either, what was kept is let go and the connection cannot resume until the other side acknowledges that far; it falls back to a full reconnect if it drops before. The bound is per connection: a manager holds up to 16 MiB for each computer it has connected, a node for its one connection; a healthy connection holds what is on its way, a round trip's worth.

When the transport ends (a read or a write fails; nothing at all was read on it for 15 s while frames written over it wait to be acknowledged, which a working transport answers within a round trip; or the manager cuts one its pings or tailcat's find dead), neither side closes the connection: it is lost, its calls waiting, its handlers and session watches running, the computer shown as connected, no pings sent. The side that finds it lost closes that transport, so that the other learns at its next read instead of by its own checks: a manager whose read loop was held up past the node's silence check (a slow handler) reads what was written up to then, finds the end and resumes at once. The manager tries for 30 s from when it noticed (`nodeproto.ResumeWindowSeconds`); a resident node keeps the connection 60 s from when it noticed (`nodeproto.ResumeKeepSeconds`), longer than the manager can take to notice a drop the node saw first (its next ping, up to 30 s on, then 15 s of silence) and try. The manager first opens a new transport on the same path. If that try fails and another path is better by then (a network changed), it tries to resume over the better path before connecting anew. Whichever path a try uses, the new transport's first line asks for the connection back:

```
→ {"id":"h41","method":"rpc.resume","params":{"token":"…","read":1234}}   a line: the last frame the manager read
← {"id":"h41","result":{"read":987,"token":"…"}}                          a line: the node's last frame read, a new token
```

Then both sides frame again, each first writing again, in order, what it kept after the other's `read`; a frame that comes a second time (read over the old transport after `read` was taken) is dropped. A resident node reads each new transport's first line before it serves it, beside its accept loop: `rpc.resume` with the token of the connection it keeps takes that connection back, the same Node serving it and nothing watched again; nothing of the connection is written on the new transport before its answer, nor at all when it is refused. Any other first line is a new connection, which replaces the one kept, in the order the transports came: one that came before the connection served and speaks only after it is closed. A token it does not have (another process's, or one already used: a token is good for one resume) is answered `{"error":{"code":"resume_refused"}}` and the transport closed, the connection kept left alone. The token a resume was asked with is still taken until the new transport carries a byte, so a manager that never read the answer asks again with the token it has. While the connection is lost the node's hooks do not wait for it: their events go out in order once it is resumed (a hook waits for its own at most a second, not at all while the transport is lost; a card it asks for always goes after it), and one the connection never sent because it ended unresumed is kept in the spool as standby keeps it, for the next connection. Known limits: an event a hook sends in the moments after its Node handed what it had not sent to the spool reaches the spool after the next connection's replay, and the manager with the connection after that; an event whose last frame was written just before the transport ended, never resumed, is lost, as with any connection that ends; and for up to the node's 60 s a connection waiting to be resumed keeps `node.sock`, so calls through it (an Agent's MCP tools, `personad ask`, `personad notify`) wait for the resume or fail at the window's end, where standby would have answered at once. The manager then lets its peer go and connects anew when the node refuses a resume, the window ends, or the node announced it is restarting (`node.restarting`). A resume over the better path that is refused or fails within the window falls back to that full reconnect over the better path. A resume that moved the connection also moves the path and transport used for path health, later path switches and the route shown for the machine; the successful resume log names the destination path. On a resume the window lets go of what it learned of the old route (its delays and rate) and measures the new one from the start; the frames written again count from then.

**Pings.** Pings, their 5 s wait and the two misses that close a connection (`devices/paths_view.go`) are the same with or without framing; framing changes what a ping queues behind, not how long it is waited for. `PingActivity` counts a reply, and the middle of a long line still arriving, read for read (a read that goes on with a line begun before it, does not finish it, and finds it past 16 KiB), which stands while that line is still arriving even when shorter lines finish beside it. The read-ahead behind a line looks at whole lines and the first pieces of lines, never at a later piece on its own. A request withdrawn before its first frame went out is `NotSent`, as a line still waiting for the writer was; one begun is written to its end. On the node, hiding handed-over values and noticing an accepted update's answer work on whole lines (`rpc.Peer.LineFilter`, `LineWritten`), framed or not. A ping can already be in the socket behind an earlier event or interactive answer. When a cumulative acknowledgement advances during its wait but only through those earlier frames, the latest such progress bounds how much response time was left. The manager applies its existing half-budget rule to that observation. Duplicate acknowledgements, silence and acknowledgements past the earlier data provide no such allowance. Peers that do not acknowledge uncredited events give no evidence for those events. Interactive answers and events can still be sent from inside a read-loop callback without waiting for credit.

**Counters.** `rpc.Peer.LaneStats` is the writer's queue per lane (frames and bytes waiting, frames sent, the longest a line waited for its first frame), the window, the bytes with credit in flight, and the latest round trip of such a frame with the time it spent queued on its way. The manager logs them, in the order control/interactive/events/bulk, on the "connected" line (`lanes=on|off`), the "connection ended" line, the line of a connection closed for unanswered pings, and the line of a call that took 2 s or more or ran out of time: `lanes=on queued=0/1/0/3 bytes=0B/1KiB/0B/24KiB maxwait=1ms/40ms/2ms/1.2s sent=12/340/88/51 window=16KiB inflight=8KiB rtt=520ms queued=90ms`. A connection that can resume adds `resume=on kept=<bytes kept> resent=<frames written again>`, the "connected" line `resume=on|off`, and the lines about a computer's connections its counts once one dropped: `drops=2 resumed=1 fell_back=1 recover=740ms/2.1s` (the latest and the longest time to resume).

hub → node requests:

| method | params → result |
| --- | --- |
| `resource.queue` / `resource.result` | `{mirror:{machine,target,port?,identity?},project?,commit?,groups?}`: fixed read-only runner SSH commands. Queue returns freshness and v1 JSON or unknown/plain text; result returns a v1 outcome or null. Older nodes return unknown method, preserving stale mirror data. |
| `node.info` | → `{hostname, os, arch, home, herdr_version, claude_version, version, system, engine, engines}` (`system`, read once at node start; `engine` is the engine the node currently uses, `engines` are those it found, see "Engines"; old nodes lack these two). If `claude_version` is empty on connect (the `claude --version` run failed), the hub asks again after 1, 2, 5, 10, 30 minutes and then hourly; once it gets a value it updates the machine and pushes it to the web app, and stops when the connection drops |
| `engine.use` | `{engine, hosts?, default?}` → `{engine}`: switch to this engine, or to the set in `hosts` / `default` for a node that takes sets ("Engines", "Host sets"; unknown ones error). If it equals the current one, nothing happens; otherwise it swaps the host, drops the old engine's Agents (refresh results started before the switch and returning after it are discarded), ends all terminal streams (each pushes `terminal.end` with an error saying the engine changed), swaps the event stream, and pushes one `sessions.changed`. Multiple `engine.use` calls run in order |
| `launchers.list` | `{host?, source?, refresh?, cache_only?}` → `{launchers, shell?, rc_file?, host?, host_runtime?, source?}`. `source:"external"` returns only the enabled local adapter's sanitized catalog before shell/host/runtime discovery; `refresh:true` joins its bounded inventory load, and missing registration or refresh failures are typed errors, not a healthy empty source. Without an explicit source or host, the Assistant picker's fallback uses `cache_only:true` to return the last completed shell list and live runtime entries without waiting for a shell. An explicit `refresh:true` takes precedence. Ordinary requests retain their original source errors and last-seen behavior. Without `host`: the machine's own launchers (Settings, the main chat's menu: the assistant runs them on its command line). With `host`, a start's engine host: what a start there can run; where that host is an engine runtime that runs only its own launchers (`caps.same_kind`, Paseo), its launchers in its own order (its default first), the other runtimes' and the desktop apps', with `host_runtime: true`: the hub adds no managed launcher (but an Antigravity one, which its own runtime runs) and no plain `claude` then, since the engine would run one of its own in their place; any other host answers as without it, saying `host`. A runtime's launcher whose Agents' approval is a switch a start in `bypassPermissions` turns on (Paseo's Auto Accept) has `auto_accept: true` ("Runtime ↔ node"). A Codex launcher has `agent: "codex"`, `prompt_optional: true` when the node starts it with no first message too (`node/codex_waiting.go`), and `run_here: true` when the node starts it in a shell pane the user picked and keeps that pane when the start fails (`panes.agent`); a runtime's launcher has `display_name` when the runtime names its provider (Paseo's label: the web app's pickers say "Grok", not `grok`) and, when its agent is not Claude Code, `permission_modes`: the modes a start on it takes (Paseo: `["default","bypassPermissions"]` where the provider has Auto Accept or full-access, else `["default"]`), from which New Agent offers "Launcher default" (sent as no mode) and Full access, and only the efforts its model lists; `source: "claude_desktop"` is the launcher `claude-desktop`, which starts the session in Claude's desktop app, and `source: "codex_app"` the launcher `codex-app`, which starts the chat in the Codex App. A login-shell launcher with the same name takes precedence. Desktop launchers need no terminal engine; `codex-app` still requires a first message |
| `launchers.zshrc` | `{}` → `{aliases:[{alias, env:{K:V}, args, command, file}]}`: lines of the form `alias x="K=V … claude [args]"` in this machine's `~/.zshrc` (`$ZDOTDIR` first), `~/.bashrc` and `~/.bash_aliases`, the login shell's file first (zsh: `~/.zshrc`, `~/.bashrc`, `~/.bash_aliases`; bash: `~/.bashrc`, `~/.bash_aliases`, `~/.zshrc`); only those whose `command` is claude. `file` is that file's label (`~/.zshrc` for `$ZDOTDIR`'s too); inside a file the last definition of a name counts, across files the first file that defines it. A missing file has none; the login shell's own file there but unreadable is an error naming it, another unreadable one is skipped. `env` carries keys, which are handed to the manager only over this RPC (import, over the hub-to-node connection) and never logged; old nodes return `unknown method`, and nodes that report no `file` read only `~/.zshrc` (the manager takes their aliases as `~/.zshrc`) |
| `launchers.repair` | `{name, action: "upgrade_cli"}` → `{ok, unsupported?, output?}`: auto-repair from the launcher health check. The node only applies fixed repairs (for Claude, it runs `claude update`) and accepts no commands; old nodes return `unknown method` |
| `launchers.catalog` | `{launchers: [ManagedLauncher]}` → `{ok}`: the Persona-managed providers in this computer's device scope, on every connection and after every change. An entry with `withheld: true` has no `api_key`, `headers` or `env`; the node asks `launchers.pull` for them when it needs them, and right away for one with `delivery: push`. `rev` changes on every save: what was pulled at another rev is dropped. Old nodes return `unknown method`, and the manager sends `launchers.managed` with this computer's providers instead |
| `launchers.managed` | `{launchers: [ManagedLauncher]}` → `{ok}`: the same with every secret, for nodes that do not know `launchers.catalog` |
| `launchers.check` | `{name, model?, host?, purpose?, assistant_turn?, effort?, conversation?, config_dir?}` → `{ok, agent?, model?, answer?, millis?, error?, assistant_turn?}`: a real one-word availability probe. Optional `model` is validated as a model id and forwarded to the CLI or native runtime, to verify a model-family quota limit. A returned model from another family cannot clear that limit; this keeps older nodes/runtimes that ignore the field conservative. `assistant_turn: true` (the main chat readiness probe; capability `launcher_check_assistant_turn`) runs a Claude Code launcher's check as an assistant turn of `conversation` runs: in that conversation's recorded profile (else `config_dir`, else the launcher's own, else Persona's for it; only read, never chosen or saved), with `PERSONA_ASSISTANT=1`, the turn's `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH`, the launcher started as the assistant starts it, Persona's own MCP server alone (`--strict-mcp-config`) with the chat's `--tools` / `--allowedTools`, and `--model` / `--effort`; still one word, one turn, nothing saved, no hooks. A tool call the one turn did not run (`error_max_turns`) counts as an answer. The answer says `assistant_turn: true` when it ran so; an older node, or a launcher that is not Claude Code, runs the plain check. Without it the check is unchanged (Settings › Models' Test, launcher health). |
| `launchers.own_service` | `{agent}` → `{agent, known, own, via?}`: whether the harness (`claude`, `codex`) already has a usable service of its own on this computer (`via`: `login`, `api_key`, `launcher`); others are `known: false`. Cached ten minutes; old nodes return `unknown method`, read as not known |
| `launchers.models` | `{name, agent_type?, refresh?, host?}` → `{agent, models, locked?, supports_start_effort?}`: same as REST `…/launchers/{name}/models`; `agent_type` is this launcher's type in the hub config (if omitted, whatever the node detects itself). `host` is the start's host, the machine's default when omitted: where it is an engine runtime that runs only its own launchers, a name it offers is its provider's, whatever launcher of the shell's or of Persona's has the name too. `launchers.check`, `launchers.model.check` and `session.start.options` take `host` the same way. A node sets `resolved_offered:true` on an alias row when the gateway catalog independently lists its complete `resolved` spelling as a selectable ID. An omitted field leaves this unknown. The manager uses this for legacy sessions and keeps the REST picker rows in their original order. A locally registered external adapter returns its bounded inventory models without running a shell probe; `refresh:true` joins a fresh inventory read. `supports_start_effort:true` enables a creation-time Codex effort from the selected model's listed levels. |
| event `launchers.changed` | node → manager `{}`: an opted-in local adapter's sanitized inventory or stale status changed. The manager invalidates that machine's model cache and refreshes its existing launcher snapshot in the background; this event grants no execution authority and does not restart conversations. |
| `session.skills` | Manager-owned `{session_id,skill_owner}` → the versioned ordinary Agent catalog above. Derives live Claude terminal launcher/cwd/profile, or the uniquely owning Codex app-server and its actual home/cwd/connection. Reads do not join or resume threads. `session.send` validates explicit leading skill contexts before delivery; Claude receives exact-file instructions, Codex native typed skill input. Plain text requires no catalog. Unsupported nodes must not receive selected references as literal text. |
| `skills.list` | `{cwd?}` → `{skills: [{name, description, source}]}`: the legacy prepared inventory, unchanged. Optional manager-owned catalog mode `{catalog:true,skill_owner,machine_id,cwd,session_id?,launcher?,runtime?,config_dir?}` → `{catalog_version:1,skills:[{id,name,description?,source}],complete}` resolves the actual supported execution environment; paths stay on the node. The new manager requires `catalog_version:1` so an old node's legacy inventory is not mistaken for a complete runtime catalog. |
| `skills.import` | Manager-only `{dir,scope,op,archive?:base64,reference?}` → skill import result (REST above). `dir` is the server-derived assistant state directory; `scope` binds assistant and machine. Strict fields and directory/scope agreement are required. The node resolves the existing user skills directory, validates/stages in isolation and atomically adds a new safe name; preview/cancel/install/unchanged-new-only Undo/status use bounded ten-minute in-memory receipts. The original preview key remains an alias for the installed/undone outcome until expiry or node restart. No arbitrary-path management, script execution or runtime/model call. |
| `dirs.list` | `{path}` → same as REST |
| `workspaces.list` | `{}` → `{workspaces:[Workspace],errors?:[{source,error}]}`; Workspace is the same as in "Workspaces"; the node omits machine_id, and id/source_id are host-local IDs. Includes spaces with no running Agent, saved Codex projects and Claude Desktop folders without a terminal engine. Scoped nodes do not enumerate desktop projects. Each source reports errors separately; if all fail it returns an RPC error and must not pretend to be an empty success. Sources not running on this computer (`host.ErrNotRunning`: Orca not open, botmux has no daemon or is too old to have `observe`) count as having no workspaces, not an error; if only non-running sources exist, it returns an empty list. An engine runtime that keeps workspaces (Paseo, `caps.workspaces`) is a source too: its `runtime.workspaces` rows, with the runtime id as `source`, `project_id` / `project_name` its space, `project_path` the repository's main checkout, `is_main` true for a main checkout, `workspace_kind` `git` or `folder`, and `owned` true on a worktree the runtime made (the only rows Delete worktree is offered for); while it is not connected it lists none |
| `fs.task.list` | Lists entries for a scheduled prompt picker. The selected directory and resolved entries must stay within the task working directory, including across symlinks. Requires the node capability `task_input`. |
| `assistant.content` | Validates the leading file and skill selections in `text` against the selected computer, directory and launcher before a task save. Applies the same Guest, public-input, and Inbox restrictions as `assistant.send`. The manager passes its origin decision for the source conversation when known. File refusals before delivery use `file_unavailable` with `delivered: "none"` and `retryable: false`, including the unsupported Runtime case. Requires the node's `task_input` capability. |
| `assistant.directory` | `{path}` → `Workspace` with physical `cwd`; existing directory read/search validation on the execution computer, no writes. A missing path returns `task_directory_missing`, which lets the manager prepare the managed default directory for scheduled selections. Requires node capability `task_execution`. |
| `workspace.resolve` | `{path, terminal?}` → `Workspace`; validates a real directory and resolves symlinks. On success source is `directory`, id/source_id/cwd are the physical path, available is true. Accepts local absolute paths or home expansion (`~/`, Windows `~\`); rejects missing paths, non-directories and protected iCloud paths. Performs no host, Agent or Git operations. `terminal: true` (the task manager, for the directory an Agent starts in) makes `cwd` the spelling a terminal there opens: under a home reached through a link (`home_real`), the home's own spelling of the same directory; id/source_id stay physical, and the git links of the linked worktree the directory lies in are made portable (`node/worktree_links.go`; files only, no git run). The manager compares task directories with the home's two spellings folded. Older nodes ignore it |
| `sessions.history` | `{since, until?, cursor?, limit?, source?, runtime?}` → `{rows, next_cursor, complete, sources}`: sessions active in a time window, every source of the node (its Claude Code transcripts, Codex rollouts, paginated TRAE records and runtimes) or the one asked. See "Session history"; older nodes report unknown method |
| `sessions.list` | optional `update_handoff` → `{sessions, update_busy?}`: `update_busy` (with `node_update_idle`) is whether `node.update.commit` would refuse now, the node's own check; older nodes leave it out. After the update grace, `update_handoff: true` makes current nodes refuse new headless turns while other RPCs and current turns continue; `false` reopens them after a failed deployment. Older nodes ignore the flag |
| `session.start` | `{cwd, launcher, agent_type?, prompt?, images?, resume_session_id?, resume_automatic?, resume_delegated?, resume_outside_health?, task_id?, workspace_id?, desktop_project_id?, workspace_label?, permission_mode?, effort?, speed?, ultracode?, tab_name?, async?, in_pane?, secret_ticket?}` → `{session}`; `desktop_project_id` selects an exact Codex App project or Claude directory project; Claude named-environment selections are refused before side effects (see "New session", including selection limits and desktop partial-start recovery). `images?` (`{mime,data}`) accompanies a non-empty prompt: the node decodes and saves the bytes on its own machine and adds them to the prompt through the same `<attached_images>` path as `session.send`; an empty start takes no images. `secret_ticket` (capability `secret_env`) is a `secret.stage` ticket: only a new Claude Code start in a terminal with a Persona-managed provider or plain `claude` takes one (`secret_env_agent` otherwise, `secret_env_gone` when the ticket is unknown, used, expired or another start's: the first start that names it takes it), and the Agent then starts through `personad launch --ticket`; `in_pane` starts in a failed start's kept tab (`shell_waiting` / `agent_start_stalled` data `pane`) instead of a new one while the node still keeps it, else opens a new tab; an Orca terminal takes one launch, so a kept Orca tab whose start already typed its line there (`agent_start_stalled`) is closed once the start passes its checks and the start opens a new tab; a refused start leaves it kept, and one Orca will not close fails the start and stays kept. A synchronous and an `async` start hold the tab the same way (`node/startremedy.go`), and a kept tab another start holds is refused with `start_tab_taken`; `async` returns immediately and starts terminal Claude in the background (`node/starting.go`); terminal Codex launchers are synchronous, and without `prompt` answer with a row waiting for the first message (`node/codex_waiting.go`); the desktop `codex-app` launcher requires a prompt. `ultracode:true` is best effort once Claude is up (never a failed start); `false` is the same as leaving it out. A Claude `resume_session_id` the node has no transcript, start (one that failed included) or record of is refused with `resume_unknown` before any tab opens: started under it, a new conversation would be listed under the id of another. `resume_outside_health: true` (capability `resume_outside_health`) is the hub's mark on an extension's resume of a conversation it does not list: before anything else reads the id, the node refuses it with the same `resume_unknown` unless something no resume rewrites says where the conversation started (its transcript or rollout, its omp session file, or the record of an engine runtime's start: the node keeps one of every session an engine runtime starts, marked `engine_runtime`) and every directory it knows it by (where its transcript starts, where it last was, the record's, a start's, the running agent's, the omp file's) is outside a track and the blocked Agent folders; one whose transcript's head names no directory is refused too, and so is one the node knows only by a terminal record, a start or a running agent (a resume writes a terminal record anew with the directory it names). Before that `resume_unknown` the node answers what holds for any id: a host it does not enable, or an engine runtime that is not connected (`engine_missing`, as for the owner's resume). The hub sets it after the manager's `agents.start_params`, and never takes it from the caller. With `resume_session_id` for a Claude session that isn't running, whatever the start leaves out (launcher, the model picked for that launcher, directory, permission mode, effort, tab name) is what the session ran with, as a message that resumes it gets (`fillResume`, `node/retire.go`). An older node runs a left-out launcher as `claude` and the launcher's default model. With `resume_session_id` (the user's Resume, the one way a stopped Agent runs again), a terminal resume runs in the shell the Agent left when that shell is at rest in the session's directory, else in a new tab; `claude-desktop` instead validates and imports its existing desktop session.  `resume_automatic:true` is the assistant's guarded reuse of this same path: the node rechecks a recorded non-user stop, serializes with user closes, and rejects launcher/permission overrides as `resume_not_allowed`; omitted for the owner's explicit Resume. With `resume_delegated:true` too (the main conversation acting for the owner) it also takes an `exit` or unknown stop, never `user`, as `stop_cause` above says. A herdr leader task and its workers carry their top-level `task_id`, with `workspace_label` for a new task workspace and `workspace_id` once recorded; the answer's `task_workspace` reports actual placement, and the node keeps it with the session for a later resume. |
| `session.modes` | `{session_id, permission_mode?, effort?, model?, launcher?, from?}`: a running session's permission mode, effort and (Claude Code in a terminal) model, the model first. `launcher` (capability `launcher_switch`) other than the session's own records a pending switch to it (`pending_switch` on its row, kept in its state record so a node restart keeps it; a session Persona did not start keeps it in memory only), checked first (`switch_*` refusals); its own launcher drops one; `from` other than the session's launcher is `switch_stale`. See "Switching a running Agent to another provider". A launcher of the other engine (capability `engine_switch`) records a switch to that engine, `pending_switch.agent` naming it: see "Switching a running Agent to another engine". → `{ok, applied?}`: with a `permission_mode`, `applied` is `now`, or `restart` when a restart into it waits for the turn to end (node/mode_restart.go); older nodes answer `{ok}` alone |
| `session.ultracode` | `{session_id, ultracode?:bool, dismiss_lost?:bool}`: the independent toggle for ordinary Claude Code Agent sessions; queued while busy or while a draft / dialog is in the way (success, `ultracode_pending`); refused with `ultracode_unsupported` where it cannot be made (botmux, main chat, old CLI). `dismiss_lost:true` dismisses the resume notice. An old node's `unknown method` becomes `409 node_outdated` at HTTP `/modes`; see "Claude Code ultracode" |
| `session.send` | `{session_id, text, images?, client_msg_id?, task_id?, workspace_id?, workspace_label?, public?}` (`client_msg_id`: see "Matching pending messages"; the task fields carry herdr task placement through a resume, with `task_workspace` in the answer when a new tab opened). For an assistant conversation, `public: true` marks one public-mention input and suppresses the owner's live snapshot for that input only; it is manager-derived, never a conversation-wide origin or a saved execution setting. `owner_input: true` is set only by the devices manager, from the hub's human-input mark on the owner's own message or its consumed one-time proof for an approval clarification (any a caller sends is dropped, in any letter case, and a node honours only that exact key, once): a Claude outside Persona's terminals in a tmux pane then takes it as typed terminal input through the ordinary pane checks and transcript confirmation, with or without an inbox; one with no pane takes it through Persona's plugin as the person's input, at rest, and with a `busy_input` plugin also queued behind a running turn or a dialog other than a question (`queued`, and `waits_on_computer` behind a dialog). The answer adds `delivered_as` (`user_input` / `relayed`) and, when a no-pane message is relayed through the inbox, `relay_reason` (`no_plugin`, `busy`, `plugin_outdated`: the session works and its plugin lacks `busy_input`, `plugin_unavailable`, `plugin_refused`, `plugin_unconfirmed`); a relayed message that ends in a coded error (`peer_unconfirmed`, `peer_held`) carries both in the error's data too; an older node ignores the field. Anyone else's message to a tmux Claude keeps its peer inbox and is refused without one, never typed. `compact_if_full: true` (the assistant's `agent_send`): a Claude Code or Codex Agent whose context is nearly full when the message would go in is compacted with its own `/compact` first; the answer adds `compacted`, or `queued` with `compact_after_turn` when it is mid-turn (the node holds the message and decides again when the turn ends); a failed compaction is refused `compact_failed` with the reason and nothing sent; an older node ignores the field. An owner's message (`owner_input`) can resume a recorded terminal Agent after the CLI exits. The node reuses the session ID and launcher. A session explicitly stopped through Persona still refuses `agent_stopped` (`delivered: none`) until it is resumed. `apply_switch:true` (the user's message from the chat) carries a pending switch (`session.modes` `launcher`) out first: the agent quit in its terminal and resumed through the new launcher there, or the switch dropped and the message refused with a `switch_*` code and nothing typed; while the agent is busy the message goes as always and the switch waits. `switch_now:true` (the assistant's `agent_switch`, capability `launcher_switch_now`) implies `apply_switch` and carries the switch out now or not at all: where the message would go on the old launcher or leave the switch waiting it is refused (`switch_busy`, `input_draft`, `dialog_open`, `switch_stale`, `switch_unsupported`, `switch_other_agent`) with nothing typed and the switch dropped. A switch to the other engine (`pending_switch.agent`, `engine_switch`) starts that engine in the same terminal with the message behind its handoff, or resumes the conversation's earlier session of it; the message is consumed by that start |
| `session.switch` | `{session_id, launcher?, from?, model?}` → `{}`: the switch `session.modes` just picked (`pending_switch`), carried out now with no message (the assistant's batch switch, capability `launcher_switch_idle`): the agent is quit and resumed on the new launcher in the same terminal and waits there, idle. Refused with nothing done and the switch dropped as `switch_now` is (`switch_busy`, `input_draft`, `dialog_open`, `switch_stale`, `switch_unsupported`, `switch_other_agent`); a failed switch as for a message (`switch_failed`, `switch_failed_stopped`, `switch_not_stopped`). For a session that is not running, with `launcher`: nothing starts; Persona's record of it is pointed at that launcher and `model` (else the launcher's default), so its next Resume, or the message that resumes it, comes up there. The same launcher checks as a switch (`switch_launcher_missing`, `switch_other_agent`, `switch_config_dir`, `switch_model_locked`, `switch_pick_model`); `from` must name the launcher it is on (`switch_stale`); a session Persona keeps no record of is `switch_unsupported` |
| `session.echoes` | `{echoes: [{session_id, client_msg_id, text, images, sent_at, after_seq, line?, in?, history?, accepted?}]}` → `{ok}`. The hub hands back sends recorded for this machine within the last day, before `sessions.list`. The node merges evidence for records it already knows. `history` identifies the transcript version and `accepted` records an acknowledged send, including queued input. Old nodes return unknown method and the hub ignores it |
| `session.echo_status` | `{session_id, client_msg_id}` → `{state}`. Capability `session_echo_status`. `seen` means the node recorded a matching line. `known_unseen` requires the node's record, an unacknowledged attempt within the echo-matching window, a live idle agent, and a complete read from the original transcript position through a turn that ended after the send. `unknown` covers missing evidence, including a turn that may still be holding queued input |
| `session.send_unseen` | Same params and success reply as `session.send`. The devices manager calls it only after the owner selects Retry and the node reports `known_unseen`. The node rechecks after taking the session's input lock. A match answers success without sending, an unseen attempt can replace its ambiguous cached receipt, and missing evidence returns `echo_unconfirmed` |
| `session.keys` | `{session_id, keys, text}` |
| `start.keys` | `{pane, text?, keys?}` → `{ok}`: types `text` as is (no enter, at most 32 characters), then presses `keys` (at most 8, Persona's key names) in a failed start's kept tab while no agent runs there (`node/startremedy.go`); any other pane is refused with `start_tab_gone`, too much with `too_large`; the tab is marked typed, so a start named to it next waits out an answered question's line |
| `start.continue` | `{session_id, choice}` → `{session}`: answers the question an async start's kept tab stopped on (`shell_waiting`) with one of its `choices`, only while the tab is kept and its last line is still that question, then starts the session again in that tab under the same id (`node/startcontinue.go`, see "Answering a start's question"); a question no longer on the tab's last line gets nothing typed and the session starts again there all the same. Refusals, nothing typed: `start_not_waiting`, `choice_not_offered`, `start_tab_gone`, `secret_env_gone`. Capability `start_continue` |
| `start.answer` | `{pane, line, choice}` → `{ok, typed}`: the same answer to `line`, the question a failed start's kept tab on `pane` stopped on, with the same checks (only while the tab is kept, no agent runs there and its last line is still `line`; only an answer `line` offers; Ctrl-C alone into a password prompt), for a start the hub runs again itself in that tab (a planned task's, `POST /api/v1/todos/{id}/start/answer`); it marks the tab typed, so the next start named to it waits out the question's line (`node/startcontinue.go`); a question no longer on the tab's last line gets nothing typed or marked, and `{ok, typed: false}` (`typed: true` once it typed the answer; the hub records the owner's answer in the task's history only then, and takes a reply without `typed`, from the first `start.answer`, as typed). Refusals, nothing typed: `start_not_waiting` (no `line`), `choice_not_offered`, `start_tab_gone`. Capability `start_answer` |
| `session.rewind` | `{session_id, prompt, occurrence, prompts_after?, restore}` → `{prompt, restore, code_restored, input_cleared}`: uses the owning tool's native rewind ("Rewinding to a message"); refusals carry `code` |
| `session.restore_model` | `{session_id}` → `{restore: "next_start", restore_to, closed}`: closes a Persona conversation's idle headless process so its next start uses the configured model; sends nothing ("Going back to the configured model"); refusals carry `code` |
| `session.interrupt` | `{session_id}`. For a verified hub owner request, the devices manager uses the internal `session.owner_interrupt` RPC when the node advertises `owner_controls_v1`. |
| `session.screen` | `{session_id, lines, source, format?}` → `{text, status}` (`format: "ansi"` includes colors) |
| `panes.list` | `{}` → `{hosts:[…]}`, same as REST `/machines/{mid}/panes`: the node answers with spaces / tabs / all panes from its latest host snapshot (taking a new one only if older than 3 seconds), without starting its own polling |
| `panes.new` | `{workspace_id, kind?}` → `{pane, terminal, tab_id}`: the host's `CreateSlot` opens a shell tab (directory is the space's own); errors if the space is gone or the host can't open tabs. With `cwd` and no `workspace_id`, the first workspace of a host that opens tabs; when that host has none, its `CreateSpace` opens a new workspace in `cwd` (home for `~`; capability `pane_new_space`, which clients ask for with `new_space`) |
| `panes.close` / `panes.split` / `panes.agent` / `panes.git` / `tabs.close` / `tabs.rename` | node menu actions, params as in the REST above. The pane / tab must be one the host lists (if not, take a snapshot first and check again); the directory is the pane's own. Closing an Agent's pane goes through `session.close` (asks it to exit first). `panes.agent` reuses the whole new-Agent launch flow (same launcher command, wait for the session to be ready, bind); on failure the pane is not closed |
| `panes.close_finished` | `{panes?, preview?}`: "Close finished terminals", as the REST above (`node/stopped.go`) |
| `claude.auth_status` | `{name}` (launcher; empty means `claude`) → `{state: logged_in\|not_logged_in\|unknown, auth_method?, api_provider?, key_source?, version?, reason?}`: runs `claude auth status --json` with the same command and the same `--settings` used to open a chat; sends no model request. `auth_method` is Claude Code's `authMethod` (`claude.ai`, `api_key`, `api_key_helper`, `oauth_token`, `third_party`, `none`); `key_source` is only the variable name (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`); email, organization and keys are never returned. `reason` for `unknown`: `old_claude` (before 2.1.41 there's no `claude auth`; not run), `not_claude` (the launcher runs Codex / a runtime), `unreadable` (status can't be read: claude not found, the launcher swallowed the arguments), `timeout` (20 seconds). A name that isn't a launcher on this computer errors without running; old nodes return `unknown method` |
| `node.doctor` / `node.doctor.fix` | `{fix?: bool, preflight?: bool, locale?: string}` / `{}` → the same `DoctorReport` shape as `personad node doctor --json`: checks run inside the node process. Absent `locale` preserves the canonical zh-Hans report byte for byte, including for the assistant's readiness; an explicit supported locale words only human `detail` / `hint` / human `items` in that language, leaving names, statuses, states, fixed identifiers, order and machine items unchanged. Older nodes ignore `locale`. `node.doctor` without `fix` writes nothing; `fix` (or `node.doctor.fix`) only rewrites files Persona itself generated (`writeGeneratedConfig`) and then checks again; never the LaunchAgent. `preflight: false` leaves the `path-access` check out (the assistant's readiness passes it without a locale: it only reads `claude-version`; older nodes ignore it). The hub's GET never passes `fix` and forwards `locale` only from an explicit `Accept-Language` |
| `machine.diagnose` | `{sections?: ["processes","disk","tools"]}` → `Diagnosis` without `machine_id` (see `GET /api/v1/machines/{mid}/diagnosis`): process groups from `/proc/<pid>/stat` (Linux, CPU over two readings half a second apart) or `ps -axo pid=,rss=,pcpu=,comm=` (macOS), names only; the home directory's folders and the cache catalog sized within 20 s on one filesystem without following links (`partial` when cut short); the tool catalog's versions, probed at most every 10 minutes. An unknown section is refused with code `bad_request`. Capability `machine_diagnose` |
| `machine.cleanup` | `{ids}` → `CleanupResult`: each id must be in the cache catalog (else code `bad_request`); the node resolves its folder itself, empties it only when it is a real folder inside the home directory reached through no link and no process of its toolchain runs (`in_use`), and keeps the folder. Capability `machine_diagnose` |
