| `machine.exec` | `{command, cwd?, timeout_ms, caller?}` → `{exit_code, timed_out, duration_ms, stdout, stderr, stdout_omitted_bytes, stderr_omitted_bytes}`: the main conversation's `machine_exec`, one non-interactive command in the user's login shell (`-lc`: on macOS `$SHELL` when it is zsh or bash, else `/bin/zsh`; elsewhere `bash`) in `cwd` (the home by default, `~` expanded), stdin empty, in a session and process group of its own. At `timeout_ms` (at most 120 s), when the caller goes away and when the shell leaves something running in its group, the group gets SIGTERM, 2 seconds, then SIGKILL until it is empty (`timed_out: true`, `exit_code: -1`). Each stream keeps its first 8 KiB and last 24 KiB around a marker. A command or `cwd` naming Persona's credential files (`hub.json`, `manager.json`, `link.json`, the keys beside them, the data directory's secrets) is refused, as is Windows. The hub writes `exec` before and `exec_result` after to the computer's `machine_audit`, never the output; the node logs only the command's length and exit code. An older node answers `unknown method` |
| `secret.run` | `{check: true}` → `{ok: true}`: nothing runs, the password card's pre-flight; refused on Windows. `{commands, password, timeout_ms}` → `{results: [{command, exit_code, timed_out, output, truncated, output_withheld}]}`: the commands the user approved on the password card (capability `secret_run`), 1 to 5 one-line commands of printable ASCII, each with `/bin/sh -c` in the home directory with `PATH=/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`, in its own session and process group. `password` is base64 of its bytes, without control characters; a command that runs one `sudo -S` (not after a pipe) gets it and a newline on stdin, any other command an empty stdin. It stops at the first command that exits non-zero, cannot start or runs out of `timeout_ms` (the whole run, at most 30 minutes; the group gets SIGTERM, 5 seconds, then SIGKILL until it is empty; `timed_out: true`, `exit_code: -1`, and a root command sudo started may still run). A command whose shell exited while a background child still holds its output runs out of time the same way; a command whose turn comes after the time is used up does not run and gets no result. `output` is stdout and stderr together, the last 16 KiB; a command whose output held the password returns none of it (`output: ""`, `output_withheld: true`). The node zeroes the password when the run ends and logs neither params nor output; it is not told when the caller stops waiting. A node without the capability gets `node_outdated` from the manager |
| `secret.stage` | `{check: true}` → `{key, key_id}`: a one-time key for one hand-off (base64 of an uncompressed P-256 point), good for 2 minutes; also the hand-off's pre-flight (refused on Windows). `{key_id, sealed}` → `{ticket, expires_at}`: values a provider extension resolved for one Agent start after the user approved the hand-off card (capability `secret_env`), sealed to that key (HPKE: DHKEM(P-256, HKDF-SHA256), HKDF-SHA256, AES-256-GCM, info `persona secret stage v1` NUL `key_id`; the plaintext is the JSON array `[{name, value}]`, `value` base64), so whatever relays the connection sees none. The key works once. 1 to 8 variables; `name` an environment variable name that is not the computer's, Persona's, the Agent's own or one that changes how programs load, run or connect (`PATH`, `HOME`, `LD_*`, `DYLD_*`, `PERSONA_*`, `ANTHROPIC_*`, `CLAUDE_*`, `GIT_*`, proxies, CA bundles, editors and the like); `value` 16 bytes to 16 KiB without NUL. The node keeps them in memory only, under a random one-time `ticket` (64 hex characters) good for 2 minutes that `session.start`'s `secret_ticket` names; it logs neither params nor values. Only the manager that connects the computer sends it: a `device.call` of it from the hub or another manager is refused with `handoff_refused`, as is a `session.start` with `secret_ticket` (in any letter case). From staging on, the node process hides each value in everything it sends. A node without the capability gets `node_outdated` from the manager |
| `worktree.snapshot` | A reviewer's own copy of an agent's change: `{cwd, name_hint?, kind?}` → `{path, root, head, skipped?}`. `git worktree add --detach` of the HEAD of the repository `cwd` is in, at `<checkouts>/review-<slug of name_hint>` (made unique), with the folder's staged, unstaged (`git diff --binary HEAD` applied) and untracked, not ignored files (at most 2000 files / 64 MiB; `skipped` counts the rest). Nothing is written in `cwd`'s tree. `worktree.remove` with `force` takes the copy away, as the plain worktree it is on every engine: on a runtime engine (Paseo) too, the node removes it itself rather than through the runtime, which made no workspace of it. Refusals: `not_a_repository`, `no_commit`, `worktree_failed` |
| `worktree.prepare` / `worktree.create` | Same as the REST above (`workspace_id`, `kind?`; create also has `branch`, `path`): the workspace must be one the host lists, and the directory is the workspace's own. Instead of `workspace_id`, `cwd` names it (the assistant's `agent_start` with `worktree`; the REST routes do not pass it): the host's space whose directory holds `cwd`, the deepest one; none holding it is an error. herdr with `worktree` uses `worktree.create`; older herdr falls back to `git worktree add` + `workspace.create`; Orca uses its runtime's `worktree.create`, after refusing a branch checked out in another worktree, which Orca would rename instead of failing. On failure it returns git's `fatal:` line; Paseo, while its bridge is connected (`caps.workspaces`), makes the worktree itself as a Paseo workspace in Paseo's worktrees folder (runtime ↔ node `workspace.create`), after the same checks: `path` must be in the folder prepare returns (only its last element can be chosen, and it is taken as Paseo names a folder: `[a-z0-9]` runs joined by single hyphens, at most 50 characters; a name with nothing left, or one whose folder exists at all, an empty one too, is refused, since Paseo would put the worktree beside it), `auto_name` lets Paseo name the branch and the folder, and a parent other than the source is refused; with Paseo not connected it fails with a sentence saying so, without `worktree_unsupported`. Only while Paseo is one of the computer's enabled engines: a bridge that is connected but not enabled makes, lists and deletes no workspaces. A whole create (prepare, the checks and Paseo's work) has one deadline, 145 s, inside the hub's 150 s; running out of it says so rather than the hub timing out. An engine with no checkouts (Cindy, a runtime without `caps.workspaces`, or a host without checkout support) fails with code `worktree_unsupported` (message `unsupported: <kind> cannot do this`), which the assistant reads as "run an inferred task in its own directory"; a repository with no commit on any ref (an unborn HEAD and nothing fetched) fails both with code `worktree_no_commits` and a sentence in the request's `locale` instead of git's "invalid reference"; a checkout path that holds something fails create with code `worktree_path_taken` (data `path`) and a sentence in the `locale`, adopting nothing. `open_workspace:false`, only for a herdr leader task's checkout, creates the Git worktree without opening a workspace; omitted leaves the existing workspace-opening behavior unchanged. prepare with a `branch` checked out in the repository answers `existing: {path, branch, in_checkouts?}` or refuses with `checkout_dirty`, `checkout_in_use`, `checkout_changed` or `checkout_unverified` (data `branch`, `path`, `owner`) |
| `terminal.watch` / `terminal.unwatch` | `{session_id, control?: {cols, rows, takeover}}`; watch → `{cols, rows, control}`, after which the node pushes `terminal.frame`. A watch while already pushing reopens a stream (new epoch, starting from a full frame). If herdr has no observe it reports `unsupported: …`. With `control` the node takes over via `herdr terminal session control` (reply has `control: true`; old nodes lack this field); if the slot is taken and there's no `takeover`, it errors with `code: attach_busy` |
| `git.pull` | `{cwd}` → `{status, updated}`, same safe pull as REST |
| `git.branches` / `git.pr` / `git.stage` / `git.commit` / `git.push` / `git.switch` / `git.stash` / `git.pr_create` / `git.pr_merge` | Params and answers as the REST above |
| `fs.list` / `git.status` / `git.diff` / `git.show` / `git.log` | same as REST (same param names) |
| `git.review` | `{cwd, scope, base?, paths?}` → the same answer as REST `git/review`; refusals are `rpc.Error` codes (`not_git`, `no_folder`, `bad_scope`, `bad_base`, `no_default_branch`, `no_merge_base`) |
| `fs.watch` | `{dirs: [{path, cwd}], git: [cwd]}` → `{ok}`, **replaces the whole set** of folders and Git directories the node watches (at most 32 folders and 8 Git directories; an empty set stops the watch loop). Old nodes report unknown method; the hub logs a line and the page keeps refreshing manually |
| `file.read` | `{path, cwd, offset}` → same as REST `file` (old nodes don't know `offset`, and their reply has no `offset` / `next`) |
| `fs.stat` | `{paths, cwd}` → `{stats}`, same as REST `stat` (old nodes report unknown method) |
| `session.items` | `{session_id, user_inputs?, before_seq, limit, turns, after_seq, lazy_images, fold_work, from_seq, through_seq}` → `{items, has_more, more_after, history, to_seq, from_seq}` (with `through_seq` it is the folded rows: `{items, more}`) (`from_seq` is only present in `after_seq` requests; without `lazy_images: true` the node reads image data back, for compatibility with old hubs). With `user_inputs:true`, returns only `{total, inputs:[{id,seq}], history}` for the full conversation, with no body/image data; runtime sessions use their existing item pages server-side. |
| `session.image` | `{session_id, item_id}` → `Image{mime, data}` (the node's items don't keep image data in memory; it rereads that line at the recorded line offset) |
| `session.visualization` | `{session_id, item_id}` → the visualization item's HTML fragment as a string: only a file under the node's visualizations tree belonging to that session (its Codex session id, or the session's main thread), symlinks resolved, at most 1 MiB; anything else is `not_found` |
| `session.item` | `{session_id, item_id}` → `Item` (full text, no images) |
| `session.watch` / `session.unwatch` | `{session_id, since_seq?}`; after watch the node reads new lines every 250ms and pushes `session.items` (with `history` / `from_seq` / `to_seq`); with `since_seq` it first resends everything after it, 500 items per page. The hub sends only one watch / unwatch at a time per session, and when its turn comes decides which to send, or whether to send at all, by the subscriber count at that moment (the node does nothing on a watch for a session already watched, so the two arriving out of order would leave the last subscriber without live content); a failed one is retried next time. A client's connection only counts the subscription when it reads `subscribe` / `unsubscribe` (and when it ends); the call itself is made off its read loop, so a node slow to answer does not keep that client's other messages unread, and a subscribe's backlog still follows its watch |
| `session.close` | `{session_id, force?: bool}`: `force: true` is the confirmation-only close used above; refuses a session no longer blocked, and never approves its dialog |
| `session.archive` / `session.unarchive` | `{session_id}` → `{native, already?, via?, reason?}`: archive (restore) the session in the tool that owns it, with the tool's own reversible archive; the manager calls them after the user archives or restores it in Persona ("Agent session archives"). `native: "done"` (now in the asked state; `already: true` when it was before, with no call to the tool; `via`: `app_server`, `cli` or `runtime`) or `"unsupported"` (no archive of its own: Claude Code, Orca, opencode, pi, a runtime without `caps.archive`, an older Codex with no `archive` command; `reason` says why). Codex: `thread/archive` / `thread/unarchive` on a connected app-server of the thread's `CODEX_HOME`, else `codex archive|unarchive <thread>` with that `CODEX_HOME` ("Archive"). Refused, to be tried again later: `code: native_archive_busy` (working), `native_archive_live` (a Codex process still has the thread open and no app-server can close it), `native_archive_failed` (the tool refused or failed; what Codex did is read back from where the rollout is). A runtime's session whose runtime is away is refused like `session.close`. Old nodes report unknown method (the manager treats it as unsupported). Nothing is deleted, and the node moves no file itself |
| `session.fork` | `{session_id, at_item_id}` → `{session_id}`: see HTTP `/fork`; old nodes report unknown method |
| `session.stop` | `{session_id, retire?: bool, stop_cause?: string}` → `{stopped}`: quits the Agent (Ctrl+C twice, up to three rounds, until the engine no longer shows it in its pane) and **keeps its terminal**, the tab with the shell it ran in; `stopped: false` when it isn't running. With `retire` only a still Agent: working, waiting on the user, starting, or another tool's returns `code: not_retirable`. Without it (a cancelled task) a working Agent is stopped too; a session with no terminal (another tool's, an engine that runs Agents itself) returns `code: no_terminal`, which the assistant then closes with `session.close`. An Agent that does not quit returns `not_stopped`; its pane is never closed to make it go. Old nodes report unknown method (the assistant treats it as refused: nothing closed). With `retire`, the manager may record `stop_cause: idle`, `task_completed` or `restart`; other explicit stop requests record `user`. Legacy `session.retire` without a cause remains unknown. The cause is committed only after a confirmed automatic stop; failed/uncertain stops grant no recovery eligibility. |
| `session.close_task_terminal` | `{todo_id, accepted_at, terminal}` → `{status: "closed" \| "skipped" \| "pending"}`. The manager sends it once after saving a supervisor's acceptance for a task whose owner opted in. `terminal` is the original `task_terminal` receipt from `session.start` with `task_terminal_token`, binding the session, pane, tab, workspace and process. A node needs a fresh Herdr inventory and an idle task process in the workspace's exclusive tab, with another tab remaining in the workspace. The node sends `agents.task_terminal.authorize` with the same request and closes only that pane upon `{authorized: true}`. The manager authorizes once after checking that the task still owns the run and the owner's choice still applies. |
| `session.retire` | `{session_id, close_terminal?: bool, after_exit?: bool, stop_cause?: string}` → `{closed}`: a finished task's Agent: the node answers like `session.stop` with `retire` (the Agent stops, its terminal stays). With `close_terminal` (the user's **Archive and close**, or the owner's `close_ended_terminals` setting) it closes the pane after the same checks, as `session.close` does; an older node closes it either way. `stop_cause` (`idle`, `task_completed`) is what an automatic close records, anything else records `user`. With `after_exit` too, an Agent that is no longer running has the marked, idle Herdr shell it left closed, with the checks of a Close after the Agent exits (`close_after_exit.go`); its stop cause stays; `closed: false` when there is no such shell or the engine is not Herdr. A node that does not know these fields ignores them (nothing is closed for an Agent that is not running). Refusals: `code: not_retirable`, `agent_busy` (the shell changed or something else runs in it) |
| `workspace.close` | `{task_id, workspace_id}` → `{closed, gone?}`: closes the herdr workspace only when the node's own session records prove that exact task/workspace pair and no live Agent remains in it. Another task's, a user-opened or an unrecorded workspace is refused `not_task_workspace`; a live one is `task_workspace_busy`. A rename does not change ownership and matching only a label is never enough. Already gone answers `closed:false, gone:true`; repeated closes are idempotent. Git checkouts and transcripts are untouched |
| `file.upload.begin` | `{name, size, dest?, dir?, cwd?, conflict?}` → `{upload_id, chunk_bytes, dest?}` (over the limit reports `too_large`; `dest` `dir` / `inbox` / `file` is echoed, see "Sending files") |
| `file.upload.chunk` | `{upload_id, offset, data}` (data is base64; offset must continue from what was received) → `{received}`; any error voids the whole upload |
| `file.upload.end` / `file.upload.abort` | `{upload_id}`; end checks the size and renames → `{path, name, size}` |
| `interaction.resolve` | `{id, resolution}` |
| `port.probe` | `{port}` → `{port, listening, http, title?}`: one GET / (Host is `localhost:<port>`) |
| `model.http` | `{method?, url, header?, body?, timeout_ms?}` → `{status, header?, body?}`: one request of a direct API connection that sends through this computer (capability `model_http`). `method` is `GET` or `POST` (left out: `POST`), `url` http(s) without user info; `body` is base64. The node sends it with its own network and proxy settings, never follows a redirect, reads the answer (a whole event stream) to its end, at most 16 MB, and returns it with `body` base64. `header` carries the key for this call only: the node never logs, keeps or repeats it, and errors name the URL at most. `timeout_ms` bounds the whole request (60 s when left out, at most 10 minutes); the manager's `rpc.cancel` ends it sooner. A node without the capability gets `node_outdated` from the manager |
| `model.run` | `{launcher, configured?, model?, effort?, system?, prompt, timeout_ms?}` → `{text, model?, usage?}` (`usage`: the CLI's `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `cache_read_input_tokens`, `cache_creation_input_tokens`, left out when it reported none): one request of an API purpose answered by a launcher's CLI on this computer (capability `model_run`). The node runs the launcher once, headless, as a start does (its environment, settings and default model; `model` / `effort` override them), in a temporary directory removed afterwards, with no tools, no MCP servers, no hooks and no session kept; Claude Code gets `system` as its system prompt and `prompt` on stdin. `launcher` must be one this computer offers or the manager vouches for (`configured`), and only Claude Code launchers answer (`codex exec` can't be kept from its tools). At most two runs at a time on a computer, a run waiting for its slot within its time; `timeout_ms` bounds it (2 minutes when left out, at most 10) and `rpc.cancel` ends it sooner. Errors: code `model_run_timeout` (no answer in time), `model_run_logged_out` (the CLI is not logged in there), otherwise the end of what the CLI printed without keys, URLs or addresses. The prompt and the answer are never logged. A node without the capability gets `node_outdated` from the manager |
| `clipboard.get` | `{}` → `{kind, text?, image?:{mime, data}}` (see `GET /api/v1/machines/{mid}/clipboard`): the clipboard of the session the node runs in; text first, else an image as PNG. Errors carry a code: `clipboard_unsupported` (message: a reason code, `no_display` / `no_tool` / `no_session` / `os`), `too_large`, `clipboard_failed` (message: what failed, never the content). Capability `clipboard` |
| `clipboard.set` | `{text}` or `{image:{mime:"image/png"\|"image/jpeg", data}}` → `{}`; also `clipboard_bad_image` when the bytes are not the image type named. Whether the user allowed it is the manager's to check, not the node's |
| `preview.servers` | `{cwd}` → the `…/preview/servers` answer: the nearest `.claude/launch.json` from `cwd` up to the repository's root, each entry probed (capability `preview`) |
| `preview.start` | `{cwd, name, workspace, kind?}` → `{pane, terminal, port}`: a new tab in the workspace named after the entry, in its folder, typing its command (each word quoted, `env K=V` in front for its `env`). For a runtime's workspace (a Paseo session's), the terminal engine's workspace whose folder holds the entry's, the deepest (one in the home folder or at the root holds everything and does not count), else a new workspace in the entry's folder with the tab named after it; never one that only happens to be first. With no host that opens tabs: refusal `preview_no_terminal` |
| `preview.open` | `{id, port, path, w, h, dpr, mobile}` → `{browser}`: a tab of the node's headless browser at `http://localhost:<port><path>`, on stream `id` whose bytes are length-prefixed frames (`internal/preview`); `port_gone`, `no_browser`, `browser_failed` |
| `computer.status` | `{}` → `Computer` (`enabled` filled in by the hub): probes the local cua-driver (path, version, daemon, `permissions status --json`) and the desktop session (IOConsoleUsers from `ioreg`: active / locked / away). The hub only asks when the `cua` plugin is enabled for this machine |
| `computer.call` | `{session, tool, args, call_id?}` → `{output?, text?, image?}`: `cua-driver call --screenshot-out-file … <tool>`, args via stdin, `session` filled into the args (element_token stays valid across calls); screenshots go separately in `image` (`{mime, data, width, height}`, converted to JPEG when smaller than PNG). Only reads and `run_script` / `run_steps` are accepted; if the daemon isn't running it first runs `open -g -b com.trycua.driver`. Not installed: error code `not_installed`. `call_id` is a canonical UUID present only for an opted-in MCP call and correlates a nested LCU elicitation with it. No originating-machine field is sent; older nodes ignore the optional id |
| `computer.install` / `computer.grant` / `computer.cancel` | `{}` → `Computer`: one background job (one at a time); its state comes back in `computer.status`'s `job`. install: the three install scripts are first downloaded to a temp directory, checked, and then `install.sh --no-modify-path` is run from disk (`CUA_DRIVER_RS_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=0`); after install, `telemetry disable`, then grant automatically. grant: `cua-driver permissions grant` (pops a system window on the Mac). cancel only stops the install |
| `browser.status` / `browser.install` / `browser.open` / `browser.cancel` | `{}` → `Browser`: whether ego lite is installed, first-time setup, stats, read-only probes. Install downloads the official DMG, verifies its signature (Team `JGQLC6YQYJ`) and notarization, then ditto's it into Applications, keeping quarantine. Open runs `open` on it on that Mac |
| `browser.call` | `{session, script?, look?, full?, screenshot?, timeout_ms?}` → `{output, image?}`: `ego-browser nodejs` (script via stdin) runs the assistant's script in the task space named `session` (`task` and `page` are ready-made), or takes a snapshot for look. The last result line is marked with `@@persona-browser@@` (NUL can't be used: ego drops the whole output); screenshots go separately in `image` |
| `plugin.node.have` / `plugin.node.put.begin` / `.chunk` / `.commit` | the plugin's package on this computer: `{id, version, digest}` → `{have}`; `begin {id, version, digest, size}` → `{upload_id}`, `chunk {upload_id, offset, data}` (in order, 1 MB), `commit {upload_id}`: verifies sha256 and unpacks into `~/.persona/plugins/<id>/<version>/` |
| `plugin.node.start` / `plugin.node.stop` | `start {id, name, version, command, args?, env?, rpc, http?, keep, lease_seconds, init}` → `{id, version, state, error?}`: starts it (if identical to what is running, leaves it alone and just renews the lease; if a new version doesn't come up within 30 seconds, rolls back to the previous version and reports an error). `init` is the program's `initialize` (config, secrets sent to the computer, never written to disk). `stop {id}` |
| `plugin.node.sync` / `plugin.node.renew` / `plugin.node.status` | `sync {programs: [{id, version, digest}], installed: [id]}` → `{programs: [state]}`: those not in `programs` are stopped and their packages deleted; those not in `installed` are deleted along with their data. `renew {ids, lease_seconds}`; `status` → `{programs}` |
| `plugin.node.dial` | `{id, plugin}` → `{}`: connects to this plugin program's HTTP socket and opens a stream `id` (after that, bytes flow over `stream.*` events, same as `port.dial`); if the program isn't running or doesn't serve HTTP it returns `code: not_running` |
| `plugin.node.call` | `{id, method, params?}` → the program's answer: a plugin protocol method (programs on the hub call it via `nodes.call`); if the program isn't running it returns `code: not_running` |
| `port.dial` | `{id, port, keep_awake?, pair?, link?, attach?, stream_version?}` → `{}`, `{stream_version: 1}` for negotiated directional EOF, or `{link: 1}` when it opened a screen session for 5900 with `pair` (`link`; `attach` rejoins a live one without dialing, else `session_gone`). Dials this local port (the address it was bound to at scan time, otherwise 127.0.0.1 then ::1; local only) and opens stream `id`. If nothing is listening, it returns `code: port_gone`. Both sides pass bytes over the `stream.*` events below. |
| events `plugin.node.state` / `plugin.node.event` | node → hub: `{id, version, state, error?}` (came up, stopped on lease expiry), `{id, event, params}` (events the program sends; the hub forwards them to programs on the hub) |
| `credential.gh_token` | `{host}` → `{token}`: runs `gh auth token --hostname <host>` non-interactively on this machine, for the GitHub connector (`github.auth.from_machine`). Only the hub can call it (the hook / MCP `node.sock` doesn't accept it); the token is never logged. gh not installed reports `code: no_gh`; not signed in (or signed in via the keychain, unreadable over ssh) reports `code: not_signed_in`; old nodes report unknown method |
| `connector.list` | → `{connectors:[{id, status, error?, guide?, via}]}`: connectors this computer itself can provide (currently only `imessage` on Mac; other systems return an empty list). `status` is `ok` / `not_configured` (no Messages data) / `no_permission` (no Full Disk Access; `guide` gives step-by-step instructions to enable it on this Mac, worded two ways depending on whether `via` is `ssh` or a resident `launchd` node) / `error` |
| `connector.chats` | `{id, limit?, before?, keep?}` → `{chats:[{id, name, group?, members:[{handle, name?}], services, last, preview?, from_me?, unread?}], more?, before?}`: chats, newest first. One person's chats across iMessage / SMS / RCS count as one; each group counts separately. `id` is a hash (`imessage-<12 chars>`) and contains no phone number. Read-only. `keep: contacts` (used by the Inbox and assistant) lists only chats handed to Persona; the web app's own browsing doesn't pass it |
| `connector.older` | `{id, chat, limit?, before?, keep?}` → `{chat, messages:[{id, at, kind: message\|event, from_me?, sender?, text?, service?, attachments?:[{kind, name, mime, size}], reply_to?, edited?, unsent?, unread?, undecoded?}], more?, before?}`: a chat's latest page or the page before `before`, oldest first. Tapbacks don't count as messages; attachments are descriptions only. No permission reports `code: no_permission`; no such chat (or, with `keep: contacts`, it isn't handed to Persona) reports `code: no_chat`. Only the hub can call it; nothing is logged (no numbers or bodies); old nodes report unknown method |
| `connector.search` | `{id, query, limit?, days?, keep?}` → `{hits:[{chat, message}]}`: messages from the last `days` (default 365) days whose text contains `query`, newest first (the assistant's `imessage_search`); `keep` defaults to contacts (someone from the address book among the members, or a chat the user has spoken in). `all` searches every chat. Verification codes are masked. Matching only; `query` is never spliced into SQL |
| `codex.answer` | `{session_id, id, resolution}`: answers a Codex card the node listed, or a command-input card ("Commands waiting for input"); a refusal is an error with `code`, and nothing is typed (but `command_input_unconfirmed`: the line may be in). The devices manager uses the internal `codex.owner_answer` RPC when the hub relays verified full-device provenance and the node advertises `owner_controls_v1`. |

`git.status` also accepts `{cwd, identity_only: true}` for manager authorization matching. It reads local metadata only and returns `{version: 1, path_resolved?, is_repo, cwd, root?, common_dir?, origin?, head_oid?}`. `path_resolved: true` certifies physical path resolution before cleaning parent segments; managers require it for paths named by standing-authorization cards. Older nodes omit it and those cards remain manual. `cwd` and Git paths are resolved on the node; `origin` is a credential-free canonical repository identifier. Linked worktrees share `common_dir`, the only cross-directory repository authorization evidence. Clones can share `origin`, but a copied URL proves no identity; independent clones require separate standing grants. Other status requests keep their existing response.

Stash selections carry the full lowercase object ID (`oid`, SHA-1 or SHA-256) from the list.
`apply`, `pop` and `drop` require both `index` and `oid`; missing identities and moved, removed or mismatched
entries return `git_stash_stale` before applying or deleting anything. Refresh and explicitly reselect; never
retry a mutation automatically. Apply uses the OID, so a later stack change cannot substitute other content.
Pop holds the removal boundary across OID application and deletion; conflicts retain the stash. An apply or pop that
stopped on merge conflicts (git printed `CONFLICT` and paths are unmerged) is `git_stash_conflicted` with those `files`, not
`git_conflict`, whose files are ones the apply would overwrite and so left alone. Removal uses
Git's files-backend common-directory reference/reflog locks (also shared by terminal Git and linked worktrees),
rewrites the reflog chain and updates the reference, including a packed final reference. Reftable, symbolic or
redirected stash storage, and installed reference-transaction hooks return `git_stash_unsupported` before pop/drop;
OID-only apply remains available. Publication failures are errors and may require inspection after content was applied.
A request sending only an index is refused by the node. The web app disables apply/pop/drop on rows from nodes
without a valid `oid` and show an update notice; push/list remain available. The hub forwards these fields unchanged.

Streams (`internal/streams`, both directions):

| Event | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `stream.data {id, data}` | Base64 bytes, at most 32 KiB per chunk. The sender waits at 512 KiB unacknowledged in each direction. |
| `stream.ack {id, n}` | Acknowledges `n` bytes written to the local endpoint. |
| `stream.eof {id}` | In stream version 1, the sender reached EOF and will send no further data for this direction. The receiver writes all preceding data and calls `CloseWrite` on its socket. The reverse direction remains open. |
| `stream.close {id, error?, abort?}` | Full stream close. By default the receiver drains queued bytes before closing. With `abort: true` it closes immediately and drops pending bytes. Older receivers ignore `abort` and perform their usual full close. |

Directional EOF is negotiated separately for each `port.dial`. A hub with a TCP endpoint that supports `CloseWrite` offers `stream_version: 1` on the outer `devices.call` envelope. A capable manager copies that version into the node's `port.dial` parameters. An older manager forwards only the original parameters, so the node sees no offer. A capable node echoes version 1 only if it accepted the offer and its endpoint supports `CloseWrite`. An absent or unsupported offer, or a reply without the matching version, selects the legacy mode, where EOF sends a full `stream.close`. This requires no protocol floor change or dial retry. Browser-side WebSocket half-close is outside this contract. The hub's binary WebSocket bridge uses full close. Screen sessions, previews and plugin sockets use their existing stream behavior.

The hub registers the stream before `port.dial`, and the node registers it before replying. The hub can queue bytes and EOF received before the reply, then start pumping in the selected mode. Each sender places its EOF after its last data in the same ordered queue. After sending its own EOF and applying the peer's EOF to its socket, each endpoint can release the stream. The dialing node then sends a full `stream.close` so the manager retires its tracking. A single EOF leaves that tracking in place. On cancellation and errors, a version 1 endpoint can send `stream.close` with `abort: true` even after sending EOF. RPC disconnect closes the local sockets.

A full close may arrive before the node opens a stream, for example when the hub gives up on a slow `port.dial` or `preview.open`. Each side remembers for 2 minutes (at most 1024 ids) the ids it heard closed without holding them and refuses to register them. The first data or EOF for an unknown id gets a full close back. The hub's stream ids include a process token so a surviving node never sees an id reused after a hub restart.

### External adapter advertisements and execution

`launchers.list` may contain `source:"external"` and an optional `external` object:
`{adapter_id,id,name,engine,revision,capabilities:{contexts,runtimes,platforms},credential_state,models,unavailable_code?,stale?}`.
`id` is the target's stable ID, distinct from the shell-safe `persona_ext_` launcher identity; models use the existing
`AgentModel` shape. Advertisements are per machine, not credentials or executable recipes. No URL, environment,
command, local path or secret belongs in this object. Unconfigured nodes omit the field and keep the original wire.

Only the manager's resolved parameters for the actual main chat's saved explicit model pick may carry
`external:{scope:"main-chat-pick",session_id,adapter_id,target_id,revision}` on `assistant.send` or headless
`session.send`; `assistant.model` returns the same binding for a legitimate resume. Client-supplied bindings are
removed before resolution. `session_id` is the real main conversation, not a caller's self-declared purpose.
The node requires its own registered target, an exact model ID, CLI runtime, POSIX and no required agent sandbox.
Missing scope on an older manager is a refusal, never permission to treat a reserved name as a shell command.

External targets are excluded from coding/terminal starts, purpose defaults, profiles/tiers, background tasks,
prewarming and automatic fallback. A directory update alone does not restart an active process or change its
confirmed model: the process binding keeps its revision until a genuinely new start. Configuration mismatch or an
unsupported combination returns a stable `adapter_*` error with `delivered:"none"` before user input is handed over;
there is no silent provider/runtime substitution or automatic message replay.

hub → node events (handled in the order sent): `terminal.input {session_id, text}`, `terminal.resize {session_id, cols, rows}`, `terminal.scroll {session_id, lines, up, column?, row?}` (scroll wheel: herdr hands it to programs that take the mouse, such as Claude Code's full-screen rendering and Codex; otherwise it scrolls herdr's own history.
The node splits it into `lines` one-line events, landing on the `column` / `row` cell, or the center of the screen if not given), `terminal.click {session_id, column, row}` (left button down + up), `terminal.keepalive {session_ids}` (every 20 s, for terminals under takeover; the node lets go after hearing nothing for 75 s).

Full herdr interface (feature `herdr_client`): hub → node RPC `herdr.client.open {client_id, cols, rows, session_id?, focus?}` (`session attach` starts a herdr client inside a PTY; at most 4 per computer, the 5th gets `code: too_many`; unsupported returns `unsupported: …`),
events `herdr.client.input {client_id, data | b64}`, `.resize {client_id, cols, rows}`, `.ack {client_id, bytes}` (cumulative), `.close {client_id}`, `.keepalive {client_ids}` (every 20 s; the node closes after hearing nothing for 75 s); node → hub events `herdr.client.data {client_id, data}` (base64; the node stops reading the PTY when the browser is 256 KB behind), `herdr.client.end {client_id, error}` (client exited, lease expired, browser not reading; not sent for closes the hub requested).

Focus sync (feature `herdr_focus`): hub → node event `herdr.client.focus {client_id, session_id}` (the page is showing another pane: the node has herdr focus it; requests for the same view replace each other; if the pane isn't one the host lists or the view is gone, nothing happens); node → hub event `herdr.focus.changed {workspace_id, tab_id, pane_id, session_id?, source, client_id?}` (herdr's focus changed: `persona` = just requested on behalf of `client_id`'s view, `client` = that client was actually typed in / clicked within 1.5 s, `other` = anything else; herdr's event itself doesn't say who changed it).

node → hub events: `session.mode_set {session_id, from?, to, actor?}` (a plan hook returned a selected permission mode with authenticated display provenance; manager-only, "Session mode changes"), `session.mode_restart {session_id, mode, outcome, reason?}` (what became of a queued restart into a permission mode, `done`, `failed` or `dropped` with why; the manager keeps it and passes it on to no one, "Session mode changes"), `fs.changed {dirs?, git?}` (the listing of a folder in `fs.watch` changed (names, sizes, times), or a Git directory's `git status` changed; the hub turns it into `fs_changed` for the relevant pages), `terminal.frame {session_id, epoch, seq, full, cols, rows, data}` (frames less than 30 ms apart are merged by the node into one: diff bytes are concatenated, and a full frame drops the diffs before it), `terminal.end {session_id, error, control?, taken?}` (the stream stopped and can't restart: the session isn't running, herdr keeps refusing; with `control`, the takeover ended: `taken` means someone else grabbed it, otherwise the lease expired),
`session.items {session_id, items, history, from_seq, to_seq}`, `session.delta {session_id, text}` (the message being written as one text, "" when there is none: the headless assistant's from its stream, a Claude session Persona started from its MessageDisplay hook while the session is watched, a runtime's as it sends it), `session.live {session_id, live}` (status line of a watched, working Claude (on hosts that can read the screen: herdr, herdr-core, Orca), sent only on change, with a trailing `null` when it ends; see "Live status"), `session.echo {session_id, client_msg_id, text, images, sent_at, after_seq, line?, in?}` (pushed once when the node records a send and once when it recognizes its line, again when it finds the line anew in the transcript a runtime's session moved to (`in`, "Matching pending messages"); the hub stores it in `sent_messages.echo`; an already-recognized one is never overwritten by a late "still waiting"), `sessions.changed {sessions}` (a list byte-identical to the last one written on this connection is not written again; after a `sessions.revs`, an answer to `sessions.list`, an engine switch or a reconnect the next list goes even when it is the same),
`sessions.revs {revs}` (checked every second, only changed revs are sent; when the list itself changes, revs go with `sessions.changed`),
`usage {buckets:[{minute, model, launcher?, agent?, in, cache_write, cache_read, out, req}], full?, add?, load?, cpus?, launchers?}` (every 10 seconds, only changed minutes, with full per-minute values;
a minute has a bucket per model, launcher and agent (`agent`: `proto.Session.Agent`'s names, absent from an older node); `launchers: true`: the buckets name their launcher;
the first one after connecting is `full: true` with the whole last 26 hours of file-metered agents (plus legacy unknown-agent rows), preserving runtime-only agents; `add: true` instead adds the buckets as per-request deltas, without replacing load/CPU metadata, and cannot be combined with `full`),
`metrics {sample: MetricSample}` (every 10 seconds, aligned to whole 10 seconds; the manager stores it in `machine_metrics`),
`codex.interactions {interactions}` (all open Codex / compatible forks questions and approvals on this machine, the questions of Claude sessions outside Persona's terminals and the commands waiting for input in agy panes ("Commands waiting for input"), sent in full on any change; the manager adds and removes cards; old versions that don't know it keep using screen cards).
(All of these first reach the manager connected to this computer; interactions, status, usage and monitoring belong to it, and it forwards what the web app needs to the hub; see "Computer events" below.)

node → manager / hub requests (`interaction.create`, `computer.elicit`, `mcp.*`, `assistant.lark`, `lark.sent`, `gate.relay`, `mail.attachment` answered by the manager; `notify` answered by the hub):
- `usage.backfill.status {agents?}` → `{done, since?, before?, agents?}` and `usage.backfill {buckets:[{minute, model, launcher?, agent?, in, cache_write, cache_read, out, req}], through, done, agents?}` → `{stored}` (answered by the manager): the token usage backfill. A few minutes after connecting the node asks whether its history wants one; unless `done`, it reads its transcripts from `since` to `before` (Unix seconds: where the history begins or the hour after the last one stored, and the start of its live window), rate-limited, sums the replies by the hour (`minute` is the hour's start), model and launcher, and sends them a week at a time, oldest first, whole hours a request (`through`: the last hour in it, a week's last request the week's last hour; `done` on the very last, which may have no buckets). Only numbers are sent. The manager stores an hour only when the machine has no usage in it yet and records `through` and `done`, so a scan cut off goes on from there and one sent again adds nothing (`stored`: hours added); an older manager answers `unknown method` and the node does nothing.
  By agent: the node names the agents it reads (`agents: ["claude", "codex", …]`) and the manager answers each one's `{done, since?, before?}` under `agents` as well (its own fields stay the first record's, what an older node reads); Claude Code's is the machine's first record, any other agent has its own. A request says the agents it read through `through` (`agents`; the manager stores only their buckets and moves their records on), and an hour is stored for an agent only when the machine has none of that agent's usage in it.
- `interaction.create {interaction}` → `{resolution}` (blocks until handled / expired; on expiry returns `{"dismiss":true}`). A detachable assistant command-gate card returns after at most 75 seconds with `{"dismiss":true,"pending":true,"approval_id":"<original card>","message":"…"}` instead of holding its turn; a later ordinary Allow stores a one-time grant for the exact original call and messages its conversation to retry once. A matching retry receives `{"allow":true,"approval_id":"<original card>"}` only after that grant is atomically consumed and persisted; a changed input or second retry does not. When the manager answers from an "Always allow in this session" it kept (or one a card answered meanwhile covers) rather than from an answer to this card, the resolution has `"remembered":true` next to `allow` and `always`; only the manager sets it, a client's answer never carries it (the sent-as-user ledger records such a write as `conversation_always`)
- `mcp.tools {assistant?, session_id?, guest?, revision?, leader_only?, tool_set?}` → `{tools, revision?}` or `{unchanged: true, revision}`. An optional revision matching the manager's current task-link cursor waits until it changes or a 30-second heartbeat expires; unchanged heartbeats do not compute the tool list. The cursor is captured before listing and invalidated on manager restart. Older managers omit it and retain one-shot discovery. With `leader_only: true`, an empty session returns the task-leader tool definitions for registration, and a named session returns them only for an active task leader eligible to use them. This query does not long-poll or fetch the general tool list. `tool_set: "supervise"`: a background supervisor's round asks for only the tools supervision uses, from `PERSONA_TOOL_SET` in its `personad mcp`'s environment; a manager that does not know the value, or an older one, answers the whole list. The set is fixed for the process, so the revision cursor applies to it unchanged. A manager may mark an Assistant tool with `work_guide_tool: true`. When the managed skill is installed, the MCP server keeps those definitions behind `work_tools_search` on each connection. Selecting exact names triggers `notifications/tools/list_changed`. Older servers ignore the marker.
- `mcp.call {name, args, session_id, wait_updates?, call_id?}` → `{content, is_error, error_kind?, retry_after?}` (`error_kind` is the failure category: `declined` the user or `connector_gate` didn't agree, `unavailable` the connector isn't signed in / can't connect, `rate_limited` rate limited; `retry_after` is how many seconds of rate limiting remain. Included only when the hub knows; `personad tool` sets its exit code from it). `wait_updates` and the node's canonical UUID `call_id` are present together only for an opted-in call on a capable hub. A malformed or oversized id disables wait reporting without failing the tool call or publishing an event

`source_permissions_v1` adds optional outer `source_permission: {at, session, generation, class, digest}` to a node's message-producing MCP calls. `class` is `bypass` or `prompting`; it is observed by the source node, not accepted from tool arguments. The call digest binds the source session and exact tool name/JSON arguments after RPC JSON compaction/escaping. Only authenticated node transport installs manager-side provenance. The manager retains creation-time evidence across delayed reports and retries; missing/mixed evidence states no class. In its initial `node.info` call, the devices manager includes `source_permissions_v1` in `manager_features`. A target node accepts reserved `session.source_send` only when this first call announces support. The manager uses it to send a rebuilt source observation; ordinary `session.send` never uses a supplied source class. All caller spellings of `source_permission`/`from_mode` are removed before this internal RPC is chosen. It is not owner input, permission approval or a new public device method. Older nodes or intermediaries keep ordinary sends with no source declaration.

- `computer.elicit {conversation, params, call_id?}` → the MCP elicitation result: LCU's nested permission or question, shown through the existing cards. An opted-in outer `computer.call` carries the same canonical UUID `call_id`, which the node includes here. The manager resolves only a live id in its own registry, joining the originating machine's existing reporter and card state; the eliciting node cannot choose a destination machine. It reports `approval` or `answer` and then restores the newest still-open card or the call's base state. An unknown, malformed, oversized or completed id gets no reporter and no event, without failing the elicitation
- `lark.sent {command?, method, path, text?, session_id?, message_ref?, let_through}` → `{}`: the node's gate proxy forwarded a write and the API answered with a 2xx; the manager keeps it in the sent-as-user ledger. `let_through` is `{kind: "rule", rule: {method, path, body?, action}}`, `{kind: "conversation_always"}`, `{kind: "permission_mode"}` (a classified ordinary write allowed by assistant bypass), or `{kind: "card", interaction_id, answered_by?}`; `text` is at most 4000 characters; `message_ref` is the id the API's answer gave for the message the write made (absent when there was none, the answer could not be read or the id was longer than 200 characters: it is not cut), which the manager keeps only for a route that creates one message in a conversation. The computer is the connection's, never a field; `permission_denied` for a computer the manager does not know, `invalid_params` for a read or a `let_through` that is not one of these, `no_database` without a ledger; an older manager reports an unknown method, which the node only logs
- `gate.relay {command, method, path, query?, header?, body?}` → `{status, header?, body?}`: a call of a relayed command gate (`relay` in `assistant.lark`'s gates, gate file `socket_env`) that the node's gate proxy let through by the gate's rules; the manager asks the extension that has the gate for its credentials, dials its unix socket, puts the token on the call and answers status, body (base64, at most 8 MiB each way) and a few headers (`Content-Type`, `Content-Encoding`, `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified`). `permission_denied` for a computer the manager does not know, `not_found` when no enabled extension has a relayed gate with that command, `unavailable` when it gave no socket or credentials or does not answer; an older manager reports an unknown method, and the node answers the script 502
- `mail.attachment {account_id, uid, mailbox?, attachment_id, session_id?, assistant?, guest?}` → `{filename, mime, size, data}` (`data` base64): the bytes of a mail attachment for `mail_save_attachment`, which the node answers itself and writes on its machine. The manager checks the caller as for `mcp.call` (work machine, assistant conversation, guest given the tool), then answers only while the mail connector offers `mail_save_attachment` to it; at most 25 MB (`attachment too large` otherwise). `filename` is the sender's, uncleaned. The computer is the connection's, never a field; an older manager reports an unknown method, which the node returns as the tool's error
- `agents.closeout.check {session_id}` → `{reason?}`: an Agent is about to stop after a turn that did work, without a closeout; the manager answers with the reason to hold the stop with while its `closeout` triage switch is on, and with nothing otherwise. The node holds a stop at most once per turn (`stop_hook_active`).
- `agents.closeout.brief {session_id, cwd?}` → `{context?}`: an Agent's session is starting (Claude Code's SessionStart hook, in a session with Persona's own hooks); the manager answers with the closeout's form to hand it as the hook's additional context while its `closeout` triage switch is on, and with nothing otherwise or for a review's reviewer. The node waits 1.5 seconds and asks once per session.
- `assistant.view.check {session_id, message}` → `{reason?}`: the persona-view check on the trusted assistant's Stop; the devices manager passes it through to the hub. The hub decides whether to check based on the session's identity. When reason is non-empty, the node returns decision=block the first time, and stops asking when stop_hook_active=true. Replies up to 1 MB, 4 errors of 2000 characters each; the node waits at most 5 seconds. Not applicable, or a disconnect, keeps the original Stop behavior. This is not a public web app / extension action interface, and it accepts no machine identity supplied by the client.
- `launchers.pull {name, own_service?: {agent, known, own, via?}}` → `{launcher: ManagedLauncher}`: a withheld provider's secrets for this connection's computer (that computer's own key when it has one). The manager checks the connection's machine, never params, against the scope and refuses with `launcher_out_of_scope`, or `launcher_own_service` when the provider says `own_service: skip` and the node reports a service of its own (sent only for such a provider), or `launcher_key_unresolved` when the key is a reference that did not resolve; the message is in the user's language. A pending computer is refused like every other request from it.
- `launchers.agents_default {}` → `{launcher?, model?, effort?}`: Model Settings › Agents for pi on this connection's computer, only when it names a Persona-managed provider pi can use and the computer is in its scope; names only, the key still comes through `launchers.pull`. Empty otherwise; an older manager answers `unknown method` and pi keeps its own default.
- `notify {title, body?, level?, silent?, id?, session_id?}` → `{sent, reason?}` (`personad notify`: `machine_id` is this connection's machine; extension `actions` / `ui` / `state` are not accepted; otherwise the same as `POST /api/v1/notify`, with mute and "Needs you" preferences applied the same way)

### Computer link (persona-link, kind link)

Computers the hub can't connect into (laptops) have persona-link connect out to the hub's TLS port and open streams on that link; inside a stream is the RPC above (bytes forwarded as is to that machine's resident node).
Once the hub has checked the credential it hands the link and its streams as is to the manager (`devices.accept` + `GET /api/v1/bus/relay`, "Computers (devices.*)" below); the messages "the hub" sends below are sent by the manager, and close codes are passed through.
When the manager isn't connected, `GET /api/v1/link` returns `503 assistant_offline`. Only what is on the wire is listed here:

- `GET /api/v1/link` (WebSocket, a credential with `role: link`, TLS only, loopback excepted). Text messages, one JSON each:
  - persona-link → hub: `{"type":"hello","machine","version","address","features"?}` (the first message, within 10 seconds), `{"type":"open_failed","id","error"}`,
    `{"type":"presence","active"?,"notifies"?,"ttl_ms"?}` (only from persona-link with a compatible parent: whether you are at this computer and its notifications show, as the link comes up and for every line the parent writes; `ttl_ms` how much longer an active one counts, at most 120000; a missing field is false),
    `{"type":"rang","interaction_id"}` (only from persona-link with a compatible parent: the parent confirmed the notification of this card, as the summary names it; sent only on the link whose summary listed the card: persona-link numbers its links for the parent, and drops a confirmation for an earlier one; a confirmation only wakes the pushes waiting for it and changes no computer's being a desktop);
    `features` lists what this persona-link takes besides streams: `attention` (the "Needs you" summary below).
  - hub → persona-link: `{"type":"endpoints","endpoints":[{"url","kind"}]}` (https candidates only), `{"type":"open","id"}`,
    `{"type":"node","online","error"}` (when the manager's connection to the resident node comes, goes or is resumed, and after `endpoints` to a link that connects while the node is already connected; never `online` while the connection waits to be resumed), `{"type":"attention","attention":{…}}` (only to a link whose hello listed `attention`: once right after `endpoints`, then on every change; a computer waiting to be confirmed or marked `trust: "work"` gets an empty summary, which also takes back what it had; while the hub cannot say which computers wait, nothing new is sent to one not known to be a work computer).
    Both sides ignore a `type` they don't know.
  - `attention` is the "Needs you" summary of the manager that carries the computer, a full snapshot each time:
    `{"rev","needs_you","more","web_url"?,"items":[{"machine_id","session_id","title","place","kind","detail","muted","notify","interaction_id"?,"since"?,"route"}]}`.
    `needs_you` is the web app's "Needs you" count (muted agents and agents waiting only on the assistant's decision included), `items` at most 20 of them (one per agent, by its oldest card handed to the user, else its oldest card; newest `since` first, then by machine and session id, so past 20 the oldest are cut; `kind` is `permission` / `plan` / `question` / `screen`), `more` the rest;
    `title` and `place` are at most 80 characters and `detail` 60, an ellipsis included;
    `notify` is whether the push rule would push the item: once a card of the agent is the user's (rung, as a push is sent; not a question the assistant is still deciding on; a terminal dialog once the screen card made for it is; a card made again after a reconnect or a restart only when it is known to have rung: a screen card read again as the card that rang), and never when `muted`: clients notify on `notify` alone, the first time an item shows with it (which may be after it was listed without it: the assistant handed its question to the user), and `muted` is for showing; `since` is RFC 3339 UTC to the second; `route` is the web app's `/s/<machine>/<session>`, percent-encoded; `web_url` is the hub's https `public_url` (sub-path included), else the `address` of the hello.
    `rev` is a hash of the rest: the same summary has the same `rev`. Nothing needs you: `needs_you: 0`, `items: []`.
  - Close codes: 4001 replaced by a new link from the same machine, 4002 credential revoked, 4003 hello doesn't match the credential, 1001 hub shutting down. Both sides ping every 10 seconds and disconnect after 5 seconds without a pong (configurable).
    When hub.json sets `link.ping_seconds` / `link.ping_timeout_seconds`, `endpoints` also carries `ping_ms`, `ping_timeout_ms` (milliseconds), and persona-link uses them on this link
    (clamped to 50 milliseconds through 10 minutes; ignored unless both are positive). When not set, these two fields aren't sent.
- `GET /api/v1/link/stream?id=<id from open>` (WebSocket, same credential, permessage-deflate): binary messages whose content is the RPC byte stream;
  the hub treats it as failed if it doesn't arrive within 15 seconds. When the link drops, its streams drop with it.

## hub ↔ hub (linked hubs)

- `POST /api/v1/peer/pair` (`Authorization: Bearer jx_…`, the other side's link code): `{hub_id,name,version,fp,tls_port,endpoints,token,center,term}` →
  the same fields (`token` is the link credential given back to the other side; `center` / `term` are the center and term of the code issuer's group: the side using the code joins that group). Invalid / used / expired code: 401; this hub has no TLS: 409.
- `GET /api/v1/peer` (WebSocket, TLS only, a credential with `role: peer`, permessage-deflate): binary messages whose content is the byte stream of the JSON-line RPC from hub ↔ node above:
  - Calls: `hello {hub_id,name,version,epoch}` (once each way), `stream.open {id}` (the stream carries one HTTP/1.1 connection to the other side's peer server),
    `relay {to,from,ttl,method,params}` (`creds.import {tokens:[{id,name,kind,role,created_at,last_seen,hash}]}` → `{added}`: a member hands credentials to the center;
    `creds.revoked {tokens:[{id,name,kind,role,hash}]}` (other fields unused) → `{revoked}`: tells the group's hubs about revoked credentials;
    `pair.code {}` → a pairing code: `personad hub pair` on a member), `unpair {}`;
  - One-way: `rec` (the hub's record: links, `center`, `term`, computers in hub.json), `stream.data` / `stream.ack` / `stream.close`.
  - Close codes: 4011 duplicate link, 4012 unlinked, 4013 can't keep up sending, 1001 hub shutting down. Both sides ping every 10 seconds and disconnect after 5 seconds without a pong (configurable).
- HTTP on a stream always carries `X-Persona-Peer-Ttl` (starts at 8, decremented each hop; at 0 returns `508 mesh_loop`) and is forwarded hop by hop to the target hub:
  - Web app requests a member forwards to the center: as is (including `Authorization`), plus `X-Persona-Peer-Source: <lan|public> <client address> <tls|plain>` (the member's judgment of the source).
    Can't forward: `503 center_unreachable`; forwarding failed: `502 hub_unreachable`.
  - Node streams the center opens through a member: `GET /api/v1/peer/node`, `Upgrade: persona-node`, `X-Persona-Peer-Node: <member hub_id>/<machine id>`, `X-Persona-Peer-From: <center hub_id>`;
    the member returns `101`, followed by the node's byte stream. A request from a hub that isn't its center gets 403; not in hub.json gets 404; can't open gets 502 (`error` is the reason).
- Admin interface (after signing in to the admin UI): `GET /api/v1/admin/mesh`, `GET /api/v1/admin/peers`, `POST /api/v1/admin/peers/code`, `POST /api/v1/admin/peers`,
  `POST /api/v1/admin/peers/probe`, `DELETE /api/v1/admin/peers/{hub_id}`, `POST /api/v1/admin/peers/{hub_id}/center`;
  the same set under `/api/v1/admin/cli/…` is for the command line on the hub machine (loopback + main token).

## hub → connector (kind service)

- The hub connects to `<address>` pinned to the `fp` in the pairing link (optionally via a `socks5://` proxy): `POST /api/v1/connector/pair {code,token,machine,hub_id,hub_name}` once;
  after that `GET /api/v1/connector/info` (every 30 seconds, liveness and RTT) and `GET /api/v1/connector/stream` (WebSocket, the node's byte stream), both with `Authorization: Bearer <credential>`.
  `info` answers `{"machine","version","features"?,"attention_rev"?}`: `features` as in a link's hello, `attention_rev` the `rev` of the summary the connector holds (absent: none).
- `POST /api/v1/connector/attention` (same credential), body one `attention` object above and nothing after it but white space, the whole body at most 64 KiB → `204`; `400` without a `rev`, with anything else in the body or over the cap, `401` with another credential. The manager posts only to a connector whose `info` listed `attention`:
  on every change, and after an `info` whose `attention_rev` is not the summary's (a post that failed, a connector that restarted). The connector drops the summary when another hub pairs and after 2 minutes without the hub coming in.
  When hub.json sets a heartbeat (`link`), the stream request also carries `X-Persona-Ping: <interval ms> <timeout ms>`, and the connector pings on this stream accordingly; when not set it's omitted.
- 401: don't dial again for 5 minutes; 429: follow `Retry-After`; 503 `node_unavailable`: show the reason and back off as usual; stream closed with 4002: needs re-pairing, stop trying; 1001: back off as usual.

## Bus (service ↔ hub, `GET /api/v1/bus`)

The hub is a channel: the assistant is a separate process that connects out to the hub's bus and stays connected, rather than living inside the hub. The hub knows nothing of any service's business semantics.
By default the hub starts the assistant as its own child process (`personad assistant`); the assistant can also run elsewhere.
The channel itself is authentication, handshake, a roster, dispatch by method name, and calls in both directions; the assistant and hub call each other through it; see "Methods the assistant uses" below.

**Identities and tokens**

- One identity per service. There is one role, `manager` (a manager process such as the assistant; ids look like `assistant`, start with a lowercase letter, at most 32 characters); tokens for other roles are rejected at upgrade (401).
- Tokens start with `jb_` and can only open `/api/v1/bus`: neither device tokens nor the main token can open the bus, and `jb_` can't open web app endpoints either (401). The hub stores only the sha256 (table `bus_identities`).
- Only `Authorization: Bearer` is accepted, not `?token=`. Public sources need TLS (otherwise `403 tls_required`); failure counting and `429 rate_limited` are the same as for web app endpoints; loopback and LAN aren't counted.
- Creating and revoking are functions inside the hub (`createBusToken`, `revokeBusToken`, in `server/internal/hub/bustokens.go`). Every time the hub starts it creates one for the assistant and passes it via the child process's stdin;
  when the assistant runs elsewhere, create one with `personad hub assistant-token` (`assistant.external` in `docs/operations/config.md`). There's no endpoint or UI.
  Creating again for the same identity replaces the old token: the old one stops working immediately, and connections using it are closed with 4002.
- Member hubs in a linked group don't forward the bus to the center: a service belongs to whichever hub it connects to.
- Installation codes: `GET /i/<code>` is the install script and `GET /i/<code>/docker` the one for a container: no credential, and fetching them does not use the code up. Every manager may use every bus method and event: the hub keeps what each reports as its own. An identity with role `manager` is a manager. The roster also records the location it reported at its last handshake and `last_seen`; a new manager exchanges a one-time installation code for a token (`POST /api/v1/bus/join`, no credentials required).

**Managers (`/api/v1/managers`, answered by the hub itself)**

| Method | Path | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GET | `/api/v1/managers` | `{managers:[{id, name, online, default?, builtin?, hide?, hidden?, host?, os?, arch?, deploy?, version?, since?, last_seen?, installing?, needs_update?, inbox_needs_you?}], default, bot_conflicts?:[{platform, managers:[id, ...]}]}`: `hide` (the built-in manager only) is the user's choice to keep it out of the switcher while it is not used, and `hidden` says that is in effect: not the default, owning no machine and with nothing in its inbox that needs the user, so a machine that falls back to it shows it again by itself; the web app leaves a `hidden` manager out of the switcher. `needs_update` is `true` for an online manager whose `manager.hello` named no `config.own` (it runs on its built-in defaults, "Handshake" below); conflicts name managers sharing an enabled Feishu bot or bound WeChat account (latest reports, including offline managers; no raw bot identities). `inbox_needs_you` is how many open items of that manager's inbox are under "Needs you" (the listed items' `status` `action`, the ones not triaged yet and the connectors' among them: what `GET /api/v1/inbox?sources=all` lists open with that status for it), an integer ≥ 0 the manager reports itself (`inbox.needs_you`, "Methods the assistant uses" below); it is absent when not known (the manager is offline or being installed, or could not read its stored items), which is not 0. Agents waiting for the user are not in it. The default manager first, installations in progress last; `builtin` is the assistant started by the hub, `installing` is the installation code's expiry time. Roster changes (creation, rename, connection, disconnection, deletion, reported bot identities, and a changed `inbox_needs_you`, one second after it changed so that the numbers changing together are one push) push `{"type":"managers"}` to the web app when it requested `managers` (`?features=` or `client_hello`'s `features`), without entering the event log (the web app rereads the list after reconnecting) |
| POST | `/api/v1/managers` | `{name}` (1–40 characters) → 201 `{manager, code, expires_at, commands}`: a one-time installation code, valid for 10 minutes and one use; `commands` are the commands that install it, `{service, join, docker?}` (install commands) |
| POST | `/api/v1/managers/{id}/code` | A new code for an existing manager, or for one being installed (its code still good, or expired less than 7 days ago: `installing` in the past) → `{code, expires_at, commands}`; the hub's own assistant returns `409 builtin_manager` |
| POST | `/api/v1/managers/{id}/machines` | `{machine_id}` → `{machine_id, manager, from}`: one of the hub's own machines is carried by this manager from now on (`assistant`: back to the carrier); `400 not_movable` for a machine not in the hub's own list, `409 installing`, `404 no_manager` (removed meanwhile), `503 owners_unknown` (the hub could not read who carries which machine yet) |
| PATCH | `/api/v1/managers/{id}` | `{name?, default?: true, hide?}`: rename, set as default, or (the built-in manager only, `400` for another) keep it out of the switcher while it is not used; `hide: true` returns `409 builtin_in_use` while it is the default (or made it in the same request) or owns a machine, `hide: false` is always accepted; an installation in progress returns `409 installing` |
| DELETE | `/api/v1/managers/{id}` | Revoke (invalidate the code for an installation in progress) → `{ok}`; the default returns `409 default_manager`, the hub's own manager `409 builtin_manager`, a missing one `404 no_manager` |
| POST | `/api/v1/bus/join` | `{code}` → `{id, name, token, hub_id}`; an incorrect, expired or used code returns `401 bad_install_code` (counted per source); plaintext from the public internet `403 tls_required`, which voids the code it carried (it expires at once). A request may carry `builtin: true` (`persona-manager join --builtin`): a code is traded only by the join of its kind, the built-in manager's (`persona-hub manager-code`) only with it and every other only without it (`409 builtin_code` / `409 not_builtin_code`). The built-in manager's code is also refused while the built-in manager is not a bound service here (`409 builtin_not_service`: `assistant.mode` not `service`, or `assistant.external`) and from a public address (`403 builtin_local_only`); a code the hub cannot look up is refused (`503`). None of these refusals spends the code. Only the latest code of a manager works: a new one voids the unused ones before it, a join uses up all of them |

Editing the roster, creating codes and deleting require a full-permission device (read-only devices get 403).

**Per-manager routing (ownership)**

- **Which manager receives the request**: header `X-Persona-Manager: <id>`, or query `?manager=<id>` (for WebSockets and links opened in a browser; the header wins when both are supplied). Omitted means the default manager (`default` in `GET /api/v1/managers`), except for an extension's token, which acts as the manager whose extension it is (the one that recognized the token) and only as it: routes that name no object, merged lists (its manager's only) and an extension API prefix several managers serve go to it, and naming another manager, or another manager's computer, session, pending card or conversation (in the path, the query or the body), gets `403 other_manager`; `GET /api/v1/machines`, `/interactions` and `/sessions` list its manager's only ("Ownership"). An id absent from the roster returns `404 no_manager`; one present but disconnected returns `503 assistant_offline`, as when the assistant was offline before. One exception: on `GET /api/v1/sessions` `manager` is a filter, not routing: the header is not read there and a disconnected manager still gets 200 (see "One manager's sessions").
- **For requests tied to an object, the hub resolves ownership itself; specifying a manager does not override it**: `/machines/{mid}/…` belongs to the computer's manager, `/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/…` to the session's (a manager's own chat belongs to the one reporting it, other chats to the computer's), and `POST /interactions/{id}/resolve` or `/choose` to whoever reported that card. Everything else (assistant page, chats, schedules, Inbox, to-dos, model config, extensions and sources, usage…) uses the header / parameter above. When a list item (an Inbox item, an extension) carries `manager`, include it in requests for that item.
- **The `manager` field**: computers (`GET /api/v1/machines`, `machines` pushes), sessions (`GET /api/v1/sessions`, `sessions` / `sessions_delta` pushes) and pending cards (`GET /api/v1/interactions`, `interaction` pushes) each carry top-level `manager` (the manager id). With one manager, responses are unchanged except for this extra field. A manager's own live updates (`ws.broadcast`, "Messages to clients" below) carry it only when they are another manager's than the assistant the hub starts.
- **Merged lists**: without a manager specified, `GET /api/v1/inbox` (`items`), `/api/v1/todos` (`todos`), `/api/v1/extensions` (`extensions`), `/api/v1/plugins` (`plugins`) and `/api/v1/connectors` (`connectors`) query the default and other connected managers in turn, concatenate their lists (default first) and add `manager` to every item; other fields (`as_of`, `triage`, `can_install`…) come from the default manager, except the to-dos' `counts`: the hub adds up those of every manager it merges, member by member (numbers added, objects such as `sections` key by key, anything else the first's; one manager's as sent), before it takes the list's `ETag`, and leaves `counts` out when no manager sent them (an older manager adds nothing, so they cover every manager only while `features` lists `todo_view`). `GET /api/v1/todos/places` is joined the same way (its row in the REST table). With a manager specified, only its list is returned. Managers that do not answer, or answer with something other than a JSON object (`null` included), are omitted; if none answers, the default manager's response is returned unchanged (for example `503 assistant_offline`).
- **Inbox validator**: the merged `GET /api/v1/inbox` (no manager named, not an extension's token) answers a request that sends `If-None-Match` with `ETag: W/"i1-<32 hex digits>"`, a hash of the answer as localized for that request, leaving out the value of its top-level `as_of`. When a tag sent is that one (weak comparison, or `*`), the answer is `304 Not Modified` without a body, still `Cache-Control: no-store`: the list the client has is still the hub's, and the client keeps it with its `as_of`. Only a 200 that every manager answered with a 2xx carries a tag. The validator is the hub's: the managers are asked for their lists without the client's `If-None-Match`. A request without `If-None-Match` gets no `ETag`; a client with no tag yet sends one no answer has (the web app sends `W/"i1-"`). Each manager lists its items newest first and, among items of the same moment, by id, so the same items always give the same bytes and the same tag. The hub may give a request the merged inbox it made for the same query, language, role and managers in the last 2 seconds, unless a manager told the web app `{"type":"inbox"}` or a request other than GET or HEAD went to a manager since.
- **Inbox delta**: the merged `GET /api/v1/inbox` (no manager named, not an extension's token) with `since=<cursor>` answers only what changed since the list that cursor names: `{"as_of", "cursor", "delta": true, "items": […], "removed": [{"id", "manager"}], "triage"}`, where `items` are the items added or changed, each whole and stamped with `manager` as in the whole list, and `removed` the items gone from it, for whatever reason (filed more than three days ago or past the newest 200 done, forgotten, dropped). A client applies them by `(manager, id)`; each manager's items stay together in the managers' order, newest first and by id among items of the same moment.
  - **A cursor the hub cannot follow gets the whole list**, as without `since`, plus `cursor` and no `delta`; the client replaces its list. That covers `0` (what the web app sends before it holds a cursor), a cursor from before a manager restarted, and one past the 16 lists each manager keeps or unused for an hour. Nothing goes wrong: it costs one whole list.
  - **How the hub works it out**: each manager keeps the lists it answered with a cursor (each item's sum of the bytes it was listed with), and the same items listed again get the same cursor. The merged cursor holds each manager's part; it is opaque to clients. The answer is a delta only when every manager could follow its part; otherwise every manager is asked again without one.
  - **Older managers and requests without `since`**: a manager that fails, or that is older and answers without a cursor, gets the request answered as without `since`, with no cursor; the client then asks with the validator.
  - **Done items' chains on open (`chain=last`)**: with `since` (any cursor, `0` included), `chain=last` lists each done item whose chain has more than one entry with its newest entry alone and `chain_count`, how many it has; open items, and every item of a list asked without it, keep their whole chain. Done items are nearly all of a busy hub's list and their chains about half of its bytes, while the web app draws a chain only on the item's page, where it reads the item (`GET /api/v1/inbox/{id}`). A cursor follows only a list asked the same way (`sources`, `chain`). Hubs and managers without it ignore the parameter and send whole chains, with no `chain_count`.
  - **The web app** (`web/src/lib/inbox.ts` `reloadInbox`) keeps the cursor and the list it names in memory only, as the hub answered it before the page's pending marks are laid over it: a page's first list asks `since=0`, every `inbox` push and reconnect asks with the cursor, and a delta is applied to that list (`applyInboxDelta`) as above. It still sends `If-None-Match`, so a hub that knows no `since` can answer 304. An answer without a cursor (an older hub or manager, or one that failed) turns `since` off for ten minutes, the validator alone in its place. A Refresh's whole list (`POST /api/v1/inbox/refresh`) has no cursor; the held list and cursor stay, so the next delta is still from the list the cursor names. It asks without `chain=last`.
- **Paged lists**: `GET /api/v1/inbox/done` (`items`) pages by a cursor that is one manager's, so it is never merged: the named manager answers, else the default, and every item gets `manager` as in a merged list; the rest (`next`) is that manager's.
- **Offline managers**: data the hub already retains stays retained with `manager`: their computers (`online: false`, `error` says the assistant is offline) and sessions (`unknown` state), plus GETs whose last response is retained, such as extension lists (`extwire.KeptRoutes`). Items get no additional fields; "Last synced…" uses that manager's `online: false` and `last_seen` from `GET /api/v1/managers`. Operations through it return `503 assistant_offline`.

**Wire format**: each WebSocket text message is one line of `internal/rpc` JSON (the same as hub ↔ node), at most 64 MiB per message; both directions can call. Managers offer permessage-deflate and the hub accepts it when offered; the hub's own manager (its child, or the built-in assistant's service dialing the hub on the same machine) offers none, since compression saves nothing on a local link and costs each end its flate state:

```jsonc
// "助手" is the name the hub records for the assistant identity ("Assistant")
{"id":"s1","method":"manager.hello","params":{"id":"assistant","capabilities":["config.own"]}}
{"id":"s1","result":{"name":"助手","role":"manager","managers":[{"id":"assistant","name":"助手","role":"manager","online":true}],
                     "owner":"","owner_notes":"","assistant":{"machine_id":"server","machines":["server"]},"done_delay_ms":60000}}
{"id":"s2","error":{"code":"stale_connection","message":"…"}}
{"event":"managers","params":{"managers":[{"id":"assistant","name":"助手","role":"manager","online":false}]}}
```

- Both sides ping every 30 seconds and disconnect after 20 seconds without a pong. If the handshake isn't done within 40 seconds of connecting, the hub closes with 4003.
- A new connection for an identity replaces the old one **when its handshake succeeds**; the old one is closed with 4001.
- Before the handshake and after being replaced, every call on the connection returns `stale_connection` and events sent are dropped; the hub never calls a connection that hasn't shaken hands.
- Close codes: 4001 replaced by a new connection for the same identity, 4002 token revoked or replaced, 4003 bad handshake or timeout, 1001 hub shutting down.
- A dial the hub refuses: 401 with code `token_revoked` for a bus token it has no identity for (revoked or replaced; the only refusal a manager takes for "revoked", like 4002); a plain 401 for a token of another shape; 503 `store_unavailable` when it can't look tokens up (its database): no verdict on the token, try again.

### Handshake

`manager.hello {id,host?,os?,arch?,deploy?,version?,capabilities?,…}`. `id` must match the token, otherwise it returns `wrong_identity` and disconnects (4003).
