The roster records only `host`, `os`, `arch`, `deploy` (an assistant started by the hub reports `child`, one elsewhere reports `external`), `version`, and keeps `capabilities` while it is connected.
`capabilities` (at most 32 names) are stable names of what the manager supports, never renamed or reused. `config.own`: it reads its own sections of the configuration from its `manager.json` (`docs/operations/config.md` ("manager.json")). For a manager without it, the hub logs once that it runs on its built-in defaults, and `GET /api/v1/managers` marks it `needs_update` while it is online. `http_body_stream`: it takes `http.request_streamed` (a large request body on a relay stream of its own, "Forwarding client requests" below); a manager without it gets every body inside `http.request`. `assistant_start_service_tier`: the manager forwards a new conversation's optional native `service_tier` to the node for acknowledgment before its first turn; the hub advertises the same feature only while the default manager names it and rejects an explicit tier sent to a manager that does not. `mcp_wait_v1`: it accepts and emits `mcp.wait` through `devices.notify` for explicitly opted-in MCP calls; the hub sends hub-mediated approval updates only to a manager whose current connection names it.
The answer is `{name,role,managers:[{id,name,role,online}],owner,owner_notes,assistant:{machine_id,machines,standby?},done_delay_ms,persona_view?,html_views?,models?,notify?,locale?,mutes?,legacy_config?,secret_handoff_gate?,archived_apart?}`:

- `name`, `role`: the name and role the hub records for this identity (the hub's record wins; the role reported in hello doesn't count);
- `legacy_config` (in the handshake's answer to a built-in manager whose hello's `deploy` is not `child`, not in `manager.updated`): the hub's `hub.json` sections, raw (`assistant.owner` / `notes` / `machine` / `launcher`, `agents`, `kb`, `ai`, `hook_timeout_minutes`, `inbox.triage_ai` / `judge_ai` / `agent.machine`). The manager takes each over into its `manager.json` once, unless it has it already.
- `managers`: all managers the hub has tokens for; `online` is whether they're connected now;
- `archived_apart: true`: the hub takes a machine's archived rows apart from its list (`fleet.archived`, "Computer events" below).;
- The rest is what the hub knows that the manager needs (`assistantwire.Hello`): `machines` are the machines this manager owns, `assistant.machine_id` the hub's default machine (its own machine; failing that, the first one) when this manager owns it, else this manager's first own machine (a local one first; empty with none); a machine the manager stored or its `manager.json` names that isn't among them isn't used; `models.launchers` are its own machines' configured launchers. A machine moved between managers sends both a new answer (`manager.updated`);
  `standby`: this hub is a member of a linked group (scheduled tasks run on the center); `done_delay_ms` is hub.json notify's completion push delay (how long a task's Agent must be stopped to count as stopped), and `notify` `{done_delay_ms?,long_turn_ms?,background_hold_ms?}` are hub.json notify's push timings;
  `persona_view` / `html_views` are always `true` and no manager reads them; `models.launchers` are the launchers hub.json's `machines[].launchers` add for this manager's machines; `locale` is the user's language.
  The user's time zone and main chat aren't here: they are the assistant's own settings, reported to the hub in the snapshot's `profile`.
- **The manager's own sections are not in it**: the manager reads them from its `manager.json` and lays them over the answer (`docs/operations/config.md` ("manager.json")): `assistant.owner` (`owner`), `assistant.notes` (`owner_notes`), `assistant.machine` (over `assistant.machine_id`, when the hub has that machine), `assistant.launcher`, `assistant.supervision_batch_minutes` (an administrator pin over the saved setting, only when present),
  `agents`, the models (`ai`, `inbox.triage_ai` / `judge_ai`, `inbox.agent.machine`) and `hook_timeout_minutes` (`notify.hook_timeout_ms`).
  `owner` and `owner_notes` are in the answer, empty.
- `mutes` `{spaces,sessions,allowed?}`: the hub's mutes (`GET /api/v1/mutes`) of the manager's own machines only (as `fleet.mutes`), so a manager has them before it pushes anything; left out while the hub cannot read them (they follow with `fleet.mutes` once it can). `manager.updated` carries no `mutes`.
- `quiet_push` (bool, left out when off): the hub's push tiering switch (push levels) is on; the manager then holds back what is its own to send by the same levels (`server/internal/assistant/push_quiet.go`). Turning the switch on or off sends `manager.updated`.
- The assistant keeps this answer. Where it might have changed (the linked group changed center, the machine list changed), the hub coalesces for 200 milliseconds and recomputes; if it differs from what it last gave, it sends
  `manager.updated` with the new answer as params (as above, without `name`, `role`, `managers`). On receiving it the assistant rereads its settings and its `manager.json` and reports a snapshot.

The same connection can shake hands again (to update its roster info); that doesn't count as a replacement.

### Roster

The hub keeps each identity's current connection (the one whose handshake succeeded) in memory: id, role, name, the machine info reported at handshake, and the connect time. It is empty after a hub restart; services reconnect and shake hands again.
When a manager comes online or goes offline, the hub sends the other online managers `managers {managers:[{id,name,role,online}]}`; the one that just connected gets the same list in its handshake answer.

### Methods

- Service → hub: the hub registers handler functions by method name (`handleBus` in `server/internal/hub/bus.go`; one-way events use `handleBusEvent`). Each handler's file registers it in `init`; the hub has no other method list.
  Besides the handshake, the only built-in is `ping {}` → `{}`. An unregistered method returns `unknown_method`; params that can't be parsed return `invalid_params`; an `rpc.Error` returned by a handler reaches the service with its `code` intact.
- hub → service: `callBus(identity, method, params)` calls this identity's current connection (if the caller gives no deadline it gives up after two minutes), and `notifyBus` sends a one-way event. If not online it returns a "not online" error; error codes the service returns are passed back as is.
- hub → managers: `credential.revoked {credential_id}` tells connected managers that a device was signed out.
  Both held Agent messages and kept Assistant messages from that credential become failed with `delete_only: true`.
  A manager checks `credential.is_revoked {credential_id}` → `{revoked}` before delivering a queued message with its
  sender's ID, so it can catch a revocation it missed while offline. If the check cannot run, the send waits.

### Methods the assistant uses

The hub side has a single implementation: `assistantLink` (`server/internal/hub/assistant_link.go`) answers the assistant's calls with the hub's own functions. The bus handlers registered in the same file (`handleBus`) only encode and decode
(parse params into that method's own type; on failure return `invalid_params`); no second copy of the logic. The hub doesn't run the assistant's code (`internal/assistant` isn't in `go list -deps ./internal/hub`);
the two sides share only message types, method names, error codes and the assistant's route table (`server/internal/assistantwire`), plus a few small text helpers (`server/internal/textfmt`).
The interaction-queue methods of `app.call` (`interactions.answer`…) only move data; the rules and wording of the tools that use them (`interaction_answer`) live in the assistant.
The Inbox belongs to the assistant; the hub only handles its sources, and the message shapes are in `assistantwire/inbox.go`.
`assistant.entries.changed` follows the same private extension-event path with `assistant.entries.read`; it carries only the rejected entry ID, correction record ID and wrong status.

`todo.changed` and `todo.decision` go the same way: typed one-way events from the assistant, turned into `event.todo.*` only for subscribers granted `todos.read`, not broadcast to the web app.

- Assistant → hub: `device.call`, `app.call` → the result as is; `notify.request {notification}` → `{ok:true}` (when push grading held the push: `{ok:true,held:true,reason}`, the reason being the same intercept reason as `GET /api/v1/push/intercepts`; for kind `assistant` and `done` also `devices`, how many devices it was handed to now, `kept` when offline devices keep it for their next connection, and with `devices` 0 and nothing held `reason` `no_device` or `filtered`, as `POST /api/v1/notify`; a card's push, a reply reminder and a decision have no `devices`; the assistant's `notify_user` shows all of it to the model; a notification `id` the hub took from that manager within two hours, recorded in its database, is not delivered again); `manager.outbox {items:[{id, at, notification | message}]}` → `{done:[id…]}`: what the manager kept while the hub was away, oldest first, sent after it reported its state on the connection, each id delivered once per manager and only about its own machines, sessions and cards; `manager.snapshot` → `{ok,seq}` (the snapshot carries `profile`: the parts of the assistant's settings the hub's own features need; the hub keeps the last one); one-way event `ws.broadcast` (see below).
  `connectors.lark_reply` reads only an explicitly bound named-person Lark topic through the configured built-in reader:
  `connectorwire.LarkReplyWatch` (source, brand, app/account/person OpenIDs, chat/topic and request message IDs) returns
  `connectorwire.LarkReplyObservation` (echoed checked identity, request/reply identity and provider-time bounds,
  observation time; no conversation bodies or credentials). It is manager-internal, read-only, bounded, and fails closed
  on missing source identity; older managers not implementing it leave the wait parked. It does not send, mark read,
  record an owner decision or guarantee Agent delivery.
  When `app.call` carries `timeout_ms` (how long the assistant waits this time), the hub also stops at that time (for example, one model call).
  The Inbox's sources use these `app.call` methods: `inbox.collect {round}` (the hub reads a round right away and answers after handing it over: pull to refresh), `inbox.kick`, `inbox.config` (with `extensions`: connectors provided by plugins),
  `inbox.mail_body {account_id,uid,mailbox,readable?}`, `inbox.mail_flags {account_id,mailbox,uids}` → `{seen,unseen}` (which of at most 200 mails are still in the mailbox, read or not), `inbox.reply_mail {account_id,uid,mailbox,text,send_id}` → `{already?}`, `inbox.reply {source,reply,send_id}` → `{already?}`
  (the hub sends a given `send_id` only once, and its record does not expire: asking again returns `already`; if the last send broke halfway it returns `assistant_in_doubt` and doesn't send again; a send that did not go out fails with an `rpc.Error` coded `inbox_cannot_reply`, `inbox_source_unavailable`, `inbox_source_signed_out`, `inbox_send_denied`, `inbox_send_rate_limited` (`data.retry_after`), `inbox_send_failed` or `inbox_send_unrecorded`, a fixed message and none of the source's output), `inbox.settle`, `inbox.group_tool`, `inbox.group_fallback`, `inbox.group_append {source,append,append_id}` (asking again with the same `append_id` uses the plugin's previous answer);
  one-way event `inbox.changed {items:[{id,source,kind,title}]}` (outside the read loop the hub sends `inbox.changed` to plugins and pushes `{"type":"inbox"}` to the web app); one-way event `inbox.needs_you {count}` to the hub: how many open items are under "Needs you", told after each handshake (the stored items are read then if nothing read them yet), when they are first read and after every `inbox.changed`; the manager never waits for the hub to take it (one teller counts and tells, and a change meanwhile is told once that went); the hub keeps the last one of the connection for the roster's `inbox_needs_you` (`GET /api/v1/managers` above), ignores one without a `count` or with a negative one, and pushes `{"type":"managers"}` a second after one differs from the one before (the changes within that second are one push); the snapshot's `inbox: {agents:[{machine_id,session_id}]}` (the AI twin's chats: no "done" push when they finish; on `null` the hub keeps the previous one).
  The snapshot's `todos` is the to-do report (`assistantwire.TodoReport`; to-dos belong to the assistant): `{links:[{machine_id,session_id,todo_id,title,task?}],completed?:[{machine_id,session_id,todo_id,title}],quiet:[{machine_id,session_id}]}`.
  Optional `completed` is display-only ownership for sessions with no active link, choosing the latest completion per session.
  It appears on full and compact session rows as `completed_todo: {id,title}`; it never fills active `todo` or cards'
  `task_title`, never starts supervision and never changes the quiet report. A dismissed association is omitted.
  `links` are active Agents on unfinished to-dos (`task`: a task dispatched from a chat); `quiet` are Agents of quiet tasks (unfinished or finished less than 7 days ago). From it the hub fills sessions' `todo`, `quiet` and cards' `task_title`, blocks pushes for quiet ones, and pushes the session list of whichever machine had these change; on `null` (unreadable) it keeps the previous one.
  hub errors go back with codes, and the assistant maps the codes back to the original errors: `no_device` (no such machine), `machine_offline`, `node_closed` (the node's connection dropped), `stale_snapshot`, `assistant_in_doubt` (an Inbox reply broke halfway last time and may already have been sent); an `rpc.Error` from the node itself is passed as is.
- hub → assistant, calls: `http.request` and `http.request_streamed` (forwarding, below), `manager.action` (the web app answered one of its questions), `assistant.tools {}` → `{tools:[…]}` (the hub asks once each time it connects and remembers it, also after it disconnects),
  `assistant.tool {name,arguments,machine_id,session_id}` → `{content,is_error}`, `assistant.context {session_id}` → `{text,…}` (the node asks before each message),
  `assistant.todo_handoff {todo_id,text?,new?,machine_id?,cwd?}` → `{found,title?,done_at?,text?,images?,status?,error?}` (`POST /api/v1/sessions`, `…/messages` with `todo_id`: whether the to-do exists and whether it's done; `text` has the decisions in effect prepended; with `new`, `text` is the new Agent's first message, with the background of the project `cwd` belongs to prepended at the very front; an empty `text` comes back as is and carries no images. Otherwise `images` carries the to-do's stored image bytes as `{mime,data}` entries, appended to any client-supplied images for a message and included with a new Agent's prompt; the target node decodes them through its ordinary image-save path. When it can't be handed off, `status` is 404 no such to-do or 409 already done, and the hub returns `status`, `error` to the web app as is), `assistant.todo_link {todo_id,machine_id,session_id,title?,cwd?,agent?,prompt?}` → `{title?}` (attach after handing off; when the session has no title, the manager takes the first line after the context block in `prompt` as the attached title; returns the to-do's title, which the new-session response's `todo` uses; a to-do that's gone or done returns an error).
  `assistant.start {text,images?,launcher?,permission_mode?,effort?,purpose?,machine_id?,main?,untitled?}` → `{session}` (a conversation one of the hub's features opens),
  `assistant.keep_undelivered {machine_id,session_id,params,human?,lang?,code?,error?,tried_at?}` → `{undelivered}` (the owner's message, as the web app sent it, that could not go in or waits behind kept ones: the manager keeps it and sends it again by itself; `assistant.send_params` answers `undelivered_ahead` for an owner's message to a chat with kept ones, which the hub then keeps behind them. A transport outcome whose delivery is unknown has code `delivery_unknown` and `tried_at`, the original send's start: the manager only looks for that first attempt in the transcript and never sends it again by itself; not found within minutes, it is marked failed for the owner's Retry or Delete),
  `assistant.send_params {machine_id,session_id,params,lang?,human?,reply_input?}` → `{params, launcher_note?}` (which launcher and model a message sent to one of its chats runs on, and the background prepended to the first message of a new main chat; `lang` is the web app request's language, the one a `bad_request` is said in; `human: true` is the hub's word that a full device's credential sent it, never an extension's, a link's or the hub's own token, which a secret hand-off's Always rule needs; the hub sets `reply_input: true` on direct web app input with its legacy owner credential for missing-reply recovery only, and the relayed `http.request` for a conversation start can carry the same mark for the first message),
  `assistant.rename {machine_id,session_id,params}` → the node's answer (the web app renames one of its chats). When these requests themselves are malformed they return `bad_request`, and the hub returns 400 to the web app.
  Inbox: `inbox.collected {epoch,seq,round,sources,mail?,names}` → `{}` (the hub hands over a round of sources it has read; `mail` is `{accounts, failed?}`, and `failed: [{id, email, read_error}]` names accounts with a read or folder-listing error. Each account keeps its INBOX page in `messages`, optional `uid_validity` and optional `inbox_unavailable`. Other successfully read mailboxes appear in `folders: [{name,uid_validity?,messages}]`, including empty pages. A partly readable account may appear in both `accounts` and `failed`; the assistant answers after building the entries. Within one `epoch`, a `seq` not greater than one already used is dropped. When the stored Inbox can't be read it returns `inbox_unavailable`, and the hub keeps it to hand over next round),
  `inbox.item {id}` → `{item,ok}`, `inbox.forget {source}` → `{deleted}`, `inbox.repo_mutes {source,set?,add?,repos?}` → `{repos}`.
- hub → assistant, one-way events: `session.user_spoke {machine_id,session_id,text?}` (the hub supplies text only for a person's full-device web app sending to an Agent, never a hub token, extension or link; the manager may settle an exact current-round option without resending it; older peers keep the metadata-only pause), `session.user_stopped` (the user stopped one of the assistant's chats in the web app), `session.turn_started`, `session.turn_ended`, `sessions.changed {machine_id, sessions, connected}` (the session list the node reported, with `spawn_from`: a to-do's auto-attach by project, spawn following, and herdr markers all come from it; `connected` is when this node connection started, and a change means the node reconnected, so the assistant resends all herdr markers), `interaction.resolved` (also used to record to-do decisions), `interaction.raised` (an Agent of a quiet task is asking), `session.start_ended {machine_id, session_id?, launcher, ok, error?, code?, data?}` (how a web app start the node ran before answering went, or one it refused, for launcher health; a start answered at once the assistant follows in `sessions.changed`), `session.assistant_sent {machine_id, session_id, outcome, code?, error?, client_msg_id?}` (how a web app message the hub sent to one of the assistant's conversations went: `delivered`, `failed` or `unknown`; only a send that ran, for the north star's availability; `client_msg_id` names the message when it has one), `todos.space_renamed {machine_id,old,new}` (a workspace was renamed via the hub), `models.used {machine_id,launcher,model}` (a start, a running session's model switch, or a message to one of its chats went through with a model the web app picked; an `async` start once the session is listed as started, not with a `start_error`; the manager remembers an ID the launcher's own `/model` list doesn't have),
  `manager.updated` (handshake above).
  The assistant handles them one by one in arrival order; `session.turn_ended` runs separately (it asks the model and waits for task Agents to stop).
- **Agents** (types in `assistantwire/agents.go`):
  the manager reads the triage limits and initial switch values from its own `manager.json`; the snapshot carries `work {on, sessions:[{machine_id, session_id, work}]}` (each Agent's work state for its latest turn;
  `work.turn_at` is when that turn ended; on `null` the hub keeps the previous one), and `interactions` includes triage cards (`tool_name: persona_triage`, asked in that Agent's session; answers still go through `manager.action`).
  The `device.call sessions.list` answer carries `muted` (session ids with pushes turned off).
  hub → assistant calls: `agents.start_params {machine_id, params, name_from?, lang?}` → `{params}` (before `POST /api/v1/sessions`: fills launcher, model and fingerprint from **Model configuration › Agents** and this time's choice, and names the tab when `name_from` isn't empty; `lang` is the web app request's language, the one a `bad_request` is said in;
  on `bad_request` the hub returns 400 to the web app; when it isn't connected the hub starts with what the web app gave), `agents.resume_params {machine_id, session_id, params}` → `{params}` (before resuming a session whose launcher is unknown; the hub sends no params and stamps the answer onto the message),
  `agents.tab_name {prompt}` → `{name}` (Agents started in the background, or opened from a Lark card); one-way event `session.seen {machine_id, session_id, at}` (the user viewed a session in the web app).
  When the user answers one of its questions or cards and it doesn't accept (not connected, or returned an error other than `gone`), the hub records the answer
  and sends `manager.action` again after its next snapshot (immediately if it wasn't connected, after 10 seconds if it returned an error), until it accepts, returns `gone` (this card / question no longer exists: answered, withdrawn, expired; no need to give it again), or the card would have expired anyway.
  Before `agents.start_params` / `agents.resume_params` the hub waits for it to connect (up to 60 seconds after the hub starts, 10 seconds after it disconnects); if it doesn't, the hub applies **Model configuration › Agents** itself.
  If the version it reports at handshake differs from the hub's (dev builds excepted), the hub logs a line: the two sides may disagree about who owns triage.
- **Models** (types in `assistantwire/models.go`):
  `/api/v1/model-config…`, `/api/v1/launchers…` (including quota `…/quota`) and `/api/v1/machines/{mid}/launchers…` are its routes, forwarded by the hub;
  the handshake answer carries `models` (each computer's `machines[].launchers` from hub.json; the rest of the model settings the manager reads from its `manager.json`);
  `app.call plugins.presets`, `plugins.voice`, `plugins.quota {name, machine, base_url, tz}` → `{report}`, `plugins.need_triage`,
  `device.call launchers.managed` (launchers added in Persona are handed to the node; new node connections also get them from the manager); hub → manager calls `models.usable {purpose}` → `{usable}`, `models.launchers {}` → `{launchers: [{name, base_url}]}` (launchers with a gateway address, without keys),
  `models.launcher_http {name, machine?, http?}` (error codes `no_launcher`, `no_gateway`, `machine_offline`).
- When the assistant isn't connected: forwarded endpoints return `503 {"code":"assistant_offline","error":"助手暂时连不上，稍后再试"}` (the error text is localized; this is the zh-Hans value, "The assistant can't be reached right now, try again later"); the assistant's tools fail the same way (`is_error`, same sentence), and `assistant.context` fails too (that node message carries no live snapshot).
  Events for it aren't sent (once connected it reports a full snapshot and asks for what it needs). The hub keeps its last snapshot, so the session list still shows titles and archives.
  The hub keeps reading Inbox sources and accumulates what it reads (merged, with a cap) to hand over together once the assistant connects. An Inbox reply that breaks in transit (connection dropped, timeout) returns `502 {"code":"assistant_in_doubt","delivered":"unknown","retryable":false}`: it may already have been sent, and sending the same one again won't send it twice (`send_id` above).
  When the assistant is connected but the Inbox can't read what's stored (the database didn't answer), Inbox endpoints return `503 inbox_unavailable`, and until it's read the Inbox accepts and writes nothing.

**Forwarding client requests**: requests the web app makes to assistant endpoints are (after authentication) handed to the assistant by the hub as `http.request`, and its answer is written back as is. The assistant endpoints are `assistantwire.Routes` (a test on the assistant side guarantees it serves exactly these):
`POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/archive`, `…/unarchive`, `POST /api/v1/assistant/conversations/{id}/route`, `…/today`, `…/compact`, `…/stop`, `GET …/{id}/feed`, `GET /api/v1/assistant/reporters`, `/api/v1/assistant/tasks…`, `/api/v1/assistant/runs`, `/api/v1/task-plans/{id}…`, `/api/v1/todos…` (all to-do endpoints, including `done-check`, `retry`, decisions), `GET/PUT /api/v1/agents/triage`, `GET /api/v1/agents/work/stats`, and `GET/PUT /api/v1/assistant`, `POST /api/v1/assistant/warm`, `GET /api/v1/assistant/readiness`, `POST /api/v1/assistant/readiness/dismiss`,
`GET /api/v1/assistant/memory`, `PUT/DELETE /api/v1/assistant/memory/{name}`, `POST /api/v1/assistant/conversations`, `POST /api/v1/assistant/main/new`, `POST /api/v1/assistant/main/clear`,
plus all Inbox and translation endpoints (`assistantwire.InboxRoutes`): `GET /api/v1/inbox`, `GET /api/v1/inbox/{id}`, `POST /api/v1/inbox/{id}/done`, `…/draft`, `…/reply` (the hub still records the receipt up front; when the assistant isn't connected it returns 503 directly without recording; a break in transit returns `assistant_in_doubt`, also unrecorded, so resending reaches the assistant), `…/doc/status`, `POST /api/v1/inbox/refresh`, `POST /api/v1/inbox/done`, `POST /api/v1/inbox/bulk`, `POST /api/v1/inbox/merge` (+ `/undo`), `POST /api/v1/inbox/todo` (+ `/undo`), `GET/POST /api/v1/inbox/mutes`, `DELETE /api/v1/inbox/mutes/{id}`, `GET/POST /api/v1/inbox/policies`, `PATCH/DELETE /api/v1/inbox/policies/{id}`, `POST /api/v1/translate`, `POST /api/v1/translate/mail`. `/api/v1/skills` is the hub's own.

```jsonc
// hub → assistant
{"id":"h3","method":"http.request","params":{"method":"POST","path":"/api/v1/assistant/conversations/c1/stop","query":"",
  "header":{"Content-Type":["application/json"],"X-Persona-Role":["full"]},"body":"<base64>"}}
// assistant → hub
{"id":"h3","result":{"status":200,"header":{"Content-Type":["application/json"]},"body":"<base64>"}}
```

- `path` keeps URL percent-encoding: the hub forwards with `EscapedPath()`, and after the assistant rebuilds the request the router decodes it once. `/`, `#`, `?` in a body card key must not be decoded into path separators, fragments or queries before forwarding.
- `header` carries no `Authorization`, `Cookie` or hop-by-hop headers; `X-Persona-Role` is the device role from the hub's authentication (one the web app sends itself is replaced). Request bodies are at most 32 MiB.
- `handoff_approver {device_id, device_name?}` is set by the hub, never from a header, on an answer (`POST /api/v1/interactions/{id}/resolve`) from a device that may approve a secret hand-off card, when the card is one or the hub does not hold it ("Secret hand-off cards"); the handshake's answer says `secret_handoff_gate: true` from a hub that does. A manager approves a hand-off only with it, and with an older hub shows no hand-off card.
- `human: true` is set by the hub, never from a header, on a new conversation's start (`POST /api/v1/assistant/conversations`) from a full credential with a device, the test that marks a message `human` on `assistant.send_params`. The manager does not count the start's first message as the user's own today: that first turn gets the card.
- **A large body goes beside the bus**: the bus is one WebSocket per manager that writes one message at a time, each as a single frame, so a body inside `http.request` would hold up every other call to that manager until it was written, and on a slow link the keepalive's ping (which waits at most 5 s for the frame) would fail and drop the bus. A body of 1 MiB or more to a manager that names `http_body_stream` goes as `http.request_streamed`: the same params without `body`, plus `body_stream {id, size}`. The hub holds a relay with that id (`GET /api/v1/bus/relay?id=`, `devicewire.RelayPath`, only the manager the request is for may take it) and writes the body there in binary messages of at most 256 KiB, then closes normally (`bus.WriteBody`); the manager dials it with its bus token, reads exactly `size` bytes into one buffer (`bus.ReadBody`) and only then serves the request as `http.request`. The answer comes back on the bus. A body that does not arrive whole is refused with code `body_incomplete` before the route runs; the hub then sends the request again as `http.request`, as it does when a manager answers `unknown_method`, so nothing runs twice and the web app sees one answer. Routes, statuses, error codes, operation receipts and "in doubt" answers are the same either way.
- If the assistant isn't connected, or disconnects mid-request, it returns `503 assistant_offline`; an `rpc.Error` it returns becomes `502` (with its `code`); requests with no deadline give up after 5 minutes.

**Messages to clients**: the assistant sends the one-way event `ws.broadcast {message}`, where `message` is a JSON object with a string `type` (`assistant_schedule`, `assistant_feed`, `task_plan`). The hub sends it to every web app WebSocket as it read it (adding the `event_seq` every message has, over a top-level one the message carried; an `extension_operation`, kept out of the event log, carries none); ones without `type` are dropped, and so is any type that is not a manager's (the managers' own, or one its extensions declare: never the hub's `interaction`, `sessions`, `machines`, `error`…), a message with a key twice or a case variant of `type` / `machine_id` / `session_id` / `conversation`, and one where any object names another manager's `machine_id`, `session_id` or `conversation` ("What the hub keeps of each manager"). A message from another manager than the assistant the hub starts also gets top-level `manager` (its id, over one it carried; a message with a case variant of it at the top level, such as `Manager`, is dropped, while deeper down such a key is the sender's own field and stays), so the web app can tell whose a live update is (one about a conversation still goes by its conversation; one about the page itself, such as `assistant_schedule`, is the shown manager's only); the assistant's messages carry none (one it put there is taken out): a message without `manager` is the assistant's (`assistant`), and with one manager nothing changes.

### Computer events (fleet.*)

What computers send belongs to the manager; the messages are in `server/internal/assistantwire/fleet.go`. The manager side is `internal/assistant/fleet*.go`, the hub side `hub/fleet_link.go`.

- Manager → hub (one-way):
  - `fleet.sessions {machine_id, sessions, muted?}`: one machine's session list, in the shape the web app gets (unified status, number of "Needs you" cards, seen, work state, to-do, channel…); sent only on change, and once per machine after each handshake. The hub stores it as the machine's `sessions`, pushes it to the web app (`sessions` / `sessions_delta`), and answers `GET /api/v1/sessions` with it.
  - `fleet.archived {machine_id, sessions}`, to a hub whose handshake answer says `archived_apart`: the machine's archived rows (`archived: true`, not the assistant's), the ones the hub leaves out of everything it sends the web app. `fleet.sessions` then carries only the rest. Each `fleet.archived` replaces the ones before; it is sent when they change (an archive, a restore, a record written, the node listing or no longer listing an archived session), and once per machine after each handshake, before the machine's `fleet.sessions`, so a session just archived is never in neither. The hub keeps them for everything that read the manager's list besides what the web app gets, as when they were in it: lookups by session (sending to one, deleting, pins, `Machine.session`), a port an archived agent listens on (`/ports/{port}/connect`, `/preview/connect`), the manager's `sessions.list`, an update waiting on a busy agent, space names, the node's revs and the unknown state while the manager is away. It drops them when another manager lists the machine; what the web app gets is the same bytes either way. A manager leaves archived sessions out of `muted` then too: they are never pushed.
  - `fleet.interaction {interaction}`: a new card, or one shown again; `fleet.interaction_resolved {id, answered_by?}`: it ended; `fleet.interactions {interactions}`: all pending ones, once after each handshake; the hub replaces the whole set (sending `interaction_resolved` to the web app for ones that disappeared). A card naming a machine, or a session on one, that is not the reporting manager's is dropped ("What the hub keeps of each manager"). The hub still pushes `interaction` / `interaction_resolved` events and answers `GET /api/v1/interactions`.
- Manager → hub (calls): `notify.request {notification}`; besides the assistant's `assistant`, `kind` can be `done` (a turn ended: `took_ms`, `long_ms`; devices filter by "only long ones"), `input` (a card: `interaction`, a pending one the manager reported; the hub pushes its own copy; `link_covered: true` when one of the manager's Persona Link desktops confirmed (`rang`) it handed this card's notification to Notification Center, on its current link, within the push's wait (checked again once the desktops were reported): then "Phone Muted" holds it back while the hub still has a valid record of one of the manager's Persona Link desktops, and pushes the phone when it has none; older managers leave it out and the phone gets the card) and `decide` (a to-do's decision with a recommended option: `todo: {id, asked_at, recommend}`, all three required, plus `options` and `responses` and, `ask` (the view's ask id) and `lockscreen` (`answer` or `open_only`, the view's rule); the devices that take "needs you" pushes get it with that `todo`, the options forwarded only with `answer`). A push about another manager's computer, session or card is refused `no_device`; connector, Cua and ego tools, gate command wording, and `assistant.lark` are answered by extensions inside the manager process and don't cross the bus), and `interactions.owner_action` of `app.call interactions` (the hub withdraws the owner action before a channel answers a card).
  - MCP wait correlation on `app.tool`: `{name, arguments, machine_id, session_id, call_id?}`. The optional `call_id` is the node's opaque per-call correlator. `machine_id` is the tool call's functional one, which is never overwritten, and a value different from the reporter's origin omits `call_id` and therefore wait updates. The hub uses these fields only to address the wait event: `mcpWaitReporter` checks the current manager's capability and its ownership of that machine. The `mcp.wait` event itself still carries exactly `{call_id, kind}`, with no tool or machine field added to it.
- hub → manager: call `fleet.ask {interaction}` → `Resolution` (cards the hub's own features need to ask; the hub waits until the card's `expires_at` and 30 seconds more, not the two minutes of its other calls, so the manager's own expiry answers first; when the hub stops waiting it cancels and the card is withdrawn); `fleet.ask_prepared {interaction,replacement}` → `{clarifying?,text}` for a hub-owned prepared setting, whose executable handle stays in the hub while only its opaque interaction ID crosses the bus; manager → hub `fleet.approval_apply {interaction_id,resolution}` → `{text,stale?}` consumes that manager-owned handle once after a fresh owner Allow, and `fleet.approval_discard {interaction_id,status}` releases it without applying; one-way `fleet.clients {elicitation}` (whether a web app that accepts MCP forms is connected; told again after web clients connect, say hello or go and after devices or their settings change, and to every manager once it connects), `fleet.seen {machine_id, session_id}` (the web app WebSocket's `seen`), `fleet.mutes {mutes}` (the hub's mutes, of the manager's own machines only: once after each handshake, on the manager's first call or event, and after each change; never sent while the hub cannot read them, so a manager keeps the last ones).
- Web app routes the hub forwards to the manager (`http.request`; manager absent: `503 assistant_offline`): `POST /api/v1/interactions/{id}/resolve`, `POST /api/v1/interactions/{id}/clarify`, `GET /api/v1/interactions/history` (MCP forms only with `X-Persona-Elicitation: 1`), `POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/seen`, `GET /api/v1/metrics`, `GET /api/v1/machines/{id}/metrics`, `GET /api/v1/machines/{id}/usage`, `GET /api/v1/usage`, `GET /api/v1/usage/days`, `GET /api/v1/usage/hours`.

### Computers (devices.*)

Computers are connected by the manager that carries them (currently the chief manager `assistant`); messages are in `server/internal/devicewire`. The hub side is `hub/devices_link.go`, `devices_relay.go`; the manager side is `internal/devices`.

- The handshake answer carries `devices`, for every manager with only the machines it carries (the carrier `assistant`: hub.json's, but those moved to another manager; another manager: those moved to it): `{machines:[hub.json entries, as is], machines_own?, hub_id, hub_name, hub_version, endpoints?, mesh_hubs?, web_url?, tailcat_derp_map_url?, link_ping_ms?, link_ping_timeout_ms?, mesh?, pending?}`. `machines_own` goes to a manager that named `machines.own`: its own list is the list, and the hub edits it with `devices.machines.*` (below). Once its report says it holds that list (`own_list`), its `machines` is `null`: what `hub.json` stages for it is put to it instead; until then it carries them for it to take over. `pending` and the rest are handed over as to any manager.
  `web_url` is hub.json's `public_url` when it is https (sub-path included, no trailing `/`): Persona Link's "Needs you" summary carries it.
  `link_ping_ms`, `link_ping_timeout_ms` are the heartbeat from hub.json's `link` section (not sent when unset; the manager then uses 10 seconds / 5 seconds); the manager pings connector streams accordingly and tells Persona Link (`endpoints`, `X-Persona-Ping`).
  `pending` are machine ids awaiting the user's confirmation (sorted); the manager tells their Persona Link (`pending` in `endpoints`). `mesh` (only to the carrier) is `{member?, center_name?, settle_until?, hubs:{hub_id:{name, reachable, rtt_ms}}, members:[{hub_id, machines:[{id, cfg, kind, avail?, rtt_ms?}]}], path_switch_ms}`. When it changes (a computer added in the admin UI, the linked group, the hub's addresses and name), the hub sends `devices.config` with the same params (coalesced over 200 milliseconds).
- Manager → hub:
  - Event `devices.state {machines:[{machine, config, info, connected?, connected_at?, warm_until?, derived?, paths?}], absorbed?:{entry id: machine id}, entries?:[{id, cfg, kind, avail?, rtt_ms?}], own_list?}`: `own_list`, the manager holds `entries` as its own list in its `manager.json` (the hub then moves those machines out of `hub.json`);
    all machines, in the web app's list order. `machine` is what the web app sees (with the monitoring `system`, minus `computer`, `browser` which the hub adds; its `online` also counts the warm start after a manager restart). `connected` means the node is really connected right now and calls reach it (this is what the hub's self-update waits on and what node updates are sent to); a change in `connected_at` means the node reconnected; before `warm_until` it is a warm start. `entries` are the manager's own entries, every one it was handed (absorbed ones too), each with its entry as the manager has it (`cfg`; older managers leave it out): the hub's mesh record lists them by how each one's own manager reaches it, and the hub keeps what each manager has from them. Sent only on change (coalesced over 50 milliseconds; a change to `last_seen` alone doesn't count), and in full once after each handshake.
  - Event `devices.desktops {desktops:[{machine_id, since, ttl_ms, notifies}]}`: the manager's computers whose Persona Link says you are at them, all of them, only computers in active mode (a passive connector cannot send confirmations back: no desktop yet), known to get the "Needs you" summary as it is (none while the hub cannot say which computers wait to be confirmed) and keeping up with the summary (its link took one and no send failed since); sent by one task, in order, a run of requests making one: for every presence a Persona Link says (about once a minute while active), when a delivery may change which computers count, after a `devices.state` when the list changed, and in full, as it is then, after the full `devices.state` each handshake sends (another report may reach the hub before that state: the hub drops the entry of a computer it does not yet have as this manager's, and the full one after the state brings it back). Apart from `devices.state` so a renewal doesn't resend the web app's machine list. `ttl_ms` is what is left of the presence when sent; the hub counts it on its own clock from when it takes it, at most 240000 (twice the presence TTL), so neither clock's drift stretches it; `since` is only for showing. The hub counts one of the sender's own computers as a desktop while that time runs and `notifies` holds (a mesh member's computer doesn't count yet).
  - Event `devices.event {machine_id, event, params}`: the node one-way events the web app needs, as is and in order (`session.items`, `terminal.frame`, `stream.data`, `sessions.revs`, `hook.event`…); `state.put`, `sessions.changed`, `codex.interactions`, `interaction.dismiss` / `cancel`, `usage`, `metrics`, `session.mode_set`, `session.mode_restart` are handled by the manager itself and not forwarded ("Computer events" above).
  - Call `devices.request {machine_id, method, params, request}` → the hub's answer: things the node needs the hub to answer (`notify`); `request` is a key the manager gives.
  - Event `devices.request_end {machine_id, request}`: the node connection this request came from dropped before the hub answered, and the hub stops waiting for it (same as the node's own connection dropping: resumable cards stay, waiting for the hook to claim them from the next connection).
  - Call `devices.connected {machine_id, connected_at}` → `{configure?:{key: value}, calls?:[{method, params}]}`: the node just connected (or the manager's connection to the hub was just established, once more for each online machine).
    The hub returns what to add to `node.configure` (`codex`, `hub_features`) and what to send afterward (`launchers.managed`, `session.echoes`); the manager does this before asking for the session list. `hub_features` carries the same capabilities as `hello.features`, including `persona_contracts_v1` and `mcp_wait_v1`. On a hub reconnect, `rehook` forwards the new announcement through `node.configure`; until `hubConnected` succeeds, retained node connections keep the previous capabilities. A successful reply from an older hub sends an empty list; a node also clears the previous capabilities when a full handover (`machine_id`) omits the field, while partial configuration updates preserve them. The node snapshots this connection-local feature list at assistant startup only to choose MCP namespaces. MCP wait updates instead read `mcp_wait_v1` live for every local `mcp.call`, so a later call follows a hub upgrade or rollback without restarting the assistant; a call already in flight is not retroactively registered. The hub at the same time starts the things it does on connect.
  - Calls `devices.link_switch.begin {machine_id, operation, ssh_host?, by?}` → `{link, pair_hash}` and `devices.link_switch.end {machine_id, operation, pair_hash?, outcome}` → `{}`: switching an ssh computer of its own to Persona Link. `begin` checks the entry is still kind ssh with that `ssh_host`, the computer is confirmed, the hub takes Persona Link and the computer has no link credential or unused code; then it sets `kind: link` (every other field kept, live, no restart) and makes one pairing code for that machine, answered as its link (secret, for the computer only) and the sha-256 of its token. `end` `succeeded` keeps it; `rolled_back` revokes that code and the credential it was traded for (all of the machine's link credentials and codes when `pair_hash` is empty) and puts the kind back to ssh. Refusals: `no_machine`, `not_ssh`, `config_changed`, `pending`, `link_unavailable`, `existing_link`; an older hub answers `unknown_method`. `operation` is required. `end` acts only on the computer's latest operation and changes nothing unless it can show that operation began (the hub's own record, or its `begin` / `begun` row in `machine_audit`). A `pair_hash` must be the one recorded for that operation. `succeeded`, `rolled_back` and `begin_failed` are final: a repeated rollback answers `{}`, and an operation id cannot begin twice (`invalid_params`). A manager that no longer carries the computer may only revoke the code of a switch it began itself; when the hub has undone the switch but the computer is no longer that manager's (moved or removed), `end` answers `rolled_back_gone` (taken), and `no_machine` only when nothing was undone. The manager keeps asking `end(rolled_back)` until the hub answers, for at most an hour (then `hub_unanswered`; `unknown_method` stops at once), and tells it so when it stops waiting for `begin` (`rpc.cancel`). For an operation it saw succeed it answers `already_succeeded` and changes nothing. While a switch runs, moving or removing the computer, or removing its manager, answers 409 `link_switch_in_progress`. `devices.config`'s `link_switch: true` says the hub answers them and takes Persona Link now.
  - Calls `devices.connector_cred {machine_id}` → `{machine_id, fp, token, version?}` (a kind service credential, stored sealed by the hub; empty `token` means not paired), `devices.connector_paired {machine_id, fp, token, version}` → `{}` (after pairing, handed to the hub to store).
- hub → manager:
  - Call `devices.call {machine_id, method, params, timeout_ms?, hold?, ordered?}` → the node's result: calls to the node from the web app and hub features; the manager also remembers `session.watch` / `session.unwatch` and re-watches when the node changes connection; a watch the new connection refuses (a node just started) is asked again while it lasts, waiting 1 s and doubling to 30 s, 8 times, unless no web app or Follow wants it any more; giving up is logged. `ordered` is set on a person's `session.send` to an Agent: while held messages of that session wait, the manager answers `held_ahead` (`delivered: none`) to one without `hold` instead of sending it ahead of them. `hold {lang}` is set by the hub on an owner's `session.send` to an Agent that may be held (a web app that declares `agent_message_hold`): when the node is not connected (nothing was written) or older held messages of the session wait, the manager keeps the call as it came and answers the error code `held` with data `{"delivered":"later","undelivered":{…}}`; it sends the call once the node's next connection is configured and listed.
    `timeout_ms` is the time the hub is still willing to wait, minus a bit (a tenth, at most 500 milliseconds), so the manager's timeout answer arrives first; calls where the hub gives no deadline (plugin `nodes.call` and the like) don't get one either, and wait the same as when the hub connected to nodes itself.
    Error codes: `no_device`, `machine_offline` (not sent), `node_closed` (after sending, the node's connection dropped, or the call was interrupted), `deadline` (after sending, time ran out); the node's own coded errors are passed as is.
    The hub maps them back to the original errors: offline is still 503 `node_unreachable`; `node_closed`, `deadline` and the bus breaking mid-call all count as "may have been done", so the result of sending a message is `unknown` (the same one won't be sent again), not treated as unsent.
    For other calls, a bus break mid-call shows the web app 503 `assistant_offline` (the manager is gone).
    For `port.dial` only, an optional outer `stream_version: 1` offers directional EOF as described with the stream events. The manager starts tracking the stream before the dial reaches the node, so it can clean up even if the reply is lost.
  - Call `devices.file_call` has the same `{machine_id, method, params, timeout_ms?}` and answer, but is used only for `file.copy` / `file.zip`. When its caller stops waiting, the hub sends `rpc.cancel` and the manager forwards that cancellation to the node. Ordinary `devices.call` deliberately does not propagate caller cancellation: other node operations may run to completion after their HTTP caller disconnects, and stopping only the manager would make their outcome ambiguous. A hub falls back to ordinary `devices.call` only when the manager explicitly answers `unknown_method`, preserving copy / zip on an older manager without cancellation; no other error retries the request, because it may already have reached the node.
  - Event `devices.notify {machine_id, event, params}`: one-way events for the node (terminal input, bytes of forwarded ports, MCP wait kinds). The manager queues per machine and writes each in order, so a computer that's slow to receive only delays itself; if one write is stuck for 30 seconds, or more than 32 MiB is queued, it reconnects that machine. For an opted-in MCP call, `event` is `mcp.wait` and `params` is exactly `{call_id, kind}`: `call_id` is the node's opaque per-call correlator and `kind` is only `unknown`, `approval`, `answer` or `computer`. No tool name, arguments, interaction text, path, recipient or account name is part of the signal. The manager publishes `computer` when the remote call starts and after its interaction resolves, `approval` or `answer` while that interaction waits; for a hub-owned settings card the hub relays the same two transitions while it waits. An older node ignores the event, and an unknown value on a live call is conservative (`unknown`). Completion differs by producer. Manager-published events use the manager's live registry, which is removed when the call returns, so a completed id gets no further manager-published event. The hub's settings relay does not consult that registry: after checking the id's shape, the current manager's capability and the machine's owner, it sends `devices.notify` directly, and the receiving node drops an id it no longer has pending. A hub-owned settings card always restores `computer`, independently of any manager-held card stack; it does not restore a manager interaction's previous kind.
  - Event `devices.link_rtt {id, rtt_ms}`: the round trip the hub measured from heartbeats on a Persona Link link (`id` is from `devices.accept`); the manager uses it when comparing paths.
  - Call `devices.accept {id, kind, machine_id, token_id?, stream_id?, source?}` → `{}`: the hub holds a connection for the manager (`kind`: `link` a Persona Link link, `link_stream` a stream it opened, `node` a node stream the center requested through this member); the manager dials `GET /api/v1/bus/relay?id=<id>` to take it over, and the hub waits 10 seconds.
  - Calls `devices.reconnect {machine_id}`, `devices.update_nodes {}` (after the hub self-updates, redeploy nodes not on this version), `devices.pair_connector {link, machine_id, address?, proxy?}` → `{address, version}` (pairing a kind service from the admin UI).
  - Calls `devices.machines.put {entry}` → `{}`, `devices.machines.remove {machine_id}` → `{removed}`, `devices.machines.get {machine_id}` → `{entry}`: the hub's edits of a manager's own list of computers (its `manager.json` `machines`), and an entry as the manager has it (its secrets too: a move hands it to the new manager). Only for a manager the hub handed `machines_own` in `devices` (one that named the capability `machines.own`): the first such hand-over's `machines` is taken over as its own, and from then on its own list is the list, which later hand-overs don't change. A manager not handed `machines_own`, or whose list was not taken over as its own, refuses them `not_own_list`; `get` of a machine it does not have, `no_device`.
  - Calls `devices.engine.get {machine_id}` → `{machine_id, choice?}`, `devices.engine.put {machine_id, choice: {hosts, default}}` → `{}`: a computer's engine choice as the manager keeps it in its own settings (`choice` absent: never chosen). A move reads it from the manager the computer leaves and puts it in the one it goes to before handing the computer over.
  - Call `devices.usage_gateway_accounts {}` → `{sources, accounts}`: the account list of account-pool gateways among the quota sources, as last read by the manager (it doesn't query the gateway; no keys or addresses).
    The extensions' `usage.gateway_accounts` (permission `usage_gateways`) is asked of it in-process by the extension manager inside the manager; the hub doesn't call it.
  - Routes the manager answers itself (`devicewire.Routes`) are forwarded via `http.request`: `POST /api/v1/machines/{mid}/reconnect`, `PUT …/engine`, `GET/PUT …/herdr`, `POST …/herdr/start`, `GET/PUT …/botmux`, `POST …/deploy`, `GET …/diagnosis`, `POST …/cleanup`, `GET …/claude-dirs`, `PUT …/claude-dirs/blocked`, `GET/PUT …/clipboard`, `GET/PUT …/clipboard/settings`, `GET …/files/operations/{oid}`, `POST …/link-switch`.
- **Relay channel** `GET /api/v1/bus/relay` (WebSocket, the manager's bus token, same authentication as `/api/v1/bus`; only the manager that carries computers can open it): `?id=` takes over a connection the hub holds; `?hub=<hub_id>&machine=<id>` asks for a node stream to that hub's computer through that hub (if the hub can't open it, it returns 502 before upgrading, with `error` as the reason).
  The hub forwards message by message (text and binary as is), and passes one side's close code and reason to the other; the Persona Link side's heartbeat is the hub's, and without a pong it closes the manager's side with 1001 "no pong within …".
  For `kind: node` (a member opening a node stream on behalf of the center), the manager first opens the node; once open it sends a text `open`, or if it can't, closes with the reason. Only then does the member answer the center: `101`, or 502 with the reason (waiting at most 1 minute).
- On every handshake (the hub restarted, or the bus dropped), the manager closes on the node side what the hub had open on the node through the previous connection: forwarded streams (`port.dial`, `plugin.node.dial`, `preview.open`) get `stream.close`, watched terminals get `terminal.unwatch`.
  If the manager forwarded a directional EOF offer for a port, its reconnect close includes `abort: true` so a half-open or write-blocked socket is released.
  At the handshake the hub also ends streams and terminals opened through the previous connection (terminals end with `助手暂时连不上，稍后再试`, "The assistant can't be reached right now, try again later", and the web app reopens them); ones still waiting for their first watch are left alone.
- When the manager isn't connected: machines show offline (`error` `助手暂时连不上，稍后再试`), endpoints that go through it return `503 assistant_offline`, terminal streams end with the same sentence, forwarded ports close, and `/api/v1/link` returns 503.
  In the 30 seconds after the hub starts and before the manager's first report, calls wait for it instead of failing immediately (machines are shown as the manager handed them over); `/api/v1/link` and members' `/api/v1/peer/node` wait at most 5 seconds.
- When a single node message exceeds 60 MiB the manager doesn't forward it (a bus line is at most 64 MiB): events are dropped, calls return `too_large`.

### Extensions, connectors and bots (extensions.*)

All belong to the manager; messages are in `server/internal/extwire`:

| Direction | Method / event | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| hub → manager, call | `extensions.accept {id}` → `{}` | the hub takes a web app request on the manager's behalf (`extwire.Routes`, extension API prefixes, extension pages in the admin UI): the manager dials `/api/v1/bus/relay` with this id and serves HTTP/1.1 on that stream (SSE and WebSocket stay streams): this request, then any later ones the hub sends on it while it stays open (keep-alive; the hub keeps a few idle per manager connection); who is asking is in each request's `X-Persona-*` headers |
| | `extensions.authorize {hash, pattern, method, path}` → `{ok, extension, name, scopes, scope?}` | an extension token hitting a hub route: whose it is and whether this route is open to it (empty `extension`: no such token) |
| | `extensions.hub_call {method, params}` → result | the hub's own features asking extensions: `settings.list`, `settings.tool` (node MCP tools, gate command wording and `assistant.lark` are asked directly inside the manager process and don't cross the bus); a change through `settings.tool` is a card the manager shows and waits for, so the hub waits for it as long as its own caller does (a read, like every other call, two minutes); when the caller stops waiting it sends `rpc.cancel` (the card is withdrawn with it, and the manager makes no change afterward) |
| hub → manager, event | `extensions.emit {event, params}` | things extensions subscribe to: `agent.finished`, `agent.needs_you` |
| manager → hub, event | `extensions.report {features, apis, machines, screen_keep_awake, looks, bot_identities?}` | the full set: extension features, API prefixes and receipts, each machine's `computer` / `browser`, and the avatars of enabled extensions with their files (`looks`; the hub serves them together with its own avatar packs); the hub keeps it (stored in `hub.extensions_report`). `bot_identities: [{kind, id}]` lists enabled Feishu app IDs and bound, enabled WeChat account IDs (`kind`: `feishu` / `wechat`), without secrets or tokens; used for the shared-bot warning in the managers roster |
| | `extensions.looks_gone {ids}` | an extension carrying avatars was uninstalled: the manager first sends a report without these avatars, then this; if the selected avatar is in `ids` and no other source provides it, the hub switches the selection back to the default avatar; if the saved choice cannot be read, the hub logs the error and leaves it unchanged |
| manager → hub, `app.call` (app `hub`) | `push.localized`, `push.mail_targets`, `extensions.token_revoked` | pushes (cards live in the assistant's interaction queue, in-process); `push.localized`'s `collapse_id`: a later push with the same id from the same manager replaces the earlier one; the push's collapse id is `ext:` and a hash of the manager and the id, so it never replaces another manager's push or the hub's own; `extensions.token_revoked` `{hash}`: an extension token the manager dropped, whose relayed connections the hub ends. Model configuration's `plugins.*` and `models.*` are inside the manager process and don't go through the hub |

### Methods channels use

The "talk to Persona" half of the Lark bot and plugin channels belongs to the assistant: the hub only sends and receives, hands the owner's messages and button presses to the assistant, and does whatever sending or editing the assistant asks for.
Types are in the channel section of `assistantwire`; the hub side is `hub/assistant_channels.go`, the assistant side `assistant/channels*.go`, `feishu*.go`.

- hub → assistant, calls: `channels.receive {channel, message, action}` → `{}` (one message from the owner on a plugin channel; `message` is a `channel.Message`), `feishu.message {event, action?, from?}` → `{}` (one message from the owner in the Lark DM or in a topic of a group on the list; the `event` of `im.message.receive_v1` as is; `from: "elsewhere"` marks the owner's `@bot /ai …` from a group that is not on the list; `from: "read"` the owner's `@bot /read …` from any group with the `read_group` switch on):
  the assistant dedups by message id and answers as soon as it has accepted, processing in the background (for Lark it first reads `feishu.status`; if that can't be read it returns `try_again` and doesn't accept); `feishu.card_action {event, action}` → the answer to the card callback (`{toast?, card?}`; Lark waits 3 seconds, the hub gives 2.5); `feishu.view {}` → `{target?, agents?}` (the assistant's two fields in `GET /api/v1/bots/feishu`).
  `action` is a one-time **owner action** issued by the hub (`oa_…`, valid for 10 minutes and only in the issuing channel; a card press can answer only that card; a message can answer only the card kinds that channel accepts as text: questions in Lark, questions / plans / permissions / terminal choices in plugin channels). The assistant must include it when answering a card (`interactions.resolve`).
  For owner messages, the hub first waits up to 60 seconds for the assistant to connect (at most 500 messages at a time), and hands them over again on a broken call, timeout or `try_again` (the assistant accepts each id only once). If it waits in vain, the hub replies to the owner itself: in Lark "Couldn't send: the assistant can't be reached right now, try again later", as a card toast "The assistant can't be reached right now, try again later", and on plugin channels via `channel.send` (`kind: note`) "Not sent: the assistant can't be reached right now, try again later" (only once per message).
- extension manager → assistant, call: `channels.unbound {channel}` → `{}` clears that channel's pending turns, text questions, and late-answer reminder synchronously. Connector sign-out and completed sign-in call it for every channel backed by that connector; cleanup errors prevent a success response. WeChat also calls it when saved credentials lose their bound account (including automatic unbinding). It does not resolve the underlying cards.
- hub → assistant, one-way events: `interaction.announced {interaction}` (a new card, except those of quiet tasks), `interaction.ended {interaction, resolution?}` (the card ended: answered ones carry the answer, withdrawn or expired ones don't; the same card arrives once with the answer and once without),
  `session.items {machine_id, session_id, items}`, `session.delta {machine_id, session_id, text}` (new entries and in-progress text of chats the assistant follows), `feishu.owner {paired, greeted?}` (bot paired / unpaired; `greeted`: the hub already greeted the owner),
  `channels.noted {channel, machine_id, session_id}` (a channel message entered a chat via the web app's endpoint: voice's `voice-…`).
- Assistant → hub, `device.call` (answered by the hub itself): `session.follow {session_id}` / `session.unfollow {session_id}` → `{}` (follow a chat: the hub watches it the way a web app opening it would, and forwards new entries and text; when the assistant disconnects the hub drops them all, and the assistant follows again after reconnecting),
  `session.send_once {session_id, text, client_msg_id, images?, …}` → `{}` (the node's `session.send` with the same send-once protection as the web app: what was sent isn't sent again, and one that broke halfway last time is refused). A clarification may carry an opaque one-time proof and card ID reserved for this path. The hub consumes a valid proof only after the once-only guard agrees to send, checks its exact manager, card, destination, text and `client_msg_id`, removes both reserved fields, and attaches its own clarification submission so devices writes `owner_input`; a manager cannot write that attestation itself. A missing proof sends the message unmarked, and an invalid proof fails before the node call without making delivery uncertain.
  `assistant.answer_again {session_id, text, client_msg_id, answer_again_after, …}` → `{}` uses the same send
  ledger. The hub passes the ID to the node as `once_id` so the transcript marks the prompt as Persona's input.
  The node checks the idle Assistant conversation and the last item ID under its send lock. A changed turn returns
  `assistant_answer_again_changed`. An older peer refuses the guarded method.
- Assistant → hub, `app.call`:
  - `feishu`: `feishu.status {}` → `{ready, enabled, features, owner?, paired_at?, public_url?, chats?, home_chat?}` (`owner` + `paired_at` identify which pairing: if they change or disappear, the assistant's chat state starts over); `feishu.post {reply_to?, card, fallback?, uuid?, chat_id?, in_thread?}` → `{message_id}` (a card replying to that message, otherwise sent into the owner's DM; a card Lark rejects is sent as rich text instead; `in_thread` makes a reply open or continue the parent's thread; `chat_id` names the chat to send into, and to fall back to when the parent was withdrawn: the hub refuses any chat but the owner's DM; `reply_to` is not checked against it),
    `feishu.text {reply_to?, text, chat_id?, in_thread?}` → `{message_id}` (same `chat_id` / `in_thread` rules), `feishu.update_card {message_id, card}`, `feishu.pin {message_id, exclusive?}` (pins one of the bot's own messages in the owner's DM; `exclusive` takes off the bot's other pins there, never the owner's), `feishu.recall {message_id}` (withdraws one of the bot's own messages in the owner's DM; both refuse any other message), `feishu.react {message_id, emoji}` → `{reaction_id}`, `feishu.unreact {message_id, reaction_id}`,
    `feishu.messages {message_id}` → `{items}` (quoted, merged-forwarded), `feishu.resource {message_id, key, kind, machine_id, as_file?}` → `{data, mime}` (images up to 3 MiB), `{path, mime, name}` (larger images or `as_file`, saved on the selected computer from the same download), or `{too_large: true, name}` (above 50 MiB; accompanying text still goes through). Download failures remain errors; saving downloaded image bytes fails with `feishu_save`, so the assistant keeps its file-save failure message. No large image bytes cross the bus,
    `feishu.save {message_id, key, kind, name, machine_id}` → `{path}` (the file is saved to that computer's temp directory, up to 50 MB; content doesn't cross the bus), `feishu.user_name {open_id}` → `{name}`,
    `feishu.configure {enabled?, features?: {id: on}}`, `feishu.test {}`. When the bot isn't on, isn't connected or isn't paired (`ready` is false), sending and editing methods return the error "the bot isn't on or isn't paired yet"; messages go only to the paired owner.
  - `channels`: `channels.list {}` → `{channels: [channel.View]}` (each channel's transport state; without the target and plugin-channel features, which the assistant fills in), `channels.send {channel, ref, text, kind, reply_to?}` → `{message_id?}` (one segment; on failure retry with the same `ref`; with nowhere to send yet it returns error code `cannot_send`),
    `channels.typing {channel, on}`, `channels.enable {channel, on}` (the switch for a plugin and its connector, or the Lark bot; returns `needs_triage_model` when the Inbox triage model isn't configured), `channels.unbind {channel}`. Binding isn't here: `POST /api/v1/channels/{id}/bind` is the hub's own route (credentials don't pass through the assistant).
  - `interactions`: `interactions.resolve {interaction_id, resolution, action, channel}` → `{ok, status?}` (answers this card with the user's reply in `channel`; `action` is that reply's owner action. Missing, used, wrong-card or wrong-channel actions, and message replies to card kinds the channel does not accept, are rejected. Recorded as answered by the user; if it is no longer waiting, `ok` is false).
- The snapshot gains `channels: {marks:[{machine_id, session_id, channels}], turns:[{machine_id, session_id, answered?}]}`: the hub fills sessions' `channels` from `marks` (pushing that machine's session list on change),
  and from `turns` (empty `answered` means it's following now, otherwise it's the time answering finished, within the hour) it doesn't push "done" for that chat's turn; on `null` (unreadable; the snapshot counts as incomplete) it keeps the previous one.
- The assistant's routes gain `/api/v1/channels*`, except binding `POST …/bind`.
- The assistant's event queue: `session.delta` keeps only one entry per chat (new text replaces old); when the queue is full only `session.delta` and `session.items` are dropped; others wait for room and are never dropped.

### The service side (`server/internal/bus`)

`Dial`, `Conn` (the adapter between WebSocket and rpc lines), `Keepalive`, and `Client`: dial, handshake (`HelloMethod`, `HelloParams`, `OnHello`), answer the hub's calls and events, and reconnect when dropped:
starting at 1 second and doubling up to 1 minute; if a connection lasted over 1 minute before dropping, counting restarts at 1 second. When the token is rejected (401, close code 4002 / 4003, handshake returns `wrong_identity`), it waits the full 1 minute every time.

- **A wait ends early when the hub comes back**. A laptop that slept failed a try at each dark wake, so its wait is usually at the full minute when it wakes. A wait longer than 3 seconds therefore asks the hub's `GET /api/v1/health` every 2 seconds, giving each request up after 2 seconds. Only a 2xx whose body says `"ok": true` counts as the hub answering.
  - The probe uses the client's own HTTP client, or the default one as the bus dial does, so it goes the bus's own way to the hub: pinned to its key, through a proxy, over an SSH local forward. Something that accepts connections for a hub it cannot reach does not pass for the hub: a forward whose tunnel stalled gives no answer in time, and a proxy whose upstream is gone answers 502.
  - If the hub did not answer when the wait began and answers now, the client tries again at once.
  - If the hub answered when the wait began, the try failed past its health (a reset during the handshake, a bus that refuses for now), and that wait runs to its end. A hub whose health answers but whose bus does not is still tried only as often as the backoff allows, and it gets one probe per wait.
  - A rejected token's wait is never cut short.

While not connected (or the handshake isn't done), `Call` and `Notify` return `ErrOffline`.
The assistant uses `assistant.BusHub` (`server/internal/assistant/bus.go`), a wrapper around it: it keeps the handshake answer, maps the hub's error codes back, handles the hub's events in order, and reports a full snapshot on every connect.

## hook / mcp ↔ node (unix socket `~/.persona/node.sock`)

The client side (socket path, dialing, request / reply types, resuming) is `server/internal/nodeclient`. `personad hook`, `personad mcp` (`internal/mcpserver`), `personad ask` / `personad notify` (`internal/scriptcli`) and `personad tool` (`internal/toolcli`) use only it and the contract packages, never `internal/node`; a guard test (`nodeclient_test.go`) keeps the node, the manager and the hub out of their dependencies, so the device's own program can carry these commands. The node writes the commands into the settings it manages as `<its own binary> hook` (`hook --persona-global` in the user's own settings) and `<its own binary> mcp`, so whichever binary runs the node serves them.

One question and one final answer per connection, one line of JSON each. The sole exception is an MCP call that explicitly opts into wait updates: zero or more one-line `wait_kind` updates may precede its one final answer.

- `{"kind":"hook","input":<the stdin JSON Claude Code passes to the hook>,"pane":"…","attempt":"<the hook process's own id>","resume":<whether this is a reconnect>}`
  → `{"output":<JSON to print to stdout, or null>}`, or `{"retry":true}` (the node is exiting; ask the next node)
- `{"kind":"mcp.tools","input":{"revision":"…","session":"…"},"pane":"…"}` → `{"tools":[…],"revision":"…","session":"…"}` or `{"unchanged":true,"revision":"…","session":"…"}`. `input` is optional. The node resolves caller identity on every request and forwards the revision only if the previously resolved session still matches; a cursor never supplies identity. Old nodes omit the revision. `personad mcp` advertises `tools.listChanged`, long-polls after its first successful list, and sends `notifications/tools/list_changed` only when definitions change. Its 45-second request deadline and 1–30 second retry backoff cover disconnects without replacing the last list with an empty one.
- `{"kind":"mcp.call","name":"…","args":{},"session_id":"…"}` → `{"content":[…],"is_error":false}`
- A `personad mcp` call with a progress token adds `"wait_updates":true`. A new node whose authenticated hub currently announces `mcp_wait_v1` generates an opaque `call_id`, forwards both fields on its manager `mcp.call`, and may write `{"wait_kind":"unknown|approval|answer|computer"}` lines before the same final `ToolResult`. The local interim line contains no other field. Without the opt-in or current hub feature there are no interim lines; an old MCP client therefore never has to parse them. An old hub, manager or upstream node likewise produces no updates, which the MCP client presents as `Still waiting`. A different case is a new upstream path delegating `computer.call` to an old target node: the manager deliberately publishes `unknown` for that RPC, then restores the preceding state. The node removes the call before its synchronized final write, so a late `mcp.wait` cannot produce a line after that answer.
- `{"kind":"cli.call","name":"…","args":{},"pane":"…","codex_thread_id":"…"}` → the same tool result, with `error_kind` (`personad tool`, `internal/toolcli`). The node, not the caller, says whose call it is (`node/clicall.go`): an Agent's own tool (`callerTools`: `task_spawn`, `assistantwire.AgentToolNames`, dispatch, a task leader's `task_plan` / `task_review`) goes to the manager's `mcp.call` as the Agent the Codex thread names, else the pane's, with `assistant: false`, as `mcp.call` resolves it; any other tool, and an Agent tool that names no known session, only from a process the node runs for the assistant (or its descendant) and only for its signed-in connectors' tools. `session_id` and `assistant` in the request are never read.
- `{"kind":"ask","input":{"question","options?","timeout_seconds?","cwd?"},"pane":"…","attempt":"…","resume":…}`
  → `{"status":"answered|denied|dismissed|timeout|unavailable|invalid","answer?","error?"}`, or `{"retry":true}` (`personad ask`; with options it gives a `question` card, without options a `permission` card)
- `{"kind":"notify","input":{"title","body?","silent?","error?"},"pane":"…"}` → `{"sent":true|false,"reason?","error?"}` (`personad notify`)
- `{"kind":"hook.display","input":<a MessageDisplay hook's stdin JSON>}` → `{"ok":true}`, answered before the node does anything with it: Claude Code shows the lines only once the hook is done. `personad hook` sends it for a MessageDisplay input (only the Agents' live replies plugin has that event, loaded while `node.configure` `claude_live_replies` is not false), waits at most 150 ms and prints nothing; an older node answers `{"error":"unknown kind"}` and standby `{"away":true}`, and the lines are simply not streamed.
- `{"kind":"claude-plugin.status"}` → `{"protocol":1,"sessions":[{"session_id","pid","plugin_version","engine_version","polling","seen_at"}]}`: the live sessions whose Persona plugin for Claude Code polls this node (Persona Link's installer, diagnostics). An older node answers `{"error":"unknown kind"}`.
- An HTTP/1.1 request line instead of JSON (`POST /claude-plugin/v1/poll`, `/ack`) is Persona's Claude Code plugin: one request per connection, answered only for the claude process at the socket's other end that has the named session open (`integrations/claude-code-plugin/README.md`). A node in standby, or an older node, gives it no HTTP answer, and the plugin backs off.
- `{"kind":"preflight","locale":"<optional language>"}` → the `path-access` check of `personad node doctor` as `{name, status, state, detail, hint, items}`: the node reads what a claude start reads with its own permissions. Omitting `locale` keeps the original zh-Hans check; an explicit supported locale words its human fields for the terminal. An older node ignores the additive field, one without preflight answers `{"error":"unknown kind"}`, and standby answers `{"away":true}`; the doctor then checks in its own process and says which of these it was. The doctor waits 23 s for the answer, longer than the node's longest run. The hidden child's separate C-locale tab-separated protocol is unchanged.

When the node can't be reached (hub not online), the hook exits 0 immediately with no output, so the TUI handles it normally; mcp returns an error text.

### Interactions survive restarts

Deploys are frequent (hub restarts, node binary swaps). Questions / plans / permissions being answered in the web app survive them instead of falling back to the computer's TUI:

- **hook**: if the node goes away after the hook has connected but before it gets an answer (connection dropped or `retry` returned), it reconnects to `node.sock` every second and resends with the same `attempt`,
  for up to 2 minutes (`nodeclient.ResumeWait`). If it can't reach the node at the very start, it still hands over to the TUI immediately.
- **node**: the interaction id is deterministic: a hash of `session_id + event + tool name + tool_use_id` (without a tool_use_id, the hook's attempt is used),
  so a reconnecting hook gets the same id. Interactions with an attempt are marked `resumable: true`, and the reconnecting one doesn't send `hook.event` again. For AskUserQuestion, the attempt also retains PreToolUse's exact `tool_use_id`; a replacement Node recovers an unambiguous pairing and any terminal tool_result from the recent transcript, while ambiguous identical calls are handed back to the terminal as one generation and their restored cards are withdrawn until their tool_results arrive, rather than guessed.
- **hub**: `resumable` interactions aren't withdrawn when the node connection drops; they're kept for 3 minutes (`resumeGrace`) for the hook to reclaim. An `interaction.create` with the same id
  reattaches to the original card (no repeat push; the web app dedups by id), and if it was answered in the web app in the meantime, the returning hook gets the answer straight from the database. At startup, pending `resumable` interactions in the database
  are reloaded (also waiting 3 minutes), and the rest are marked cancelled. Old nodes don't send `resumable`; behavior is unchanged.
  The assistant's `ask_user` raised with `wait: false` is `resumable` too: no hook waits on it, the manager's own record of the question claims the card back after a restart ("Asking without holding the turn"). A waiting `ask_user` that lets go of its turn becomes `resumable` while it is up: the hub is sent the same card again with the flag set, and its history row is marked.

### When the manager is away (resident nodes)

A resident node (`personad node --attach`: Persona Link, the Mac's launchd node, a service node) outlives its manager connection.
